Despite	being	transported	by	fourteen	years-of-age,	Mary	had	at	least	one	 previous	conviction.	Her	first	appearance	in	the	courts	was	in	September	1831,	 when	she	was	just	nine-years-old.	The	case	was	acquitted	as	having	‘no	bill’.	 However,	she	was	again	brought	before	the	court	in	April	1834	under	another	 charge	of	Larceny	and	this	time	she	was	given	a	one-week	prison	sentence.		 
Through	exploring	Mary’s	Description	List,	we	find	she	was	fourteen	years-of-age	when	transported.	This	matches	her	birth	record	which	states	she	was	 born	 in	 late	October	 1822.	 Therefore,	Mary	was	 convicted	 aged	 twelve	 and	 reached	VDL	by	fourteen	years-of-age.		 
Mary	was	sentenced	to	seven	years’	transportation	for	stealing	a	watch	to	 the	value	of	one	pound	from	a	widow	named	Ann	Moore.	 In	 fact,	Mary	had	 broken	into	her	prosecutor’s	house	while	she	was	asleep,	waking	her	up	in	the	 process.	This	gave	 rise	 to	an	alarm	and	the	presence	of	police.	According	 to	 John	Fitzgerald,	the	police	constable,	Mary	stated	it	was	the	first	time	she	had	 ever	stolen.	Yet,	she	was	indicted	twice	in	the	same	session	which	includes	a	 guilty	plea	for	stealing	a	shawl	worth	one	pound	from	Elizabeth	Naylor.	It	is	very	 possible	that	it	was	because	of	these	two	successive	prosecutions	against	Mary	 that	she	gained	an	actual	transportation	voyage	to	Australia.	Especially	coupled	 with	the	fact	that,	despite	being	classified	as	Simple	Larceny	in	the	Old	Bailey	 Online,	 she	did	 in	 fact	break	 into	a	Dwelling	House	at	night.	Breaking	 into	a	 house	at	night	was	seen	as	a	particularly	serious	crime	because	it	was	thought	 that	the	owners	would	be	put	in	fear.	The	fact	that	Mary	committed	the	offence	 alone	is	not	uncommon	for	females.		 
Just	 one	 of	 the	 165	 convicts	 transported	 on	 the	New	Grove	 in	October	 1834,	Mary	arrived	at	VDL	in	March	1835.	The	Conduct	Record	holds	a	wealth	 of	 information	 about	 offenders.	 While	 confirming	 Mary’s	 two	 Old	 Bailey	 convictions,	the	record	also	reveals	further	information	about	Mary’s	contact	 with	the	criminal	justice	system.	Namely,	that	she	was	in	Newgate	prison,	and	 that	she	also	spent	time	in	a	refuge	and/or	at	Mrs.	Fry’s	school.	Elizabeth	Fry	
 
established	 The	 House	 of	 Discipline	 and	 School	 of	 Reform	 for	 Girls	 in	 1825	 which	 later	 became	 known	 as	 the	 School	 of	 Discipline	 and	 took	 in	 girls	 for	 reformation.	Mary’s	record	states	that	she	spent	time	in	‘Mrs.	Fry’s	school’	but	 it	is	also	mentions	she	spent	time	in	a	refuge.	It	is	unclear	whether	the	refuge	 being	referred	to	was	Mrs.	Fry’s	school	or	another	institution	Mary	spent	time	 in.	When	the	ship	surgeon	superintendent	refers	to	her	character,	he	stated	 she	was	‘indifferent	but	young	and	thoughtless	disposition’	but	he	also	added	 that	she	was	not	‘bad’.	Indeed,	Mary’s	behaviour	while	under	supervision	in	the	 new	 colony	 reflects	 this.	 Mary	 committed	 a	 series	 of	 non-serious	 offences	 resulting	in	several	visits	to	the	female	factory	for	hard	labour.	Most	offences	 were	absenteeism.	It	was	also	noted	that	‘through	extreme	carelessness	[Mary]	 let	 her	master’s	 baby	 fall	 to	 the	 ground	 by	 which	 its	 leg	 was	 broken’.	 This	 comment	 implies	that	there	was	nothing	malicious	 in	the	 incident:	 it	was	an	 accident.		 
Eventually	Mary	received	her	Free	Certificate	in	1841,	a	timely	seven	years	 after	her	sentence	expired.	If	a	settled	life	can	be	measured	by	such	outcomes	 as	marriage	or	steady	employment	–	Mary	did	settle.	Approved	for	marriage	in	 May	1839	(before	freedom),	she	married	a	free	man	named	George	Clarke	and	 they	went	on	to	have	nine	children.	They	migrated	to	Wallaroo,	South	Australia.	 George	died	 in	 1875	at	 Kadina,	 South	Australia	 but	Mary	 lived	 for	 a	 further	 nineteen	years.	Mary	remarried	a	Christopher	Charlton	who	survived	her	(he	 died	in	1903).		 
Mary	died	at	the	old	age	of	sixty-seven	in	January	1894	and	was	buried	at	 the	Wallaroo	Cemetery	in	South	Australia.	 
	 Mary	is	only	one	individual	and	we	are	not	privy	to	–	as	with	many	studies	of	 
historical	lives	–	her	internal	decision	making.	Yet,	we	can	still	assess	collective	life-
events	and	paths.	It	is	not	possible	to	ascertain	if	Mary	was	happy	in	marriage,	but	 
we	do	know	she	stayed	with	her	husband	until	his	death	and	formed	a	large	family.	 
Despite	her	arduous	start	to	colonial	life,	Mary	built	a	new	life	free	from	crime;	but	 
was	Mary’s	life	typical	of	these	juveniles?	By	placing	juvenile	convicts	like	Mary	in	 
their	colonial	context	and	comparing	and	contrasting	their	life-events,	this	thesis	 
aims	to	explore	the	lives	of	female	and	male	juvenile	convicts	transported	to	VDL	 
collectively.	 
	 By	using	the	method	outlined	in	Chapter	Three,	it	is	possible	to	uncover	the	lives	of	 
historical	actors	which	have	been	overlooked.	Over	the	last	four	decades	the	 
historiography	has	moved	on	from	focusing	narrowly	on	juvenile	crime	within	the	
 
early	Victorian	narrative	of	reform,	to	knowing	who	juvenile	offenders	were.	This	is	 
exemplified	in	the	significant	work	of	Heather	Shore	(1999).	By	exploring	individual	 
lives,	and	contextualising	their	experiences,	it	is	possible	to	go	beyond	the	 
circumstances	of	offending	through	to	their	punishment	period,	and	their	lives	upon	 
release;	to	allow	a	fuller	understanding	of	what	factors	inhibited	or	supported	 
‘settled’	lives.	The	following	themes	were	assessed	including:	crime;	punishment;	 
education,	training	and	occupation;	family	Life;	and	death.	 
	 In	order	to	address	questions	of	recidivism	and	desistance,	the	juvenile	convicts	will	 
be	contextualised	within	the	criminal	justice	system	of	VDL	(using	the	Official	 
Statistical	Returns),	and	compared	with	the	whole	convict	population	arriving	in	VDL	 
in	Chapter	Four.	This	two-step	comparison	process	will	allow	us	to	answer	the	 
question:	Did	juveniles	transported	commit	a	greater	number	of	offences	and/or	 
more	serious	offences,	than	the	average	convict	under	sentence	in	VDL?	If	so,	why	 
and	how	did	this	effect	their	lives?	 
	 The	punishments	endured	by	the	juvenile	convicts	will	be	investigated	to	further	 
understand	their	experience	under	servitude	to	ascertain	if	this	related	to	their	life-
outcomes	in	Chapter	Five.	From	hard	labour	and	flogging,	to	confinement	in	the	 
cells	and	extended	sentences	-	what	did	these	juvenile	convicts	experience?	Did	 
these	experiences	differ	from	other	convicts,	and	if	so,	why,	and	how	did	this	affect	 
them?	 
	 In	order	to	address	the	employment	and	occupations	of	this	group,	the	changing	 
economy	and	their	prior	education,	training	and	employment	will	be	taken	into	 
account	in	Chapter	Six.	This	will	be	done	by	turning	to	the	Official	Statistical	Returns	 
–	taking	particular	notice	of	the	state	of	the	economy,	the	average	wage	rates,	and	 
changing	populations	(referring	to	migration	and	transportation).	As	far	as	 
education	is	concerned,	particular	notice	will	be	paid	to	pre-transportation	literacy	 
rates,	the	education	and	training	in	the	colony	(for	example,	the	education	and	 
training	some	male	juveniles	received	at	Point	Puer),	and	any	subsequent	evidence	 
of	employment	(for	example,	as	displayed	on	their	children’s	birth	records	or	 
newspaper	reports).	They	will	also	be	compared	to	other	convicts	arriving	in	VDL.	
 
Allowing	the	following	questions	to	be	approached;	were	the	juvenile	convicts	 
(dis)advantaged	in	the	labour	market	of	their	new	colony,	were	they	able	to	gain	 
employment,	and	what	was	that	employment?	 
	 From	the	behaviour	of	the	juvenile	convicts	themselves,	to	the	decisions	of	the	 
administrators	and	the	conditions	of	the	penal	colony	into	which	they	were	thrust;	 
were	these	female	and	male	juvenile	convicts	able	to	form	‘settled’	familial	lives	and	 
which	factors	inhibited	or	facilitated	this	process?	This	will	be	explored	in	Chapter	 
Seven.	To	gain	a	rounded	understanding	of	their	whole	lives	it	is	important	to	assess	 
if	they	married	or	formed	relationships.	This	includes	looking	at	factors	such	as:	 
their	age	and	whether	they	were	free	when	married;	were	their	marriage-partners	 
convicts,	emancipists	or	free	settlers;	and	the	age	and	occupations	of	their	marriage	 
partners.	As	van	Schellen	put	it	‘it	is	not	only	relevant	to	study	if	criminal	convicts	 
marry	but	also	whom	they	marry’	(2012,	547).	In	doing	so	it	will	be	possible	to	 
approach	the	question;	did	the	juvenile	convicts	go	on	to	have	‘settled’	family	lives,	 
and	which	factors	influenced	this?	 
	 Chapter	Eight	explores	the	end	of	the	juvenile	convicts	lives.	Was	juvenile	convict	 
mortality	affected	by	being	transported	as	convicts	to	VDL?	This	question	will	be	 
addressed	by	comparing	the	mortality	rate	of	this	sample	with	the	rates	for	the	 
whole	population,	including	convicts.	Did	the	juveniles	in	the	sample	die	younger	 
than	the	average	population	living	in	VDL?	Also	to	be	considered	are	causes	of	 
death;	were	they	victims	of	disease	or	were	they	dying	in	old	age.	Was	there	a	 
correlation	between	repeated	punishment	and	early	death,	for	instance?	These	 
questions	will	be	answered	by	turning	to	the	Official	Statistical	Returns	with	regards	 
to	the	whole	population,	other	convict	samples,	and	by	turning	to	the	death	 
certificates	and	newspaper	reports	of	the	group	sampled.	These	contributing	factors	 
will	be	taken	into	account	to	answer	the	following	question;	did	the	juvenile	 
convicts	live	‘long’	lives?	And,	whether	or	not	they	did,	which	factors	influenced	 
this?	 
	
 
Finally,	the	Conclusion	will	bring	all	findings	and	compartmentalized	stages	of	these	 
young	offenders	lives,	and	how	they	interacted,	together.	In	doing	so	we	will	 
understand	whether	these	juveniles	were	able	to	have	‘settled’	colonial	lives	and	 
which	factors	affected	their	life-outcomes.			 
	 This	thesis	will	contribute	to	research	centred	on	juvenile	offenders,	from	the	 
crimes	they	committed	to	the	punishments	they	endured	and	the	institutions	they	 
experienced.	It	will	also	contribute	to	Australian	social	history	centred	on	VDL,	the	 
history	of	transportation,	and	the	convict	lives	caught	up	in	this	criminal	justice	 
measure.	Due	to	this	thesis’	concentration	on	the	juvenile	convicts’	experience	and	 
life-outcomes,	it	will	also	contribute	to	the	literature	on	forced	migration	and	 
juvenile	migration	generally.	The	use	of	the	method	of	life-course	analysis	and	the	 
use	of	individual	life-narratives	mean	this	thesis	will	add	to	the	continuing	process	 
of	uncovering	the	history	of	non-elite	lives.	 
	 
	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	
 
Chapter 2: Historiography  
	 While	our	views	and	understanding	of	crime	and	criminals	have	changed	over	time,	 
it	has	been	a	national	issue	within	the	press	and	parliamentary	reports	since	the	 
nineteenth	century	(Macilwee	2011,	11).	Of	course,	the	way	in	which	society	viewed	 
criminality	did	not	necessarily	reflect	reality.	Yet,	understanding	these	 
contemporary	societal	views	is	vital	because	such	changes	and	continuities	in	 
attitudes	inevitably	influenced	how	offenders	were	dealt	with	(Emsley	2010,	291).	 
This	is	as	true	for	adults	as	it	was	for	juveniles,	and	it	fed	into	ideas	about	juvenile	 
delinquency.	Important	to	the	understanding	of	the	concept	of	the	‘juvenile	 
delinquent’	was	the	changing	views	of	childhood,	the	position	of	the	urban	working	 
class	child,	and	the	emergence	of	the	juvenile	justice	system.	Such	aspects	will	be	 
explored	before	turning	to	the	practice	of	transportation	and	the	changing	 
management	of	convicts,	which	will	be	important	in	understanding	the	experiences	 
of	the	juveniles	studied	in	this	thesis.	 
	 
The	Dark	Figure	 
The	existence	of	a	dark-figure	of	crime	has	long	been	acknowledged	(Phillips	1977;	 
Emsley	2014;	Godfrey	2007).	Simply	defined,	crime	is	the	behaviour	which	violates	 
the	criminal	law,	which	if	detected	would	lead	to	prosecution	(Emsley	2014,	2).	As	 
such,	official	crime	is	produced	by	a	process	of	interaction	between	those	who	 
make	and	enforce	the	laws,	and	those	who	break	them	(Phillips	1977,	45).	Whether	 
a	crime	is	prosecuted	depends	on	the	attitudes	of	authorities	and	the	public	(Phillips	 
1977,	42).	Although	historians	have	taken	up	the	idea	of	social	construction	to	 
differing	extents,	early	revisionist’s	extreme	views	have	been	largely	dismissed.	 
While	stimulating	debate	into	criminal	research,	such	ideas	were	also	constricting.	 
Foucault	(1975),	Ignatieff	(1978),	and	Garland	(1985)	all	pointed	to	the	deep	 
structures	of	power	(Wiener	1990,	7).	These	revisionists	took	the	upward	 
movement	of	the	Whiggish	internalists	and	pragmatists	and	turned	it	into	‘an	 
onward	march	of	surveillance	and	control’	(Wiener	1990,	8).	The	humanitarian	 
reform	argument	of	the	Whigs,	and	the	revisionist’s	argument	of	social	control,	are	 
too	simplistic.	Both	the	complexity	and	variety	of	human	motives,	as	well	as	the	
 
discourse	of	power	relations	need	to	be	combined	to	begin	to	understand	the	 
history	of	crime	and	offenders	(Wiener	1990,	8).		 
	 
The	Criminal	Class	 
Much	misunderstandings	of	crime	have	resulted	from	national	histories	which	have	 
in	the	past	uncritically	relied	on	unreliable	statistics	and	contemporary	commentary	 
(Tobias	1967;	Chesney	1970).	However,	regional	investigation	has	allowed	for	a	 
more	nuanced	understanding	of	criminals	and	crime	(Phillips	1977;	Conley	1999).	 
Until	the	1970s	the	history	of	crime	in	Britain	was	told	as	one	of	reform	and	 
modernisation	(Wiener	1990,	1).	To	understand	crime	and	criminals	we	need	to	 
take	into	account	the	values,	interests	and	context	of	society,	and	avoid	a	 
positivistic	approach.	Essentially,	crime	is	not	an	‘objective	fact	which	constitutes	a	 
problem’	(Wiener	1990,	4-6).	Whig	historian,	Tobias,	took	nineteenth-century	 
contemporary	views	of	offenders	and	presented	them	as	the	‘criminal	class’.	 
Presenting	them	as	a	separate	group	who	could	be	‘distinguished	by	their	clothing	 
and	habits	and	lived	wholly	or	largely	on	the	proceeds	of	crime’	(1967,	14).	 
Historians	have	since	dismissed	the	idea	that	his	assertions	‘maybe	regarded	as	an	 
acceptable	explanation	of	the	phenomena	of	the	time’	(Tobias	1967,	70;	Phillips	 
1977,	16-17).	Even	Tobias	himself	noted:	‘…	when	dealing	with	this	material	we	are	 
faced	with	an	acute	form	of	a	general	problem	of	historical	research.	Even	if	 
contemporise	are	agreed	on	something,	we	cannot	be	sure	that	they	were	right’	 
(1967,	13).	Importantly,	if	crime	is	viewed	as	inevitable	in	the	‘criminal	class’,	crime	 
and	its	perpetrators	can	never	be	understood.		 
	 
Some	historians	(for	example	Tobias	1967	and	Chesney	1970)	uncritically	used	 
Victorian	and	Edwardian	commentators	who	did	not	differentiate	between	the	 
labouring	poor	and	the	criminal	class.	For	example,	Chesney	excluded	upper-class	 
criminal	embezzlers,	whilst	including	the	lower-classes	who	merely	went	against	 
Victorian	morality	-	such	as	prostitutes.	Whereas,	Duckworth	(2002)	asserted	there	 
were	‘emphatic	differences	within	the	lower	classes’.	Arguing	that	the	respectable	 
poor	would	have	nothing	to	do	with	the	perishing	and	dangerous	classes	 
(Duckworth	2002,	213).	As	Shore	(2015,	2)	points	out,	the	under-	and	upperworld	
 
overlapped.	Moreover;	‘criminal	organisation	is	characterised	by	the	same	 
relationships	of	exchange	and	reciprocity	that	structure	everyday	society’	(Shore	 
2015,	15).	Therefore,	to	suggest	that	there	was	a	degraded	criminal	group	who	 
were	avoided	by	the	other	poor	is	unrealistic.	Many	working-class	poor	lived	in	 
housing	among	those	who	relied	on	theft	to	live.	There	were	those	in	full-time	work	 
who	stole,	just	as	there	were	those	occasional	workers	who	did	not	(Godfrey	2014,	 
9).	Phillip’s	(1977),	for	example,	found	that	only	ten	per	cent	of	crimes	committed	in	 
the	Black	Country	were	committed	by	‘professional	criminals’.	Most	had	normal	 
jobs,	stealing	only	to	supplement	income	or	due	to	opportunity	(Conley	1991,	137).	 
As	Emsley	stated,	both	statistics	and	court	records	suggest	that	the	overwhelming	 
majority	of	theft	was	opportunistic	and	petty.	Rather	than	being	major,	planned	and	 
carried	out	by	professional	criminals	(2010,	181).	Although	historians	have	 
dismissed	the	idea	of	a	professional	criminal	class	(Gatrell	1980;	Conley	1991),	 
Phillips	(1977,	198;	287)	stated	that,	for	London	at	least,	a	criminal	class	may	have	 
existed	because	such	a	large	and	rich	city	could	have	supported	‘a	large	professional	 
criminal	class’.	It	may	be	true	that	no	other	town	could	have	individually	 
approached	the	number	of	offences	committed	in	London	(Thomas	1998,	3),	but	as	 
George	Rude	concluded:	‘even	in	London	for	all	its	reputation	as	a	centre	of	 
professional	crime	and	dangerous	deviants,	the	case	for	the	existence	of	a	definable	 
criminal	class	has	not	been	made’	(cited	in	Conley	1991,	137).		 
	 
Conley	argued	that	the	idea	of	a	criminal	class	was	really	bound	up	in	the	idea	of	 
respectability,	where	respectability	was	a	‘social	category	posing	as	a	moral	 
category’	–	meaning	that	the	middle	classes	were	born	respectable	while	the	poor	 
had	to	earn	it	(Conley	1991,	4).	Indeed,	the	notion	of	a	criminal	class	was	a	 
convenient	way	of	shifting	the	blame	of	criminal	actions	onto	an	alien	group	 
(Emsley	2010,	181).	Notwithstanding	some	individuals	which	did	live	off	criminal	 
earnings,	the	term	‘criminal	class’	implies	a	large	homogenous	group,	which	did	not	 
exist	(Emsley	2010,	88).	Historians	have	now	further	debated	the	existence	of	the	 
criminal	class	(Phillips	1977;	Conley	1991;	Shore	1999;	Godfrey	et	al	2007;	Emsley	 
2014).	While	they	have	found	that	most	defendants	were	not	professional	criminals,	 
judicial	authorities	and	the	general	public	believed	criminals	to	be	a	threatening	
 
breed-apart	(Conley	1991,	136-137).	In	many	ways	the	actual	existence	of	a	criminal	 
class	is	unimportant.	It	was	a	popular	belief	in	its	existence	that	fuelled	debate	 
(Godfrey	et	al	2007,	73).	Therefore,	nineteenth-century	attitudes	towards,	and	 
ideas	about,	crime	and	criminals	is	important	but	should	be	used	critically	and	 
cautiously	(Phillips	1977,	18).	 
	 
The	Historiography	of	Childhood	 
Along	with	nineteenth-century	concern	that	the	criminal	class	were	marching	 
against	societal	mores,	was	a	special	concern	with	juveniles	and	their	delinquency	 
(Shore	1999,	1).	In	order	to	understand	the	centrality	of	the	juvenile	delinquent	in	 
the	nineteenth	century,	we	must	consider	the	changing	ideas	of	childhood.	As	 
Pinchbeck	and	Hewitt	highlighted,	a	‘remarkable	feature’	of	our	time	is	the	 
considerable	social	and	statutory	concern	centred	on	children’s	welfare	(1969,	1).	 
By	the	twentieth	century	childhood	was	recognised	as	a	universal	condition	 
(Munchie	2009,	50),	and	historians	have	shown	a	burgeoning	interest	in	childhood	 
but	they	have	been	rarely	in	agreement.	The	1970s	saw	a	consensus	where	the	 
history	of	childhood	was	viewed	as	one	of	progress.	Yet,	just	a	decade	later,	with	all	 
historical	genres	moving	away	from	modernisation	theory,	the	accepted	orthodoxy	 
became	continuity	(Cunningham	2005,	4).	Although	this	historiography	begun	with	 
an	overarching	history	of	sentimentilization	by	those	including	Aries	(1962),	Mause	 
(1974),	Shorter	(1976)	and	Stone	(1977);	the	work	of	Pollock	(1983),	Wrightson	 
(1982)	and	Macfarlane	(1986)	have	produced	more	nuanced	histories	(Cunningham	 
2005,	3-16).	This	new	historiography	moved	towards	the	role	of	political	and	social	 
structures,	particularly	that	of	demographic	philanthropy	and	the	state.	 
	 
Partly	owing	to	Middle-Age	languages	not	distinguishing	juveniles	from	adults,	Aries	 
radically	proposed	that	prior	to	the	seventeenth	century	there	was	no	conception	of	 
childhood	(Munchie	2009,	48).	This	construction	argument	was	based	on	the	idea	 
that	many	nineteenth-century	juveniles	would	have	been	little	affected	by	concepts	 
of	childhood	(Munchie	2009,	50).	Pollock,	on	the	other	hand,	had	already	pointed	 
out	that	there	was	no	evidence	of	parental	indifference	predominating	at	any	time.	 
Instead,	she	argued	that	parents	had	always	held	an	emotional	attachment	to	their	
 
children	and,	therefore,	some	conception	of	childhood	must	have	always	existed	 
(Munchie	2009,	48).	Moreover,	Pinchbeck	and	Hewitt	demonstrated	that	children	 
were	considered	in	the	paternalistic	legislation	from	as	early	as	the	sixteenth	 
century	(1969,	1).	Notwithstanding	differing	ideas	of	harshness	from	today,	early-
modern	children	and	their	proper	place	in	society	was	a	national	concern	 
(Pinchbeck	&	Hewitt	1969,	2).	However,	Pinchbeck	and	Hewitt	also	found	a	 
‘conspicuous	lack	of	concern	for	the	welfare	of	children’	in	the	eighteenth	and	early-
nineteenth	century.	Until	a	‘pubic	re-awakening’	of	the	importance	of	child	welfare	 
in	the	late	nineteenth-century,	they	suggested	that	‘childhood	was	but	a	brief	 
introduction	to	the	heavy	responsibilities	of	the	adult	world’	(1969,	1;	299).	 
Stemming	from	the	reformers	reactions	to	the	changing	context	of	social	and	family	 
life,	in	a	country	with	increasing	population	and	urbanisation,	both	poverty	and	 
delinquency	were	re-problematised	(Pinchbeck	&	Hewitt	1969,	2).	Similarly,	 
Cunningham	(2005,	2),	while	allowing	for	differences	in	social	class,	country	and	 
gender,	argued	that	the	patterns	of	childhood	experiences	eventually	encompassed	 
all.	Indeed,	childhood	cannot	be	studied	in	isolation	from	societal,	economic,	 
demographic	and	political	changes.	For	example,	economic	development	allowed	 
the	shift	from	employment	to	education	in	childhood,	forming	the	idea	that	 
childhood	should	be	a	time	of	dependency.	Leading	children	and	childhood	to	 
become	increasingly	separate	from	adults	and	adulthood	(Cunningham	2005,	3).	 
Certainly,	the	idea	that	society	were	‘wasteful	and	heedless’	with	its	children	was	 
replaced	by	Pinchbeck	and	Hewitt’s	continuity	stance.	Yet,	this	does	not	mean	that	 
the	nineteenth	century	did	not	undergo	significant	alterations	(1969,	1).	Along	with,	 
and	largely	due	to,	conflict	over	the	history	of	childhood,	came	similar	 
disagreements	over	the	historical	origins	of	the	concept	of	the	‘juvenile	delinquent’	 
(Shore	2011,	4).	 
	 
Juvenile	Delinquency	 
[Juvenile]	 Delinquents	were	 differentiated	 not	 only	 by	 their	 offence,	 but	 by	 their	life-styles,	by	their	impatience	of	restraint,	their	dislike	of	discipline	and	 aversion	to	settled	employment	(May	1981,	106).	 
	
 
During	the	1970s	and	1980s	there	was	an	‘academic	renaissance’	in	terms	of	 
understanding	the	concept	of	juvenile	delinquency	(Shore	2011,	1).	This	new	 
orthodoxy	challenged	previous	historiographical	assumptions	that	juvenile	justice	 
developed	as	a	humanitarian	response	to	a	real	and	dramatic	increase	in	juvenile	 
offending	(Munchie	2009,	62).	Following	the	new	history	from	below	wave,	 
marginal	juvenile	offenders	were	brought	to	the	forefront	of	historical	analysis	 
(Shore	2011,	4).	However,	despite	the	term	juvenile	delinquency	being	coined	in	 
1776,	revisionist	histories	largely	placed	its	origins	as	a	creation	of	the	late-
eighteenth	to	nineteenth	century	due	to	processes	of	industrialisation,	urbanisation	 
and	criminalisation	(Munchie	2009,	62).	These	revisions	came	with	numerous	 
explanations	of	the	discovery	or	invention	of	the	concept,	along	with	various	 
chronologies.	 
	 
While	being	subsequently	challenged,	the	key	works	from	Magarey	(1978)	and	May	 
(1981),	and	later	Springhall	(1986)	and	Bailey	(1987),	introduced	the	idea	of	the	 
Victorian	invention	of	delinquency,	which	they	argued	led	to	the	Victorian	and	 
Edwardian	development	of	the	juvenile	justice	system	(Shore	2011,	2).	Magarey	 
explored	the	interplay	between	changes	in	some	juvenile	behaviour	and	changes	in	 
the	criminal	law	and	its	enforcement	in	Britain,	between	1820	and	the	1850s	(1978,	 
12).	Magarey	demonstrated	that	there	was	some	justification	for	increasing	 
nineteenth-century	fears	by	pointing	to	prison	statistics.	The	number	of	offenders	 
under	seventeen	years-of-age	imprisoned	increased	from	9	500,	in	1838,	to	14	000,	 
in	1848.	This	was	not	attributed	to	increased	lawlessness	but	instead	to	the	 
criminalisation	of	juvenile	behaviour:	behaviour	which	previously	warranted	no	 
official	response	(Munchie	2009,	54).	This	argument	was	supported	by	pointing	to	 
contemporaries,	for	example	William	Crawford	and	Whitworth	Russell	(who	were	 
newly	appointed	inspectors	of	prisons	for	the	Home	District	in	1836),	who	ascribed	 
the	‘striking	increase’	of	juvenile	male	committals	to	‘other	causes	than	the	positive	 
advance	of	crime’.	Concluding;	‘the	position	of	children	in	relation	to	the	criminal	 
law,	and	the	criminalisation	of	behaviour	for	which	an	earlier	age	would,	at	worst,	 
have	tipped	a	boy	into	a	horse	trough’	(cited	in	Magarey	1978,	17).	Magarey	argued	 
this	was	initiated	by	the	presumption	of	doli	incapax	for	those	under	fourteen	
 
falling	into	disuse,	and	the	1820s	Acts	(including:	Vagrancy	Act	1824,	Malicious	 
Trespass	Act	1827,	and	Metropolitan	Police	Act	1829),	which	she	believed	were	 
partly	designed	to	control	delinquent	juveniles.	Together,	by	broadening	legal	 
definitions	of	criminal	activity	the	apprehension	of	all	‘loose,	idle	and	disorderly	 
persons	not	giving	good	account	of	themselves’	was	enabled,	and	street	children	 
became	increasingly	liable	for	arrest	(Munchie	2009,	54).	Thus,	Magarey	argued	 
that	juvenile	delinquency	was	legislated	into	existence	due	to	a	decreasing	 
willingness	to	overlook	juvenile	crime,	and	declining	acquittal	verdicts	(Munchie	 
2009,	54;	Shore	2003,	110).		 
	 
Another	pioneer	in	the	field,	Margaret	May,	described	the	ideology	and	legislative	 
forces	which	clarified	the	conceptual	idea	of	the	juvenile	offender	as	taking	place	 
between	the	1830s-40s	(Shore	2002,	82).	May	pointed	out	that	juvenile	delinquents	 
were	identified	by	a	process	which	distinguished	them	from	both	other	children	and	 
adults,	this	was	partly	a	function	of	the	investigators’	approach	and	the	reliance	on	 
area	and	behavioural	studies.	In	surveying	the	‘moral	topography’	of	cities,	the	 
juveniles	under	question	became	associated	with	the	‘deteriorating	and	squalid	 
neighbourhoods’	they	lived	in,	which	resulted	in	the	transfer	of	the	characteristics	 
of	the	area	to	the	juveniles	in	question	(1981,	98).	May’s	seminal	thesis	explored	 
the	social	process	underlying	the	identification	of	juvenile	delinquency,	the	 
pressures	leading	to	policy	innovation	and	the	implementation	of	a	new	treatment	 
philosophy	in	the	form	of	the	reformatory	and	industrial	School	movement.	May	 
argues	that	‘consciousness	of	delinquency	stemmed	from	a	disruption	of	traditional	 
social	controls	consequent	on	industrialisation’.	It	also	reflected	new	sensitivities	to	 
childhood	and	the	demands	of	the	casual	child	labour	market	(May	1981).	May	 
(1981,	74)	achieved	this	by	specifically	looking	at	the	subjective	factors,	tracing	the	 
growth	and	changing	focus	of	investigations,	and	the	analytical	process	which	 
isolated	delinquency	as	a	specific	social	problem.	May	critically	outlined	the	 
relationship	between	the	changes	to	the	criminal	justice	system,	the	new	police	 
establishment	and	changing	attitudes	to	juvenile	criminal	responsibility.	In	doing	so,	 
she	concluded	that	Platt	(1969)	had	over	stated	his	argument.	Platt	argued	that	 
current	delinquency	controlling	programmes	could	be	traced	to	enterprising	‘child	
 
savers’,	who	in	the	late-nineteenth	century	helped	create	special	judicial	and	 
correctional	institutions	for	the	labelling	and	management	of	troublesome	juveniles.	 
Platt	concluded	that	these	reformers	brought	attention	to,	and	in	doing	so	invented,	 
new	categories	of	misbehaviour	(Platt	1969,	3).	This,	May	argued,	was	overstating	 
the	reformers	role	in	a	complex	process	of	change.	More	empirically	detailed	 
explanations	of	the	apparent	growth	in	juvenile	crime	soon	entered	the	debate	 
(Shore	2011,	9).	 
	 
Empirically	rooted	research	soon	developed,	which	allowed	for	a	more	meaningful	 
measure	of	the	growth	of	nineteenth-century	juvenile	delinquency.	King	(1998)	 
provided	detailed	statistical	analysis	of	juvenile	offenders	at	selected	courts	 
throughout	Britain,	including	the	Old	Bailey.	In	doing	so,	he	found	that	the	rise	in	 
juvenile	prosecutions	pre-dated	the	Victorian	‘invention’	of	delinquency	by	two	 
decades.1	King’s	(1998)	findings	point	to	the	issue	of	urban	growth	as	central	to	the	 
increasing	willingness	to	prosecute	juvenile	offenders.	Stressing	the	complexity	of	 
the	situation,	he	highlighted	the	shifting	cultural,	social	and	political	landscape.	 
Concluding	that	the	existence	of	a	growing	number	of	vulnerable,	poor	and	urban	 
juveniles,	and	of	a	general	increase	in	post-war	anxieties	about	rising	crime	rates,	 
resulted	in	the	conditions	for	an	increase	in	juvenile	prosecutions	in	the	1810s	 
(Shore	2011,	10).		 
	 
Rush	(1992,	6),	utilising	social	construction,	also	argued	that	juveniles	emerged	as	a	 
distinct	problem	in	the	nineteenth	century.	Conceding	that	both	social	control	and	 
the	term	juvenile	delinquency	both	existed	before	the	nineteenth-century,	he	 
nevertheless	asserted	that	the	concept	emerged	with	the	increased	administration	 
of	juveniles.	Rush	argued	that	reformers	invented	the	problem	of	juvenile	 
delinquency	in	answer	to	urbanisation	and	industrialisation,	which	brought	new	 
societal	needs	and	problems	(Rush	1992,	6;	12).	He	further	demonstrated	the	 
progress	of	this	‘social	imperative’	by	highlighting	the	increasing	significance	of	the	 
juveniles	age	in	trial	and	punishment.	The	extension	of	summary	jurisdiction	 
																																																						 1	This	work	was	based	on	property	offenders	aged	<17	years’	old	
 
brought	a	corresponding	emphasis	on	the	sentence	and	mode	of	punishment.	Due	 
to	concern	over	the	risks	of	juvenile	contamination	through	association	with	 
hardened	adult	criminals,	swift	justice	was	implemented	under	the	1821	Bill;2	this	 
allowed	juveniles	to	be	processed	quickly	under	summary	powers.	This	resulted	in	 
the	age	of	the	offender	taking	on	a	new	significance	but	it	had	no	‘practical	 
relevance	to	the	guilt	and	responsibility	of	the	offender’.	Still,	as	the	mode	of	 
punishment	was	gradually	distinguished	from	the	trial,	the	chronological	age	of	the	 
offender	become	important	at	the	stage	of	sentencing	and	punishment	(Rush	1992,	 
16).	Similarly,	Shore	highlighted	that	juvenile	offenders	were	increasingly	viewed	 
separately	in	the	nineteenth	century	through	stressing	the	importance	of	the	‘large	 
scale	criminalisation	of	children’	(1999,	29).	This	is	not	to	dismiss	other	factors,	 
including	the	changing	form	of	the	household	in	the	early-modern	period	(Shore	 
1999,	149).	Specifically,	the	repeal	of	the	Statute	of	Artificers	(1814)	and	the	decline	 
in	apprenticeships	which	predated	this	(Shore	1999,	18).	It	also	includes	the	 
influence	of	the	long	war-time	period	which	provided	the	government	with	 
experience	of	penal	detention	through	prison-of-war	camps	(Shore	1999,	23).	 
Essentially,	with	the	changing	definitions	of	criminality	and	legal	demarcations,	 
juveniles	who	would	previously	have	been	informally	dealt	with,	were	undergoing	a	 
more	formal	and	punitive	process	(Shore	1999,	149).	This	is	evidenced	by	an	 
increased	tendency	to	use	custodial	punishment	for	juveniles	after	the	cessation	of	 
war	in	1815	(Shore	1999,	23).	However,	it	was	relatively	early	on	in	which	prison	 
professionals	questioned	the	counter-productive	effects	of	incarcerating	children.	 
During	the	1820s	to	1840s	philanthropists	repeatedly	commented	on	the	beneficial	 
effects	of	separate	juvenile	provision	on	crime	rates	and	the	economy	(Shore	1999,	 
100).	A	decreasing	willingness	to	overlook	juvenile	crime	was	combined	with	 
decreasing	acquittal	verdicts	and	the	growth	of	secondary	punishments.	This	 
suggests	‘…that	to	some	extent	the	problem	of	juveniles	was	exacerbated,	though	 
not	created,	by	the	policy-makers	of	the	time’	(Shore	1999,	150).		 
	 
																																																						 2	1821	Bill	for	The	Punishment,	Correction	and	Reform	of	Young	Persons	Charged	with	Privately	 Stealing	from	Houses,	or	the	Person	in	Certain	Cases		
 
The	edited	collective	essays	of	Cox	and	Shore	(2003)	further	challenge	the	invention	 
of	the	nineteenth-century	juvenile	delinquent	through	exploring	different	European	 
cultures.	Significantly,	they	locate	the	continuities	between	the	early-modern	and	 
modern	periods	in	terms	of	perceptions	and	treatment	of	delinquent	juveniles.	 
These	essays	suggest	an	articulated	construction	of	the	delinquent	as	the	youth	 
who	threatened	society,	giving	rise	to	practices	and	institutions	that	catered	 
especially	for	juvenile	offenders	(Ben-amos	2005,	144).	The	idea	of	the	invention	of	 
juvenile	delinquency,	as	Griffiths	suggests,	is	problematically	tied	to	modernisation	 
theory.	Indeed,	Griffiths	demonstrates	that	confinement	of	the	young;	concerns	 
over	rough	youths	in	domestic	service	and	apprenticeships;	forms	of	policing	 
disorderly	youth	and	attempts	at	reformation;	all	preceded	the	nineteenth	century	 
(Shore	2011,	12).	Age	specific	offenses,	penalties	and	policing	measures	were	 
prevalent	in	the	houses	of	correction,	in	transportation,	and	in	the	discourse	of	 
youth	reformation	long	before	the	‘semantic	twist’	of	juvenile	delinquency	 
(Munchie	2009,	64).	By	turning	to	linguistic	reconfigurations,	however,	Griffiths	 
demonstrates	that	sharp	nineteenth-century	shifts	were	partly	introduced	by	the	 
regulatory	language	of	juvenile	delinquency	into	the	penal	lexicon	(Shore	2011,	12).	 
He	argued	that	changing	vocabulary	promoted	a	separate	discourse	and	 
engendered	this	judicial	separation.	Adding	that,	the	emergence	of	new	 
terminologies	are	key	to	understanding	both	continuities	and	discontinuities.	Thus,	 
it	is	likely	that	powerful	class-based	dichotomies	increasingly	shaped	how	juvenile	 
offenders	were	managed.	Consequently,	the	difference	between	hardened	and	 
corrupt	working	class	children	and	the	innocent	middle-class	children	fed	into	penal	 
language.	These	discourses	increasingly	focused	upon	the	‘hardened’,	‘incorrigible’,	 
‘dangerous’,	juvenile	offender,	and	persistent	juvenile	offenders	became	an	 
‘emblem	for	social	breakdown	and	domestic	instability’	(Shore	2003,	114).	 
Therefore,	while	it	is	true	that,	until	well	into	the	nineteenth	century,	there	was	no	 
formal	differentiations	according	to	age	with	regards	to	trial	and	punishment,	it	 
would	be	inaccurate	to	argue	that	the	construction	of	juvenile	delinquency	took	 
place	at	that	time	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1986,	133;	Shore	2003,	120).	Nevertheless,	 
the	combination	of	juvenile-specific	legislation	and	institutions	in	the	early-
nineteenth	century	continues	to	signify	the	nineteenth	century	as	important	in	the	
 
definition	and	management	of	disorder.	‘Juvenile	delinquency’	may	not	have	been	 
invented	but	it	underwent	a	‘dramatic	reconfiguration’	at	this	time	(Munchie	2009,	 
64).	 
	 
The	correlation	between	the	emergence	of	a	separate	juvenile	justice	system	and	 
the	increasingly	visible	categorisation	of	juvenile	offenders	in	the	nineteenth	 
century	has	been	repeatedly	highlighted	(Shore	1999,	17;	Shore	2003,	116;	King	 
1998;	Rush	1992).	Also	pointed	to	has	been	its	slow	progress,	and	significant	 
continuities	from	the	early-modern	period	(Shore	2003,	113).	Additionally,	Shore	 
points	to	the	consequences	of	the	shift	to	the	separate	treatment	of	juvenile	 
offenders.	Specifically,	as	soon	as	juveniles	were	considered	separately	they	were	 
the	first	to	be	viewed	as	having	some	hope	of	redemption	and	reformation	(1999,	 
131).	However,	the	separation	of	juveniles	from	adults	was	‘double-edged’.	They	 
were	categorised	and	consequently	problematised	in	their	own	right	(Shore	1999,	 
135).	Notwithstanding	early-modern	continuations,	the	systems	of	juvenile	justice	 
which	developed	in	the	twentieth	century	were	rooted	in	this	separate	 
categorisation	of	juvenile	criminals,	which	evolved	in	the	early-nineteenth	century	 
(Shore	1999,	148;	Shore	2003,	110).	(See	Chapter	Six	for	further	information	on	the	 
separate	treatment	of	juvenile	offenders	within	the	justice	system).	 
	 
As	we	have	seen,	much	of	this	increased	nineteenth-century	focus	on	criminality	 
was	directed	at	juvenile	offenders.	This	was	partly	fuelled	by	the	belief	that	these	 
delinquents	could	be	saved	and	reincorporated	back	into	respectful	society	before	 
they	were	lost	as	hardened	criminals	(Shore	1999,	1).	Yet,	as	Shore	points	out,	this	 
paradigm	of	explanation	is	not	neat	(1999,	14).	There	were	various	explanations	of	 
causation	from	societal	explanations	centred	on	parents	and	popular	 
entertainments,	to	the	underworld	of	crime	and	the	justice	system	itself	(Shore	 
1999,	34).	Juvenile	delinquents	were	even	subject	to	their	own	classification	system;	 
the	‘perishing	class’	and	‘dangerous	class’.	The	perishing	class	were	merely	in	 
danger	of	falling	into	crime,	while	the	dangerous	were	actual	offenders	 
(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1986,	167).	This	perception	of	crime	was	driven	by	the	 
prevailing	stereotypes.	Consequently,	when	the	ideas	of	the	criminal	class	reached	
 
its	height,	poverty	stricken	juveniles	were	seen	as	being	‘cradled	in	iniquity’	(Shore	 
1999,	35).	Contemporaries	also	thought	that	other	children,	specifically	older	 
juvenile	gangs,	were	bad	examples;	including	the	swell-mob	who	they	believed	 
‘epitomised	the	rewards	of	the	life	of	crime’	(Shore	1999,	45).	Contemporary	 
commentators	believed	there	were	numerous	child	thief-managers,	who	both	 
trained	juveniles	and	fenced	their	goods	(Duckworth	2002,	29).	While	pickpocketing	 
was	seen	as	a	progressive	step	into	the	criminal	career	(leading	it	to	be	a	capital	 
offence	until	1808),	in	reality	the	average	juvenile	offender	did	not	resemble	these	 
professional	groups	(Shore	1999,	55-59).	Nevertheless,	contemporary	fears	of	 
juvenile	offenders	maturing	into	adult	burglars	was	embedded	in	many	arguments	 
for	penal	reform	and	‘colonial	retraining’	(Shore	1999,	61),	and	much	of	this	debate	 
centred	on	the	city	of	London.	 
	 London	 
Moving	into	the	nineteenth	century,	increasingly	crime	was	seen	as	something	 
inherent,	and	external	factors	took	on	less	importance.	Then,	during	the	1820s	and	 
1830s,	juvenile	crime	was	linked	to	the	much	narrower	explanation	of	the	criminal	 
class,	as	already	discussed	(Shore	1999,	19).	Importantly,	this	increased	 
contemporary	focus	on	juvenile	criminals,	Shore	argues,	could	have	subsided	if	it	 
had	not	been	for	its	coincidence	with	metropolitan	life	pressures,	along	with	 
institutional	creations	for	the	poor	and	criminals	(1999,	23).	As	the	early-nineteenth	 
century	progressed,	it	was	no	longer	only	the	dark	alleys	which	held	danger	for	 
potential	robberies,	but	also	the	‘crowded	thoroughfares	of	the	developing	 
metropolis’	(Shore	2015,	70).	There	was	an	acceleration	in	the	industrialisation	 
process	that	had	begun	in	the	previous	century.	A	falling	death	rate	also	ensured	a	 
steady	population	growth	and	internal	migrants	moved	into	towns	and	cities	from	 
all	over	the	UK,	and	in	particular	they	moved	to	London.	Britain’s	population	 
doubled	between	1801	and	1851,	from	approximately	nine	to	eighteen	million	 
(Gray	2010,	56).	It	is	clear	from	the	social	commentary	circulating	in	the	second	 
decade	of	the	nineteenth	century	that	there	was	a	widespread	belief	in	the	rise	of	 
crime.	Contemporaries,	in	London	especially,	were	increasingly	concerned	about	 
the	perceived	increase	in	population,	and	the	‘rising	tide	of	iniquity	and	poverty’	
 
(Shore	1999,	19).	The	awareness	of	increasing	juvenile	committals,	which	 
‘dramatically	and	unexpectedly’	emerged	during	the	inquiry	into	metropolitan	 
policing	of	1811-1816,	also	first	centred	on	London	(May	1981,	76).	Consequently,	 
working-class	London	youths	were	seen	as	being	particularly	problematic,	and	this	is	 
the	group	this	thesis	will	focus	on.	But	what	of	the	management	of	those	taken	 
from	London	and	transported	to	Australia?	 
	 
	The	Practice	of	Punishment	&	Transportation	 
	 
The	Historiography	of	Australian	Convict	Transportation	 
Academics,	including	Clark	(1956),	Shaw	(1966)	and	Robson	(1971),	pioneered	 
major	professional	research	into	Australian	history.	They	used	new	data	and	 
techniques,	and	in	doing	so	overturned	Wood’s	(1922)	argument	that	transported	 
convicts	were	victims	of	British	colonial	cruelty.	Like	Wood,	Shaw	(1966)	used	a	 
traditional	qualitative	methodology	but	he	utilised	the	results	of	other	researchers	 
including	Clark	(1956),	and	later	Robson	(1971),	for	support.	These	two	researchers	 
had	innovatively	employed	what	were	then	neglected	sources,	the	Conduct	 
Records,	in	a	quantitative	manner.	Payne	(1961)	also	utilised	similar	methods	but	he	 
presented,	through	a	study	of	Tasmanian	female	convicts,	a	picture	which	tallied	 
with	Wood’s.	Yet,	it	was	the	works	of	Clark,	Robson	and	Shaw,	due	to	their	 
comprehensive	nature,	which	have	underpinned	the	subsequent	interpretation	of	 
Australian	history.	As	Oxley	explains,	Clark	(1956)	did	employ	empirical	 
methodology	but	he	was	heavily	influenced	by	‘subjective	assessments	formulated	 
by	impressionistic	readings	of	qualitative	sources’	(Oxley	1996,	5).	Robson	(1971),	 
on	the	other	hand,	was	rigorously	quantitative	and	systematic.	He	studied	7000	 
convicts	sent	to	the	eastern	colonies.	Nevertheless,	he	presented	descriptive	 
statistics	located	within	a	qualitative	framework.	Fundamentally,	the	notion	of	a	 
criminal	class	determined	his	statistical	analysis.	Accordingly,	criminal	offences	were	 
concentrated	on,	and	trades	and	skills	were	largely	ignored.	Nicholas	and	Shergold	 
(1988,	5)	argued	that,	when	statistical	results	and	their	hypothesis	did	not	correlate	 
they	were	overlooked.	For	example,	although	Clark	found	that	convict	literacy	levels	 
were	surprisingly	high,	he	characterised	convicts	as	having	‘low	cunning	and	
 
ignorance’	(Nicholas	&	Shergold	1988,	5).	Consequently,	these	publications	resulted	 
in	a	picture	of	male	convicts	as	professional	criminals,	with	female	convicts	as	 
professional	prostitutes	(Oxley	1996,	5).	 
	 
By	looking	closer	at	the	experience	of	special	categories	of	convicts	and	their	 
contributions	to	the	colony,	historians	have	presented	a	more	nuanced	picture	 
(Smith	2008,	10).	For	example,	Convict	Workers:	Reinterpreting	Australia’s	Past	 
involved	economic	historians	who	asked	new	questions	about	the	early	economic	 
and	social	development	of	NSW.	Using	empirical	and	comparative	methodologies,	 
they	explored	‘human	capital’	and	demonstrated	the	beneficial	effect	of	the	 
convicts,	and	the	convict	system,	on	the	colony.	By	assessing	the	occupational	skills,	 
education	and	physical	fitness	they	overturned	the	pervading	convict	stereotype	 
(Nicholas	1988).	In	this	vain,	this	thesis	will	explore	the	whole	lives	of	juvenile	 
convicts,	not	simply	their	crimes	and	punishments.	First,	both	individual	and	group	 
experiences	cannot	be	understood	without	knowledge	of	the	history	of	 
transportation	as	a	whole.		 
	 
The	Practice	of	Transportation	 
When	the	punishment	of	transportation	to	Australia	began	in	the	late	eighteenth-
century,	it	was	not	a	new	concept.	Transportation	had	been	increasingly	prescribed	 
since	seventeenth-century,	and	exiling	as	a	punishment	had	existed	for	centuries.	 
The	punishment	of	banishment	though	exile	was	combined	with	the	idea	that	the	 
offender	could	also	repay	the	common	good	through	colonisation.	As	early	as	1607,	 
criminals	were	transportation	to	the	Virginian	plantations	(Shaw	1966,	22-23).	 
Undeniably	this	punishment	was	makeshift	and	informal.	It	was	not	until	the	 
Habeas	Corpus	Act	(1679)	that	transportation	without	trial	was	prevented.	Later,	 
the	1655	Act	allowed	the	practice	of	mitigating	criminals	awaiting	execution	with	 
transportation,	and	transportation	became	increasingly	systematic.	The	 
Transportation	Act	(1718)	outlined	that	the	purpose	of	transportation	was	to	deter	 
criminals	and	supply	the	colonies	with	labour.	Because	of	the	need	for	servants	at	 
the	American	plantations,	all	clergiable	offences	were	commuted	to	seven	years’	 
transportation.	By	the	eighteenth	century,	transportation	became	‘a	major	
 
ingredient	of	English	criminal	law’	(Shaw	1966,	24-25).	This	left	Britain	in	a	 
predicament	when	the	American	colonies	revolted	and	they	would	no	longer	accept	 
Britain’s	convicts.	While	awaiting	a	decision	on	a	new	penal	colony,	 
decommissioned	war	ships	were	used	to	house	prisoners,	which	were	known	as	 
prison	hulks.	Parliament	authorized	the	use	of	these	hulks	for	two	years:	they	lasted	 
eight-two	(Shaw	1966,	42-43).		 
	 
Eventually	Botany	Bay	in	Sydney	(NSW)	was	chosen	to	be	the	new	penal	colony	 
(Shaw	1966,	43).	Accordingly,	the	first	fleet	departed	there	in	1787.	By	1868,	132	 
308	men	and	24	960	women	were	transported	to	the	Australian	colonies	from	 
Britain	and	Ireland	(Quinlan	2014,	220).	The	majority	were	sent	to	NSW	and	VDL.	 
Others	were	sent	to	Moreton	Bay	(Brisbane),	Queensland,	Norfolk	Island,	and	after	 
1850,	Western	Australia	(WA).	There	were	also	a	negligible	number	of	‘offenders’	 
exiled	to	Victoria	(Brooke	&	Brandon	2005,	221).	Transportation	ended	to	NSW	in	 
1841,	to	Tasmania	in	1853,	and	to	WA	in	1868	(Smith	2008,	35).	This	thesis	will	 
focus	on	VDL.	 
	 
In	1642,	some	128	years	before	Captain	James	Cook	visited	Australia,	an	island	was	 
named	by	explorer	Abel	Tasman.	He	called	the	island	Van	Diemen’s	Land	(VDL)	after	 
the	governor	of	Batavia	in	the	Dutch	East	Indies.	This	small	Island	was	about	160	 
miles	long	by	eighty	miles	wide	(Fleming	2012,	33).	It	received	73	000	convicts	over	 
fifty	years	beginning	in	1803.	It	only	became	a	separate	colony	from	NSW	in	1825	 
(Brooke	&	Brandon	2005,	221).	VDL	become	self-governing	in	1856,	when	it	gained	 
its	own	fully	elected	legislature,	which	was	after	transportation	had	ended	(Fleming	 
2012,	48).	 
	 
The	British	government	advocated	transportation	because	it	was	seen	as	a	cheap,	 
deterrent	punishment.	While	the	American	colonies	were	substituted	for	the	 
Australian	colonies,	the	economic	reasons	for	transportation	remained	the	same	as	 
stated	in	the	first	Transportation	Act	(1717),	which	was	labour	supply	(Meredith	 
1988,	14).	Practically	speaking,	those	who	it	failed	to	deter	would	be	removed	from	 
the	country,	and	would	be	unlikely	to	return.	It	was	also	initially	believed	that	
 
removal	from	criminal	connections,	in	a	new	environment,	with	‘ready’	 
employment	would	result	in	convict	reformation	(Shaw	1966,	17).		 
	 
The	practice	of	punishment	 
How	convicts	were	disciplined	in	the	colony	changed	over	time.	This	was	partly	 
because	it	was	believed	that	the	once	primitive	colony	of	the	late-eighteenth	 
century	had	become	ordered	and	civilised	by	the	mid-nineteenth	century.	 
Accordingly,	transportation	became	increasingly	seen	as	not	severe	enough.	This	 
was	largely	fuelled	by	the	perception	of	rising	crime	rates	in	Britain,	and	so	it	 
followed	in	the	minds	of	contemporaries	that	transportation	was	not	acting	as	a	 
sufficient	deterrent.	The	Governors	were	ordered	to	increase	the	severity	of	the	 
punishment	by	the	mother	country	(Shaw	1966,	17).	Consequently,	the	supposed	 
lottery	of	the	assignment	system	was	replaced	by	the	probation	system,	which	was	 
quickly	realised	to	be	a	failure.	The	experience	of	transportation	for	individual	 
convicts	would	have	varied	due	to	age,	sex,	behaviour	and	skill,	which	resulted	in	 
differing	punishments	and/or	rewards,	but	also	due	to	these	large	shifts	in	the	 
management	of	convicts	generally.	This	chapter	will	explore	these	changing	 
circumstances	in	order	to	contextualise	the	analysis	of	the	following	chapters.	 
	 
Assignment	 
When	a	convict	arrived	in	the	formative	days	of	the	colony	they	would	usually	be	 
assigned	to	a	free	colonist	for	the	purpose	of	carrying	out	labour	(Shaw	1966,	211).	 
Assignment	dated	back	to	the	first	settlers	but	it	was	formally	established	by	 
Governor	King	in	1804	(assignment	was	only	made	legal	under	the	Transportation	 
Act	of	1824).	Convict	assignment	was	handled	by	the	assignment	board	which	 
comprised	of	three	persons,	including	a	Chief	Police	Magistrate	and	the	Principle	 
Superintendent	of	Convicts	(Brand	1990,	5).	 
From	the	perspective	of	convicts,	the	benefits	of	the	assignment	system	 
were	the	increased	freedoms	it	offered.	Predicated	on	good	behaviour	and	 
provided	the	Lt.	Governor	gave	approval,	it	was	also	possible	to	earn	a	ticket-of-
leave	(ToL).	A	ToL	allowed	convicts	to	work	for	an	employer	for	wages	or	hold	a	 
government	post,	and	own	property	(Brand	1990,	6).	However,	ToL	regulations	
 
were	tightened	by	1823	and	prisoners	had	to	serve	a	fixed	period	before	they	were	 
eligible	to	earn	one.	Then	the	1832	Act	forbade	early	tickets	altogether,	which	had	 
been	locally	granted	in	special	circumstances	(for	example,	for	capturing	 
bushrangers).	On	top	of	this,	legal	protection	was	taken	away	from	ToL	holders	 
with	regards	to	their	property	(Shaw	1966,	229-231).	Nevertheless,	tickets	were	still	 
sought	after.	While	their	Certificate	of	Freedom	was	given	at	the	end	of	their	 
sentence	(introduced	in	1810),	a	revocable,	Conditional	or	Absolute,	Pardon	could	 
also	be	granted	by	the	crown	through	Governor	recommendation	(Brand	1990	6;	 
Brooke	&	Brandon	2005,	80).	 
The	merits	of	assignment	for	the	governor	of	VDL,	free	settlers	and	the	 
British	government	were	largely	financial	(Shaw	1966,	211).	Even	so,	assignment	 
did	not	come	without	criticism	even	early	on;	as	in	Bigge’s	1825	report	which	 
suggested	the	continuation	of	assignment	but	recommended	the	dispersal	of	 
convicts	into	the	countryside	to	avoid	the	‘evils’	of	association.	Convicts	would	also	 
no	longer	be	granted	land	upon	freedom.	These	changes,	it	was	hoped,	would	 
result	in	a	perceived	increase	of	severity	(Brooke	&	Brandon	2005,	245-246).	 
Moreover,	with	the	continuation	of	assignment,	employers	would	continue	to	be	 
responsible	for	the	food,	clothing,	medical	care	and	accommodation	of	their	 
assigned	servants.	As	such,	the	government	would	only	pay	administration	costs,	 
and	for	those	in	public	gangs,	gaols	and	penal	settlements.	Simultaneously,	 
colonists	benefited	from	a	low	cost	labour	force	which	required	no	wages.	 
Moreover,	it	was	at	least	initially	believed	that	assignment	encouraged	convicts	to	 
reform	through	rewarding	good	conduct	(Brand	1990,	6).		 
	 
Despite	restrictions	to	ensure	well	behaved	masters,	assignment	was	increasingly	 
seen	as	a	lottery.	Excepting	special	approval,	inn-keepers,	ex-convicts,	relatives,	 
those	without	free	overseers	and	those	who	broke	the	rules	were	not	allowed	 
assigned	convicts	(Shaw	1966,	219).	However,	while	one	convict	might	get	a	 
tolerant	and	lenient	master	who	indulged	his	servant	with	tea,	sugar	and	tobacco,	 
another	might	be	overworked	and	abused	(Brand	1990,	6).	Assignments	could	be	 
revoked	upon	complaint	but	many	unsuitable	masters	remained	and	their	actions	 
went	unnoticed	(Shaw	1966,	219).	A	master	could	not	punish	his	own	servant,	they	
 
had	to	take	their	complaints	to	the	magistrate.	However,	although	magistrates	 
were	arbitrators,	Shaw	argues	that	they	had	an	interest	in	the	subordination	of	 
convicts	because	they	had	their	own	assigned	servants	(1966,	224).	Simultaneously	 
some	magistrates,	like	other	masters,	indulged	their	servants	(Shaw	1966,	219-
220).	Material	rewards	including	extra	rations,	tobacco,	sugar	and	extra	wages	 
(even	after	government	opposition	to	the	practice	in	1823)	were	given	to	some	 
convicts	(Meredith	1988,	15).	These	inconsistencies	in	the	punishment	led	to	 
doubts	about	the	systems	reformatory	capabilities,	as	did	the	connotations	of	slave	 
labour	(Brand	1990,	6).		 
	 
Towards	the	New	Probation	System	 
Lieutenant	Governor	Arthur,	like	many	colonists,	thought	the	assignment	system	 
was	a	good	punishment.	However,	many	back	home	and	in	Australia	disagreed.	 
While	its	detractors	thought	it	a	lottery,	those	who	defended	the	system	argued	it	 
was	a	severe,	economical	and	reformatory	punishment	(Shaw	1966,	216).	However,	 
the	British	government	was	convinced	that	more	severe	discipline	was	needed	as	a	 
deterrent	to	increasing	crime	rates	at	home	(Shaw	1966,	250).	The	Select	 
Committee	(1837),	known	as	the	Molesworth	Committee,	criticised	the	lack	of	 
distinction	made	between	the	sentence,	age,	character	or	nature	of	offence,	in	the	 
treatment	of	convicts.	Finding	instead	that	their	fate	was	determined	by	their	skill	 
(Meredith	1988,	15).	The	committee	concluded	that	transportation	was	an	 
‘ineffective	instrument	of	reform’.	Not	only	did	it	recommend	the	abolition	of	 
assignment,	it	also	recommended	the	establishment	of	penitentiaries	at	home	and	 
abroad.	Yet,	until	these	prisons	were	built,	transportation	would	continue	under	an	 
altered	system	(Brand	1990,	11),	which	they	demanded	should	be	less	vague	and	 
arbitrary	(Shaw	1966,	298).	 
	 
In	1837	the	British	government	finally	stopped	assignment	(Shaw	1966,	268).	In	 
future	all	convicts	would	work	in	gangs	for	a	fixed	period	upon	arrival,	and	 
subsequently	obtain	private	employment	for	wages.	Under	the	Comptroller	of	 
Convicts,	the	probation	gang	would	be	put	to	hard	labour	of	differing	degrees	of	 
severity	according	to	conduct.	Good	behaviour	would	allow	convicts	to	progress	to	
 
the	next	stage,	in	which	they	could	earn	a	probation	pass	enabling	them	to	work	for	 
wages.	If	a	convict	lost	their	pass	through	bad	behaviour,	all	wages	earned	were	 
forfeited	to	the	Queen.	If	the	pass	holder	was	unemployed	they	could	resort	to	the	 
public	works	but	would	only	receive	food	and	clothing	in	exchange	for	labour.	The	 
penultimate	stage	was	the	ToL,	which	was	only	valid	in	the	colony	it	was	granted.	 
Only	when	they	earned	their	ToL	could	unpaid	wages	be	accessed,	and	it	could	only	 
be	earned	after	completion	of	half	of	their	sentence	(Brand	1990,	19-20).	The	final	 
stage	was	a	pardon,	conditional	or	absolute	(Shaw	1966;	272-4).	In	this	way	the	 
probation	system	was	introduced,	as	an	experiment,	in	1839.		 
	 
The	end	of	transportation	to	NSW	led	to	VDL	receiving	more	convicts	than	 
anticipated.	This,	along	with	the	abandonment	of	assignment,	meant	the	probation	 
gangs	were	bigger	than	intended	(Shaw	1966,	275-277).	This	increased	costs	and	 
many	of	the	overseers	and	superintendents	were	unqualified	due	to	low	salaries	 
(Brand	1990,	16).	Stanley	(Secretary	of	state	for	the	Colonies),	dispatched	 
instructions	for	the	new	probation	system	in	late	1842.	Sir	Eardley-Wilmot	was	 
chosen	as	Franklin’s	replacement	as	Governor	but	he	had	no	administrative	 
experience.	Captain	Matthew	Forster,	who	was	made	Controller-General	of	 
Convicts,	was	also	a	problematic	ineffectual	appointment	(Shaw	1966,	297).	Wilmot	 
arrived	(in	1843)	into	a	colony	which	had	been	under	economic	depression	since	 
1841	(Brand	1990,	24).	From	the	outset	there	were	issues	with	the	system.	There	 
had	not	been	enough	time	to	erect	appropriate	buildings,	making	classification	 
impossible.	While	Wilmot	believed	Port	Arthur	was	an	effective	place	of	 
punishment	and	that	the	conditions	at	Port	Puer	(the	juvenile	penal	settlement)	had	 
improved,	the	inspectors	disagreed	(Shaw	1966,	298).	(See	Chapter	Six	for	 
information	on	Point	Puer).	On	top	of	all	this,	there	was	also	a	labour	shortage	in	 
1840-1841.	This	was	due	to	the	end	of	assignment,	the	suspension	of	assisted	 
migration	into	VDL,	and	the	number	of	mechanics	migrating	to	the	mainland.	To	 
meet	these	labour	shortages	Franklin	promoted	free	immigration	to	VDL.	 
Unfortunately,	this	meant	that	when	convicts	emerged	from	the	probation	gangs	 
looking	for	waged	work,	there	was	none	(Shaw	1966,	279-281).	(For	more	 
information	on	the	Van	Diemonian	depression	see	Chapter	Six.)	
 
	 
Whoever	was	to	blame	for	the	failure	of	the	probation	system	the	result	was	a	 
perceived	British	indifference	which	increased	anti-transportation	sentiment	(Brand	 
1990,	103).	Charles	La	Trobe’s	report,	published	as	a	British	Parliamentary	paper	in	 
1848,	condemned	the	system	(Brand	1990,	2).	The	probation	system	lasted	for	 
fourteen	years;	from	the	formation	of	Franklin’s	gangs	to	the	cessation	of	 
transportation	(Brand	1990,	97).	Several	of	the	probation	establishments,	however,	 
remained	open	after	1853	until	the	last	convicts	served	out	their	sentences	(Brand	 
1990,	2).		 
	 
Female	Convicts		 
‘Of	the	females	less	need	be	said,	for	they	comprised	only	a	one-sixth	of	 
the	total’	(Shaw	1966,	164)	 
	 
There	were	only	around	24,960	convict	women	transported	to	Australia	 
(Hendriksen	2009,	2),	this	is	because	eighty	per	cent	of	transported	convicts	were	 
male	(Nicholas	&	Shergold	1988;	4).	Despite	Shaw’s	dismissive	quote	above,	the	 
importance	of	the	female	convict	experience	has	been	increasingly	acknowledged.	 
Robinson’s	(1988)	work	on	the	first	forty	years	of	settlement	showed	that	female	 
convicts	were	petty,	first-time	offenders	who	had	suffered	harsh	conditions	in	 
Britain.	Beddoe	(1979)	looked	at	the	circumstances,	demographic	information	and	 
occupational	circumstance	of	Welsh	female	convicts,	thereby	uncovering	their	 
convict	experience.	Subsequently,	Oxley	(1995)	who	took	an	aggregate	approach	to	 
research	female	convicts	transported	to	NSW,	found	that	they	arrived	with	much	 
needed	skills	and	trade	experience.	Other	important	works	on	female	convicts	 
include:	Robinson	1985;	Perrott	1983;	Weatherburn;	Salt	1979;	Lake	2003;	Smith	 
1988;	Fleming	2012.	This	research	will	build	on	the	work	of	these	historians.	While	 
female	convicts	have	now	been	located	in	the	historiography,	juvenile	female	 
convicts	have	been	amalgamated	with	the	adult	females.	This	research	will	look	at	 
the	juvenile	convict	experience	in	comparison	with,	but	in	isolation	from,	their	adult	 
counterparts.	 
	
 
On	arrival	in	VDL	female	convicts	were	kept	in	factories	until	they	could	be	assigned	 
(Shaw	1966,	240).	They	were	also	confined	there	when	they	offended.	(For	further	 
information	on	female	factories,	the	institutions	in	which	females	were	kept	see	 
Chapter	5).	Noteworthy,	while	some	juvenile	males	were,	in	theory	at	least,	 
separated	from	adult	males,	females	underwent	no	such	separation.	Even	during	 
voyages	after	1837,	no	such	arrangements	applied	to	female	convicts;	at	least	 
twenty-five	per	cent	of	whom	were	juveniles.	There	is	no	dispatch	mentioning	the	 
separation	of	juvenile	females,	nor	the	problems	they	faced	because	the	 
government	failed	to	separate	them	(Brand	1990,	105).	Yet,	it	is	difficult	to	believe	 
that	there	was	not	the	potential	for	abuse	under	these	circumstances.	This	is	not	to	 
say	females	were	completely	neglected.	Juvenile	females	who	were	transported	 
were	generally	slightly	older	than	the	male	juveniles	and	they	were	also	far	less	of	 
them.	This	is	partly	because	they	were	often	diverted	into	other	institutions	such	as	 
the	Philanthropic	Society,	the	Refuge	of	the	Destitute	and	the	Bridewell	House	of	 
Correction	in	Britain	(Brooke	&	Brandon	2005,	118).	Still	the	lack	of	separation	of	 
female	juveniles	in	the	colonies	has	hitherto	not	been	explored.	 
	 
The	Cessation	of	transportation	 
In	1852	the	Secretary	of	State	for	the	Colonies,	Sir	John	Pakington,	advised	 
Governor	Denison	that	transportation	to	VDL	would	cease.	No	further	convicts	 
arrived	after	the	landing	of	the	St.	Vincent	in	1853,	and	Denison	received	the	order	 
for	the	end	of	transportation	in	1854.	Certain	penal	institutions	and	settlements,	for	 
example	Cascades	and	Impression	Bay,	continued	to	hold	prisoners	until	all	 
probationers	had	passed	through	into	freedom	(Brand	1990,	95-96).	 
	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 
 
 
Chapter 3: Method & Methodology 	 In	order	to	explore	the	lives	and	criminal	careers	of	juvenile	offenders	they	were	 
nominally	linked	using	both	criminal	and	non-criminal	records.	With	the	aim	of	 
outlining	the	method	that	will	be	employed	in	this	thesis,	this	chapter	will	begin	by	 
evaluating	the	evolution	of	the	life-course	method	used.	The	focus	of	historians	has	 
shifted	from	micro-histories	concentrated	on	geographical	areas	and	events	to	a	 
more	person-centred	approach.	This	shift	has	not	been	isolated	within	the	discipline	 
of	history.	As	such	the	sociological	underpinnings	of	the	life-course	method,	which	 
is	increasingly	popular	with	historians	(Godfrey	et	al	2007;	2010;	2017;	Williams	 
2014;	Maxwell-Stewart	and	Kippen	2015),	will	be	discussed.	This	mixture	of	 
qualitative	and	quantitative	approaches	which	the	historical	life-course	method	 
incorporates	necessarily	differs	from	that	of	sociological/criminological	methods;	 
namely	through	use	of	prosopography	and	life-narratives.	Both	methods	will	be	 
discussed	along	with	the	digitization	of	historical	primary	sources	that	enable	this	 
research	to	take	place	on	a	relatively	large	scale,	the	sources	that	will	be	used,	as	 
well	as	details	of	the	database	and	sampling	that	this	research	has	employed.	 
Threaded	through	this	chapter	will	be	case	studies	(especially	one	case	study	of	a	 
juvenile	transportee3	–	George	Fenby)	which	will	be	used	as	a	device	to	exemplify	 
the	method	and	sources	being	used.		 
	 A	Person-Centred	Approach	 
Microhistories	revolve	around	significant	events	in	order	to	illustrate	wider	 
historical	phenomena.	This	is	demonstrated	by	Brown’s	(2013)	study	of	the	1932	 
Dartmoor	Prison	riot	and	Gatrell’s	(1996)	study	of	capital	justice	focusing	on	the	 
Coalbrookdale	community	reactions	to	the	rape	of	Elizabeth	Cureton.	This	 
methodology	is	not	dissimilar	to	the	focus	used	in	biographical	analysis,	which	 
instead	takes	the	lives	of	people	as	the	reference	point.	As	well	as	similar	methods,	 
both	approaches	use	similar	primary	sources;	relying	on	official	printed	documents	 
and	reports,	newspapers	and	private	papers.	Recently	the	use	of	biographical	data	 
																																																						 3	The	sample	of	juveniles	transported	to	VDL	for	this	research	will	here	and	hence	forth	be	referred	 to	as	‘juvenile	transportees’.	This	will	remain	the	case	even	when	referring	to	them	in	adulthood	as	 this	will	allow	a	differentiation	between	other	samples	discussed	in	this	thesis.	
 
to	analyse	the	life-histories	of	convicts	has	increased	in	popularity	(for	example:	 
Godfrey	et	al	2010;	Williams	2014;	Maxwell-Stewart	and	Kippen	2015).	Particularly,	 
Godfrey	et	al	incorporated	the	use	of	biographical	data	into	life-course	analysis,	and	 
it	is	this	method	that	this	research	will	closely	follow.	Beginning	by	examining	low-
level	persistent	criminality	in	Crewe,	in	the	period	of	1880-1940,	these	academics	 
then	applied	the	method	to	habitual	serious	criminals	in	Serious	Offenders	(2007;	 
2010).	Subsequently,	the	same	method	has	been	applied	to	juveniles	in	Young	 
Criminal	Lives.	This	project	considered	the	long-term	impact	of	youth	justice	 
interventions	on	400	children.	By	combining	historical	data	from	a	wide-range	of	 
sources	including	the	admissions	registers	of	reform	institutions,	they	created	life-
grids	for	juvenile	offenders	(Godfrey	et	al	2017,	9).	Other	works	using	similar	 
methods	include	Williams	(2015)	and	Turner	(2007).	Essentially,	this	method	 
requires	record-linkage	of	a	variety	of	records,	not	only	criminal	justice	records,	but	 
also	census	records,	birth,	marriage	and	death	registers,	and	newspapers	-	in	order	 
to	create	life-narratives.	Then	the	information	can	be	sequentially	ordered	by	life-
events	of	the	individuals	in	retrospect,	which	enables	an	understanding	of	the	 
progress	of	an	historical	figures	life	path.	 
	 Inevitably	the	narratives	uncovered	in	this	thesis	will	contain	personal	information.	 
The	juveniles	in	this	study	have	long	since	been	deceased	and	the	records	used	are	 
all	within	the	public	domain	and	are	even	available	online.	Yet,	descendants	will	 
potentially	be	exposed	to	un-called	for	information	about	their	family	tree.	This	is	 
increasingly	a	problem	when	an	offender	commits	a	serious	or	abhorrent	crime.	 
However,	if	names	are	anonymised	not	only	is	the	offender	stripped	of	their	 
identity,	but	also	the	research	process	misses	out	on	outside	input.	For	example,	 
during	the	initial	stages	of	this	research	George	Fenby’s	biography	(a	juvenile	 
convict	in	the	sample)	was	posted	in	a	blog	as	a	case	study,	this	resulted	in	a	 
descendent	of	George	Fenby	reaching	out.	The	great	grandson	stated:	‘Very	much	 
liked	your	site	and	the	presentation	of	your	research.	.	.’	This	is	significant	since,	 
while	George	was	convicted	at	the	Old	Bailey	of	a	petty	theft,	he	was	later	convicted	 
in	the	colony	for	‘indecently	assaulting’	a	six-year-old	girl.	Yet,	his	descendant	did	 
not	find	the	information	unwelcome.	The	remoteness	of	time	here	seems	to	have	
 
offset	any	distress	that	the	family	could	have	potentially	experienced.	Moreover,	 
the	exchange	was	a	two-way	process.	Having	spent	a	great	deal	of	time	and	effort	 
researching	George,	his	descendent	was	able	to	provide	this	research	with	further	 
information	about	George’s	family	tree.	This	would	not	have	taken	place	if	George	 
Fenby	had	been	anonymised	(Watkins	2015a).	Furthermore,	the	majority	of	the	 
juveniles	in	this	sample	did	not	take	part	in	serious	crime.		 
	 It	cannot	be	ignored	that	historians	do	not	simply	present	the	facts	as	they	are.	 
Although	it	is	always	the	aim	of	this	thesis	to	stay	as	close	to	the	facts	as	possible,	 
historians	inevitably	interpret.	Therefore,	while	avoiding	the	act	of	robbing	these	 
offenders	of	their	stories	by	not	anonymising	them	-	it	may	be	questioned	why	this	 
researcher	should	be	the	one	to	interpret	their	stories.	While	this	is	an	important	 
issue,	it	is	equally	important	not	to	further	marginalise	a	group	which	has	been	 
previously	disregarded	because	they	were	both	‘deviant’	and	children,	which	was	 
further	compounded	if	they	were	female.	Keeping	their	real	identity	is	important	in	 
the	process	of	humanising	these	individuals	and	giving	them	a	narrative	amounting	 
to	more	than	their	offences.	Therefore,	this	research	will	follow	the	trend	of	those	 
including	Godfrey	et	al	(2010),	Shore	(1999)	and	Williams	(2014),	and	not	 
anonymise	any	of	the	subjects.	 
	 While	the	life-narratives	compiled	in	this	research	are	of	interest,	the	crimes	which	 
initiated	the	juvenile	criminal	careers	are	far	from	extraordinary,	and	it	is	not	the	 
aim	of	this	research	to	romanticise	their	biographical	narratives.	This	is	in	the	same	 
spirit	as	D’Cruze	in	her	investigation	of	class,	gender	and	violence.	While	not	 
trivialising	violent	experiences,	D’Cruze	focused	on	the	everyday	violence	rather	 
than	the	sensational	and	rare	(D’Cruze	2000,	11).	Sentimentalization	too	will	be	 
avoided.	This	is	particularly	a	challenge	given	the	youth	and	the	petty	nature	of	the	 
initial	crimes	of	this	sample.	However,	this	can	be	avoided	by	remaining	true	to	the	 
facts	and	avoiding	the	interpretation	of	offender’s	narratives	with	the	attitude	of	 
giving	them	‘the	benefit	of	the	doubt’.	This	will	be	avoided	in	this	thesis	by	 
contextualizing	the	juveniles	lives.	Through	stressing,	for	example,	that	while	 
today’s	society	would	consider	their	crimes	remarkably	petty	(e.g.	pickpocketing	a	
 
handkerchief),	contemporaries	saw	property	crime	as	a	serious	offence	and	 
pickpocketing	specifically	as	the	gateway	to	burglary.		 
	 Sociological/Criminological	Underpinnings	 
In	order	to	understand	the	benefits	and	limitations	of	the	methods	being	used	it	is	 
important	to	engage	with	the	criminological	underpinnings	on	which	this	method	 
grew.	Criminologists	have	emphasized	the	link	between	criminal	behaviour	and	 
individual	background,	and	have	increasingly	applied	life-course	perspectives	in	 
their	analysis.	Increasing	in	popularity	partly	due	to	the	digitization	of	population	 
data,	these	developmental	studies	are	longitudinal	in	nature	(Vikstrom	2011,	861-
2).	This	life-course	methodology	has	evolved	from	the	‘temporal’	or	dynamic	 
approach	that	traced	the	story	of	lives	over	time.	Advanced	by	W.	I.	Thomas	and	the	 
Chicago	School,	this	temporal	approach	of	life	histories	took	a	micro-level	turn	and	 
eventually	the	life-course	approach	emerged	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	6-7).	Life-course	 
refers	to	a	sequence	of	socially	defined	events	and	roles	that	the	individual	enacts.	 
Taken	into	account	in	this	research	are	diverse	events	and	roles	which	constitute	an	 
individual’s	experience	over	time.	When	conducting	life-course	research	the	 
encoding	of	historical	events	and	social	interaction	outside	the	person	are	key	(Giele	 
&	Elder	1998,	22).	 
	 Early	works	include	Elder’s	(1974)	study	which	reconstructed	longitudinal	data	on	 
children’s	lives,	collected	since	the	1930s,	forming	one	of	the	first	systematic	studies	 
of	change	in	families	and	children.	Further	research	by	Giele	and	Elder	on	individual	 
life	records	connected	the	personal	life	trajectories	with	cultural	and	economic	 
changes;	including	depression	and	war	(1998,	7).	Later	the	historical	studies	became	 
more	demographic,	and	shifted	in	focus	from	solely	concentrating	on	wars	and	 
heroes,	to	also	include	ordinary	life-events	including	births	and	deaths	(Giele	&	 
Elder	1998,	1).	While	their	research	initially	concentrated	on	development	in	 
discrete	stages	(life-cycle	approach),	it	moved	on	to	recognise	that	any	point	in	an	 
individual	life	must	be	viewed	as	integral	to	the	outcome,	including	internal	decision	 
making	and	structural	constraint	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	19).	Life-course,	defined	in	 
terms	of	trajectories	from	birth	to	death,	allows	the	uncovering	of	a	line	of	
 
development	that	includes	phases	such	as	childhood	to	adulthood	–	including	 
getting	a	job,	having	children,	being	transported,	marrying	or	migrating.	Marked	by	 
these	events,	most	people	pass	through	a	sequence	of	transitions.	For	example,	the	 
propensity	to	be	involved	in	crime	varies	with	age,	depends	on	human	agency,	and	 
is	interfered	with	by	background	factors	(Vikstrom	2011,	863).	Giele	and	Elder	 
(1998,	1)	point	to	the	key	aspects	to	be	taken	into	account	when	using	this	method	 
which	comprised	of:	the	history,	social	structure	and	culture;	the	interaction	of	 
individuals	with	societal	institutions	and	social	groups;	human	agency;	 
chronologically	ordering	of	events	with	personal,	group	and	historical	markers.	 
	 This	thesis	has	sampled	juvenile	convicts,	and	therefore	their	criminal	activity	is	 
important	in	understanding	their	whole	lives.	However,	their	criminality	or	 
desistance	are	not	necessarily	the	most	important	factor	under	deliberation.	 
Consequently,	as	well	as	changing	criminal	legislation	and	the	importance	of	 
structural	factors,	it	is	important	to	explore	offenders’	lives	before,	during	and	after	 
any	criminal	activity	(Vikstrom	2011,	862-863;	Sampson	&	Laub	2005).	Within-
individual	changes	over	the	life-course	and	between-individual	differences	will	both	 
be	explored	by	comparing	the	respective	pathways	of	different	offenders	(Vikstrom	 
2011,	864).	In	the	same	way	as	Sampson	and	Laub	exploited	life-history	narratives	 
to	better	understand	patterns	of	stability	and	change	in	offending	over	the	life-
course,	this	research	will	use	turning	points	to	understand	life	narratives	and	 
whether	juvenile	offenders	were	able	to	settle	post-transportation	(2005,	17).	 
	 Along	with	this	growing	life-course	approach,	came	a	new	development	in	collective	 
biography	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	19).	Those	such	as	Harvey	Graff	highlighted	the	need	 
to	form	a	‘collective	portrait’	of	the	sample	based	on	their	socio-demographic	 
characteristics	and	backgrounds.	In	doing	so	it	is	possible	to	reveal	the	underlying	 
features	of	these	juveniles	lives,	which	control	mechanisms	and	structural	changes	 
fail	to	explain	(Vikstrom	2011,	861-862).	Giele	and	Elder	point	out	how	groups	of	 
individuals	who	were	‘born	at	roughly	the	same	time	and	experienced	 
approximately	the	same	historical	events’	can	be	examined	using	panel	studies	and	 
longitudinal	surveys.	Their	studies	and	surveys	collect	information	from	individuals	
 
at	discrete	points	over	a	period	of	years	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	19-20).	Since	it	is	not	 
possible	for	this	research	to	survey	the	sample,	instead	the	wealth	of	records	left	 
behind	in	the	form	of	criminal	and	social	records	will	be	turned	to.	Freed	from	 
single-factor	explanations,	Giele	and	Elder’s	model	allows	inclusion	of	many	 
variables	including	education,	peer-networks,	familial	life,	socio-economic	 
conditions	and	offending	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	22).	While	this	new	life-course	 
approach	brought	the	social	sciences	to	a	‘new	frontier	in	the	study	and	 
understanding	of	human	lives’,	methods	for	collecting	life	stories	as	a	way	of	 
capturing	the	subjective	meaning	of	experience	cannot	be	wholly	represented	by	 
quantitative	methods;	if	so	human	agency	would	be	masked	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	 
25).	 
	 This	research	aims	to	emphasize	human	agency	across	the	life-span,	underscoring	 
how	people	construct	their	lives	within	the	context	of	ongoing	constraints.	From	 
this	view,	trajectories	are	interpreted,	not	from	a	lens	of	unfolding	inevitability,	but	 
rather	as	continuous	social	reproduction	(Sampson	&	Laub	2005,	20).	Human	 
agency	is	important	for	fully	understanding	the	life-course.	Yet,	self-report	or	 
interview	data	is	inevitably	not	available	to	this	historical	research.	Of	course	 
without	qualitative	narrative	interviews,	like	those	used	by	Sampson	and	Laub,	it	is	 
difficult	to	uncover	human	agency	(2005,	17).	While	this	is	not	unusual	for	 
researchers	of	nineteenth-century	offenders,	it	is	still	a	limitation	(Godfrey	2011,	 
165).	This	is	because	attitudes	and	views	cannot	be	uncovered.	As	such,	the	idea	of	 
agency	with	a	structural	notion	of	turning	points,	known	as	‘situated	choice’,	can	 
only	be	speculated	on	using	detailed	life-narratives	derived	from	as	many	varied	 
sources	as	possible	(Sampson	&	Laub	2005,	43).	Yet,	through	using	a	variety	of	 
sources	it	is	still	possible	to	gain	an	understanding	(see	Primary	Sources	later	in	this	 
chapter).	For	example,	when	exploring	recidivism	and	desistance,	the	sources	allow	 
exploration	of	key	mechanisms	pointed	to	by	Sampson	and	Laub	(2005,	34)	 
including:	a	knifing	off	of	the	past	from	the	present;	new	relationships	offering	 
social	support	and	networks;	supervision	of	behaviour;	structured	routines	centred	 
on	family	life	rather	than	unstructured	peer	time;	and	situations	providing	identity	 
transformation	opportunities.	While	this	research	will	not	be	able	to	get	at	the	
 
internal	decision	making	process	of	those	sampled,	the	paths	individuals	forged	for	 
themselves	can	still	be	uncovered.		 
	 The	process,	used	by	Sampson	and	Laub,	of	intensive	qualitative	analysis	carried	out	 
in	response	to	quantitative	findings	will	be	emulated	in	this	research	(1998,	221).	 
Any	trends	revealed	by	statistical	analysis	will	be	further	explored	by	picking	out	 
individuals	and	forming	biographies.	This	strategy	has	two	distinct	methodological	 
benefits.	First	the	quantitative	findings	are	enhanced	by	the	analysis	of	qualitative	 
narratives,	resulting	in	more	illumination	of	the	complex	processes	leading	to	life-
outcomes.	This	process	allows	this	research	to	investigate	factors	including	 
cumulative	disadvantage.	This	is	when	negative	influences	of	structural	 
disadvantages	(e.g.	being	an	orphan)	persist	into	adulthood	(Sampson	&	Laub	1998,	 
222).	Similarly,	cumulative	advantage	will	also	be	considered	as	a	factor	which	could	 
affect	the	juvenile	transportees	‘life	chances’.	As	pointed	out	by	Godfrey	et	al	 
(2017),	cumulative	(dis)advantage	cannot	be	viewed	as	the	singular	by-product	of	 
formal	social	controls	–	such	as	transportation.	Instead	the	social,	cultural,	 
economic	and	emotional	experiences	all	work	together	along	with	the	experiences	 
of	informal	social	factors	(work,	relationships	and	networks)	as	well	as	their	 
experiences	of	interventions	including	education	and	training.	These	experiences	 
are	not	always	readily	measurable	or	quantifiable	and	therefore	are	not	easily	 
translated	into	longitudinal	methodologies.	However,	this	does	not	mean	that	they	 
did	not	count	and	such	details	should	be	sought	by	forming	detailed	biographies.	 
Individual	biographies	of	those	who	follow	statistical	trends	as	well	as	offenders	 
who	diverge	from	those	trends	will	be	chosen	for	a	deeper	understanding.	The	 
importance	of	the	qualitative	analysis	of	these	detailed	life	narratives	is	highlighted	 
when	categories	are	broken	down	in	cross-tabulation	and	numbers	can	become	 
small.	 
	 By	historically	contextualizing	this	study,	including	familial	relationships	and	 
employment,	as	well	as	significant	historical	events,	individual	development	can	be	 
understood	(Giele	&	Elder	1998,	26).	Quantitative	and	qualitative	data	in	individual	 
lives	and	social	structures	must	be	integrated	to	fully	understand	stability	and	
 
change	in	behaviour	over	time	(Sampson	&	Laub	1998,	229).	By	following	this	life-
course	method,	which	has	since	been	appropriated	and	refined	for	historical	 
research	by	Godfrey	et	al	(2007),	this	research	will	be	able	to	approach	a	fuller	 
understanding	of	the	life	outcomes	of	juvenile	transportees.	As	developments	took	 
place	in	sociology	and	criminology	–	changes	correspondingly	occurred	in	the	 
discipline	of	history	with	regards	to	prosopography	and	record-linkage.	 
	 Prosopography		 
As	described	above,	this	research	will	use	a	life-course	approach	to	trace	juveniles	 
longitudinally	across	their	life	span	by	using	a	mixture	of	historical	and	 
sociological/criminological	methods.	For	a	historical	study	to	incorporate	 
criminological	methods,	certain	practical	adaptations	must	be	made.	Specifically,	 
this	research	will	incorporate	biographical	and	prosopographical	historical	methods.	 
Using	details	from	life-events	allows	the	formation	of	biographies	which	can	be	 
combined	with	statistical	analysis	of	the	common	factors	and	experiences	present	in	 
the	lives	of	these	juvenile	transportees.	This	will	enable	both	individual	and	group	 
level	analysis.		 
	 The	breakthrough	for	prosopography	as	a	method	for	extracting	historical	 
information	was	made	by	R.	Syme’s	in	The	Roman	Revolution	(1939).	Becoming	a	 
standard	method	to	analyse	Roman	history,	the	prosopographical	method	studies	 
all	social	groups	from	those	at	the	peak	of	the	social	hierarchy	-	to	slaves.	This	 
method	investigates	individuals	as	part	of	a	network	of	personal	relationships	(Beck	 
2003,	16).	The	method	has	increasingly	been	taken	up	by	early-modern	and	modern	 
studies,	and	so	too	has	the	focus	on	the	non-exceptional.	Indeed,	this	research	will	 
focus	on	unsensational,	average	criminal	juveniles	(Nelson	et	al	2003,	155).	While	 
increasing	in	popularity,	prosopography	is	not	without	its	critics.	It	has	been	 
compared	to	the	work	of	positivist	Lewis	Namier	–	as	narrow	and	reductionist,	 
where	political	and	social	history	are	reduced	to	mere	networking	in	the	service	of	 
personal	interest:	‘as	if	history	could	be	presented	as	a	series	of	ascertainable	and	 
incontrovertible	facts’.	Yet,	provided	institutional	structures	and	context	are	taken	 
into	account	the	method	remains	relevant	(Nelson	et	al	2003,	157).		
 
	 
Prosopographical	studies	are	both	the	identification	of	individuals	(Bradley	&	Short	 
2005,	3),	as	well	as	‘the	investigation	of	the	common	background	characteristics	of
