a	group	of	actors	in	history	by	means	of	a	collective	study	of	their	lives’	(MacLeod	&	 
Nuvolari	2006,	759).	Using	the	methods	of	prosopography	allows	the	common	 
aspects	of	juvenile	offenders’	lives	to	be	uncovered,	resulting	in	an	understanding	of	 
the	group	as	a	whole.	This	allows	the	proposal	of	causal	relationships	to	questions	 
concerning	their	life	outcomes.	Inevitably,	as	with	most	historical	sources,	the	 
sources	used	in	this	research	are	fragmentary.	It	is	the	unequal	spread	of	the	 
fragmentary	evidence	of	individuals	which	makes	this	approach	vital;	where	 
individuals	with	detailed	information	can	be	used	in	group	analysis	to	supplement	 
those	few	individuals	who	have	gaps	in	their	histories	(Williams	2014,	47).	The	new	 
evolving	prosopography	has	engaged	with	a	greater	range	of	sources	for	a	wider	 
and	more	detailed	perspective.	Unstructured	and	narrative	in	nature;	the	sources	 
used	in	this	research	are	complicated	and	varied,	but	through	use	of	a	 
comprehensive	and	flexible	database	the	relevant	information	was	gathered	 
(Bradley	&	Short	2005,	5).	Successfully	employed	by	historians	of	crime	in	particular	 
(Godfrey	et	al	2007;	Williams	2015)	this	is	a	highly	contextualising	approach	–	 
placing	the	groups	of	individuals	firmly	in	the	social,	economic,	and	institutional	 
environment	of	their	time.	 
	 Longitudinal	quantitative	analysis	has	precedent	in	historical	work,	for	example,	in	 
David	Courtwright’s	work	on	violence,	which	analyzed	the	history	of	violence	from	 
the	American	Civil	War,	using	long	runs	of	data	contextualized	by	documentary	 
analysis	(1998).	Yet,	while	prosopography	allows	the	study	of	individuals	in	 
aggregate,	this	research	will	go	further	to	allow	the	narrative	and	experience	of	the	 
individual	to	emerge	in	order	to	represent	the	diversity	of	the	sample,	and	allow	the	 
experience	of	the	individuals	who	compose	the	group	to	emerge.	The	information	 
collated	to	create	individual	biographies	can	neither	be	used	to	represent	the	 
whole,	or	reveal	the	individuals	internal	decision-making	(Williams	2014,	39).	What	 
this	approach	does	do	is	force	a	perspective	in	which	offending	is	seen	as	it	was:	 
unusual	and	secondary	in	the	lives	of	most	offenders.	It	emphasises	the	humanity	of	
 
the	subject	under	study	and	encourages	a	more	empathetic	response	(Godfrey	 
2017).	Undeniably,	constructing	narratives	is	not	without	its	problems	as	it	is	a	 
creative	process;	‘a	construct	that	articulates	the	past	anew’.	Yet	this	does	not	 
mean	that	the	narrative	does	not	have	truth	(Norman	1991,	135).	A	degree	of	 
interpretation	is	inevitable.	What	is	vital	is	that	the	sources	used	to	create	the	 
database	are	interrogated	in	a	proper	and	consistent	historical	fashion	(Bradley	&	 
Short	2005,	17).	Similarly,	with	the	increasing	digitization	so	too	must	the	 
presentation	of	sources	be	questioned.	 
	 Digitization	 
‘The	availability	of	digital	data	on	the	internet	offers	a	hyper-extension	of	 
criminology’s	reach	towards	uncovering	and	recovering	the	lives	of	the	disposed	 
and	powerless’	(Godfrey	2017,	140).	However,	this	increasing	ease	of	access	of	 
online	historical	material	is	not	without	its	challenges.	Specifically,	while	 
interrogating	the	primary	source	itself	is	necessary,	it	is	also	important	to	 
understand	the	digitization	process	and	the	limitations	and	possibilities	associated	 
with	it	(Deswarte	2010,	281).	The	nature	of	historical	evidence	may	not	have	 
changed,	but	our	access	to	it	and	its	presentation	has	(Cohen	2006,	391).	The	large-
scale	digitisation	of	primary	sources	has	allowed	historians	‘new	insights’	into	 
working-class	lives.	Indeed,	the	‘elaborate	bureaucracy	of	surveillance’	established	 
in	Van	Diemen’s	Land	(VDL)	during	the	convict	period,	which	is	now	vastly	digitized,	 
is	a	prime	example.	These	records	contain	numerous	observations	for	the	same	 
individual	allowing	the	piecing	together	of	individual	criminal	lives	and	statistical	 
analysis	to	varied	research	questions	–	at	a	scale	unmanageable	using	non-digitized	 
documentation	(Shore	&	Johnston	2015,	3-4).	The	increased	accessibility	of	tracing	 
offenders’	lives,	thanks	to	the	digitization	of	historical	documents,	is	especially	 
relevant	to	the	late-nineteenth	century.	Consequently,	there	has	been	a	 
concentration	on	this	heavily	documented	period,	leaving	a	relative	neglect	of	early-
nineteenth	century	criminal	history.	Resulting	partly	in	the	concentration	of	this	 
thesis	beginning	in	1816.	The	bureaucratic	system	of	the	nineteenth	century	 
resulted	in	the	production	of	an	overwhelming	number	of	criminal	justice	sources,	 
when	combined	with	the	recent	digitization,	you	have	something	which	is	
 
invaluable	to	historical	research	and	particularly	the	method	of	nominal	record-
linkage.	 
	 Record-Linkage	 
The	increasing	focus	directly	on	criminal	lives	is	made	possible	not	merely	thanks	to	 
the	revolution	in	electronic	resources,	but	also	the	technique	of	data-linkage	of	 
multiple	documents	(Godfrey	2014,	90-91).	Despite	warnings	that	it	requires	 
‘enormous	imaginative	ingenuity’	to	match	records,	when	data-linkage	is	carried	 
out	on	a	manual,	relatively	small	scale	it	is	possible	to	become	familiar	with	the	 
details	which	allow	accurate	identification	(Winchester	1970,	110;	Pouyez,	Roy	&	 
Martin	1983,	130).	Record	linkage	is	the	bringing	together	of	information	 
concerning	a	historical	individual	derived	from	independent	sources.	This	allows	 
greater	information	about	an	individual	to	be	collected	and	corroborated.	Being	 
concerned	with	a	larger	social	pattern	and	the	everyday	life	of	ordinary	people,	 
representative	individuals	can	be	traced	through	a	historical	period.	Ideally	all	 
individuals	in	a	particular	period	or	region	would	be	traced,	but	this	is	not	always	 
possible	since	most	ordinary	people	do	not	leave	identifying	information	behind.	 
And	the	information	that	can	be	garnered	from	census	and	parish	registers,	though	 
valued,	is	limited	(Winchester	1970,	107-8).	Yet	when	it	comes	to	criminals	this	can	 
be	overcome	to	some	extent	due	to	the	details	left	by	the	bureaucratic,	document-
heavy	system.	This	is	because	most	criminal	justice	generated	documents	have	 
information	not	just	on	crime,	but	also	on	the	criminal.	When	this	is	combined	with	 
detailed	historical	newspapers,	thorough	narratives	can	emerge	(Godfrey	2014,	79).	 
This	is	highlighted	in	the	Swedish	study	which	benefits	from	the	combination	of	 
records	to	create	longitudinal	databases	of	individual	data	(Wisselgren	et	al	2014,	 
138).	In	research	which	depends	largely	upon	documents	generated	by	and	for	the	 
state,	every	additional	piece	of	information	is	welcome	in	confirming	or	altering	 
interpretation	(Frost	2011,	26).		 
	 Nominally	linking	individuals	using	this	method	is	not	new,	for	example,	Gatrell	 
experimented	with	tracing	in	his	seminal	work	The	Hanging	Tree.	Gatrell	traced	the	 
convicted	rapist	Noden	to	the	convict	transportation	destination	of	Bermuda,	and	
 
then	found	him	again	back	in	the	community	in	which	he	committed	his	crime	 
(Gatrell	1996,	493).	Now,	data-linkage	methods	have	become	mainstream	and	 
expanded.	This	allows	life-event	maps	of	individual	offenders	to	be	formed	by	 
linking	together:	penal	records	containing	information	on	previous	convictions,	 
community	ties	and	offender	descriptions;	newspaper	reports;	and	census	and	 
parish	records	which	provide	details	of	residence,	occupation,	births,	marriages	and	 
deaths	(Williams	&	Godfrey	2015,	7).	Although	all	the	information	available	will	be	 
used,	not	all	the	information	will	be	known	–	significant	interactions,	events	and	 
decision-making	will	remain	hidden	in	history.	Nevertheless,	interpretation	based	 
on	available	evidence	and	knowledge	of	relevant	social	and	economic	histories	will	 
aid	the	construction	of	narratives.		 
	 Sampling	 
Using	a	grounded	method,	all	information	on	the	juveniles	in	this	study	was	 
gathered	for	the	database	from	all	available	and	accessible	sources,	then	the	 
information	and	its	significance	was	later	evaluated.	The	column	variables	formed	in	 
the	database	spread	across	the	juvenile’s	life	spans,	stretching	from	their	lives	prior	 
to	conviction,	the	conviction	itself,	the	periods	of	punishment	and	beyond.		 
	 Sampling	Stage	1	 
Sampling	for	this	study	was	carried	out	in	several	stages.	Juveniles	were	originally	 
identified	at	the	Old	Bailey	Online	(OBO).	Those	convicted	under	fourteen	years-of-
age4,	who	were	sentenced	to	transportation	or	confinement	in	the	period	of	1816-
																																																						 4	The	age	at	which	an	individual	was	a	juvenile	varied	widely	in	social	discourse	from	fourteen,	 sixteen,	seventeen,	and	even	to	twenty	years-of-age.	As	is	demonstrated	in	the	1819	Select	 Committee	in	which	commentators	referred	to	differing	upper	age	limits	of	seventeen	and	twenty	 (May	1981,	80).	This	is	also	pointed	out	by	Magarey	(1978,	16)	who	stated	that	in	British	prisons	the	 distinction	between	juveniles	and	adults	‘was	drawn	at	a	variety	of	different	ages	in	different	local	 prisons,	but	the	maximum	age	of	juvenile	classes	in	prisons	was	seventeen’.	Within	VDL,	Point	Puer	 held	‘juveniles’	up	to	twenty	years-of-age	but	the	majority	were	fourteen.	As	such,	juveniles	under	 fourteen	years-of-age	were	sampled	in	this	study	based	on	nineteenth-century	law:	juveniles	aged	 between	seven	and	fourteen	could	be	prosecuted	‘only’	if	the	prosecutor	could	convince	the	judge	 and	jury	that	the	child	knew	they	were	committing	a	crime	(doli	capax),	rather	than	just	being	 ‘naughty’	(doli	incapax).	Those	over	fourteen	were	considered	adults	in	the	eyes	of	the	law	with	 regards	to	trial	and	punishment.	However,	while	the	juveniles	were	under	fourteen	upon	conviction,	 some	had	to	wait	several	years	for	a	transport	to	VDL.	By	the	time	they	arrived	in	VDL	the	majority	 (eighty-eight	per	cent)	were	sixteen	and	under	(the	oldest	female	was	nineteen;	the	oldest	males	 were	eighteen;	the	youngest	female	was	twelve;	the	youngest	male	was	ten).		
 
1850	had	their	criminal	proceedings	transcribed	into	an	Excel	database.	This	gave	a	 
total	of	2622	juvenile	offences.	Using	this	sample,	it	was	possible	to	investigate	the	 
types	of	offences	committed,	as	well	as	their	resulting	sentences.		 
	 Next	those	that	were	sentenced	to	transportation	were	traced	in	the	British	 
Transportation	Records	to	ascertain	which	juveniles	actually	underwent	forced	 
migration	to	Australia.	There	were	1406	juveniles	of	whom	ninety-five	per	cent	 
were	male.	There	were	1406	juveniles	sentenced	to	transportation	and	of	those	 
(seventy	females	and	1336	males)	only	879	(sixty-three	per	cent)	were	sent	to	 
Australia.	Leaving	527	juveniles	(thirty-seven	per	cent)	not	transported.	 
	 
Sampling	Stage	2	-	Males	 
Of	the	1336	males	sentenced	to	transportation	only	855	(sixty-four	per	cent)	were	 
actually	sent.	Given	the	time	restrictions	of	this	thesis	and	the	length	of	time	it	 
would	take	to	fully	and	accurately	trace	all	the	juveniles,	a	sample	was	taken.	It	was	 
also	decided	that	in	order	to	fully	understand	the	lives	of	these	transported	 
juveniles	it	would	be	best	to	concentrate	on	one	penal	colony.	This	left	the	choice	 
between	VDL	and	New	South	Wales	(NSW)	–	since	only	one	offender	was	sent	to	 
Western	Australia	(WA)	and	those	sent	to	Victoria	as	exiles	were	not	sufficiently	 
recorded;	VDL	was	chosen.	This	choice	not	only	allowed	the	full	contextualisation	of	 
these	juveniles,	but	also	the	records	of	VDL	have	been	better	preserved.	This,	 
combined	with	a	research	trip	to	Tasmania	(formerly	VDL),	made	the	decision	apt.	 
Therefore,	of	those	855	male	juveniles,	who	were	actually	transported	to	Australia,	 
only	534	(sixty-two	per	cent)	were	sent	to	VDL.	This	left	321	(thirty-eight	per	cent)	 
convicts	who	were	sent	elsewhere:	thirteen	(four	per	cent)	were	sent	to	Victoria,	 
307	(thirty-six	per	cent)	were	sent	to	NSW	and	just	one	(0.1%)	was	sent	to	WA.	 
	 	 	 Sampling	Stage	3	-	Males	 
Despite	limiting	the	sample	to	VDL	transportees	this	still	left	534	males	to	be	traced	 
longitudinally	through	their	lives;	further	sampling	was	required.	Consequently	100	 
(nineteen	per	cent)	of	male	juveniles	were	sampled	systematically	by	choosing	a	
 
juvenile	and	then	missing	a	given	number	of	juveniles	in	a	chronologically	organized	 
database.	This	process	was	followed	until	100	juveniles	were	sampled,	which	had	 
either	a	death	certificate	or	a	significant	life	event	after	freedom	(be	it	further	 
offending	or	a	social	life	event).	This	gave	a	sample	of	male	juveniles	who	arrived	 
between	1818	and	1852,	with	sentences	of	seven	years’	transportation	(seventy-
eight	per	cent),	ten	years’	transportation	(six	per	cent)	and	fourteen	years’	 
transportation	(four	per	cent),	fifteen	years’	transportation	(one	per	cent)	and	a	life	 
sentence	of	transportation	(eleven	per	cent).	 
	 Sampling	Stage	2	-	Females	 
Of	the	seventy	females	sentenced	to	transportation	only	twenty-four	(thirty-four	 
per	cent)	were	actually	sent.	Since	it	was	decided	that	only	those	transported	to	 
VDL	would	have	their	lives	traced	this	left	only	eighteen	female	juveniles.	The	 
remaining	six	were	sent	to	NSW.	Consequently,	no	further	sampling	was	required	 
here.	Arriving	between	1825	and	1846,	the	eighteen	females	who	were	traced	 
through	their	lives	were	sentenced	to	seven	years’	transportation	(seventy-eight	per	 
cent),	ten	years’	transportation	(eleven	per	cent),	fourteen	years’	transportation	 
(5.6%)	and	a	life	sentence	of	transportation	(5.6%).	 
	 Analysis	 
Along	with	the	biographies	created,	as	will	be	demonstrated	through	the	Case	Study	 
No.	2	below,	the	purpose	of	the	database	is	to	allow	for	quantitative	analysis.	 
Through	coding	of	the	relevant	variables,	both	frequencies	and	cross-tabulations	 
were	carried	out	using	SPSS	and	Excel.	The	aim	of	this	approach	was	to	analyse	the	 
interplay	of	variables	in	order	to	understand	historical	processes.	While	rich	 
narrative	data	can	be	extracted	from	the	database,	the	measurable	variables	can	 
also	be	uncovered	including	those	surrounding	crime	and	punishment,	to	those	 
involving	the	social	and	economic	aspects	of	their	changing	lives.	Where	the	female	 
sample	is	concerned	(and	also	with	certain	breakdowns	of	the	male	sample)	 
numbers	became	small.	On	these	occasions,	scrutiny	was	turned	to	the	detailed	life-
narratives	of	these	juvenile	lives	and	they	were	subsequently	compared	with	similar	 
groups.	
 
	 In	order	to	establish	whether	these	juvenile	transportees	were	able	to	settle	into	 
their	new	colonial	lives,	the	following	themes	were	assessed	including	crime;	 
punishment;	education,	training	and	occupation;	family	Life;	and	death.	Deciding	on	 
the	‘life-outcome’	for	any	of	the	juvenile	transportees	can	only	be	done	in	reference	 
to	other	contemporary	groups,	be	they	free	settlers	or	other	convicts.	Yet,	even	 
when	comparing	the	juvenile	transportees	with	other	juvenile	convicts	the	 
comparison	is	imperfect.	This	is	because,	as	pointed	out	by	Parker	(2008,	227),	how	 
one	person	evaluates	their	experience	and	how	a	researcher	evaluates	the	 
collective	experience	will	inevitably	result	in	exceptions	and	generalizations.	There	 
is	no	doubt	that	this	research	suffers	from	this	limitation,	especially	since	there	is	no	 
first	person	testimony	available.	However,	it	is	still	possible	to	uncover	the	lives	that	 
the	juvenile	convicts	forged	for	themselves	within	their	structural	constraints	and	in	 
relation	to	their	contemporaries.	 
	 It	was	possible	to	uncover	detailed	information	thanks	to	the	rich	sources	used.	 
From	the	criminal	records	created	for	surveillance,	to	the	newspapers	created	for	 
public	consumption	–	all	provide	different	perspectives	of	the	offender’s	life.	Next,	 
this	chapter	will	explore	the	sources	used	and	the	wealth	of	information	they	offer,	 
as	well	as	the	drawbacks	centred	on	their	authorship.		 
	 Primary	Sources	 
While	records	other	than	criminal	records	have	been	used	in	this	research,	there	is	a	 
concentration	and	heavy	reliance	on	them.	As	such	when	tracing	juveniles,	those	 
with	more	offending	had	more	records	generated	about	them.	Similarly,	those	who	 
were	extraordinary	in	some	other	aspect	of	their	lives	were	also	more	readily	 
identified.	It	may	therefore	be	argued	that	it	is	the	ordinary	that	fall	through	the	 
gaps.	Yet,	since	nineteenth-century	lives	are	so	difficult	to	uncover,	especially	the	 
lives	of	juveniles,	it	is	a	limitation	worth	striving	to	overcome.	And	it	can	be,	 
provided	the	limitations	and	bias	inherent	in	the	sources	and	methodology	are	 
taken	into	account,	and	as	many	varied	sources	are	turned	to	as	possible.	 
	
 
The	systematic	recording	of	crime	levels	was	started	by	the	Home	Office	(an	 
organisation	which	itself	grew	from	six	clerks	in	1817,	to	a	vast	bureaucracy	by	the	 
twentieth	century).	This	growing	‘bureaucratic	engine’	demanded	increasing	 
amounts	of	data	in	order	to	sustain	a	government	that	was	increasingly	interested	 
in	crime	and	control	(Godfrey	2011,	159).	There	are	a	multitude	of	nineteenth-
century	criminal	justice	sources	available	for	utilization,	but	they	are	not	without	 
issue.	Not	only	is	the	objectivity	of	the	historian	at	issue,	but	also	these	invaluable	 
sources	were	shaped	by	the	author’s	agenda	(Shore	1999,	12).	In	particular,	the	 
sources	overwhelmingly	utilised	in	this	research	were	generated	by	institutions	and	 
organizations	whose	motive	was	to	punish	and/or	reform	criminals	(Williams	2015,	 
39).	And	because	these	official	documents	were	shaped	by	the	needs	of	the	 
institution	they	were	written	for,	details	will	always	be	omitted.	Despite	these	 
limitations,	the	approach	employed	still	allows	the	understanding	of	the	progress	of	 
the	lives	of	juvenile’s,	who	were	overwhelmingly	drawn	from	the	poor;	allowing	the	 
exploration	of,	for	example,	how	socioeconomic	policies	impacted	individuals	 
(Godfrey	2015,	6).	These	nineteenth-century	juvenile	offenders	will	inevitably	be	 
tied	to	their	criminal	records	in	which	they	were	identified,	but	through	using	a	 
holistic	approach,	by	describing	their	lives	through	investigation	of	aspects	such	as	 
employment	and	familial	life,	a	rounded	picture	can	be	sought	(Shore	1999,	16;	 
Godfrey	2015,	5).	This	research	hopes	to	follow	the	same	theoretical	and	 
methodological	approach	as	the	‘history	from	below’	pioneered	by	Douglas	Hay	 
(1975)	and	E.	P.	Thompson	(1975);	and	continued,	for	example,	by	Shore	(1999),	 
Davies	(2008),	Rogers	(2014)	and	Brown	(2003).	It	is	thanks	to	the	sources	used	that	 
this	is	possible.	 
	 The	Central	Court	Criminal	(Old	Bailey)	Proceedings	 
In	order	to	identify	the	juvenile	offenders	for	this	research	the	Old	Bailey	was	 
utilised.	A	commercial	success,	the	Old	Bailey	proceedings	were	originally	 
inexpensive	and	targeted	at	a	popular	audience.	For	over	240	years	this	periodical	 
was	published	at	the	conclusion	of	every	session,	and	it	is	the	largest	body	of	texts	 
detailing	non-elite	lives	ever	published	(Bradley	&	Short	2005,	13;	Shoemaker	2005,	 
2).	All	surviving	records,	from	1674	to	1913,	are	now	freely	available	on	the	OBO	
 
(Shoemaker	2005,	2).	The	OBO	contains	both	images	of	the	original	proceedings,	 
and	key	word	searchable	text	enabling	sampling.	As	well	as	details	of	the	crime	and	 
sentence,	certain	demographic	information,	rich	witness	narratives,	and	criminal	 
juvenile	testimony	are	all	available	in	the	online	repository	which	contains	197	000	 
trials;	of	which	only	2622	met	this	research	criteria	(Howard	2015,	14;	Godfrey	 
2014,	85).	One	of	these	juveniles	is	nine-year-old	George	Fenby,	found	guilty	of	 
Simple	Larceny	in	1829.	 
	 Case	Study	No.2:	George	Fenby	 George,	having	stolen	two	pairs	of	shoes	from	a	shop	with	his	mother,	Hannah	 Fenby,	was	tried	along	with	her.	Despite	the	court	believing	George	to	be	nine-years-old	(he	was	in	fact	twelve-years-old),	both	him	and	his	forty-three-year-old	 mother	 were	 sentenced	 to	 seven	 years’	 transportation.5	 From	 this	 proceeding	we	learn	George’s	age,	that	both	his	parents	were	together,	as	well	 as	his	mother’s	employment	–	a	char	woman.	It	is	even	possible	to	glimpse	a	 snap-shop	of	the	care	Hannah	had	for	her	son.	The	trial	record	describes	how	 Hannah	put	herself	under	suspicion	by	going	to	‘beg	the	boy	off’.	What-is-more,	 we	find	that	Thomas	Fenby,	the	father,	was	at	the	gin-shop	during	the	offence.	 As	well	as	certain	demographic	information	about	the	offender,	we	learn	about	 the	circumstances	of	the	offence.		 
	 The	proceedings	are	useful	but	they	are	not	without	their	limitations,	it	is	important	 
to	consider	why	they	were	published	and	who	had	access	to	them	(Mahood	1995,	 
14).	Trial	records	are	official	and	public	texts	–	they	construct	accounts	of	behaviour	 
in	terms	of	legal	and	public	guilt	or	innocence	within	the	value	system	which	they	 
are	written.	Yet,	a	trial	is	one	of	the	rare	moments	in	which	any	information	of	the	 
lower	classes,	especially	that	of	juveniles,	is	recorded	in	any	detail.	It	may,	as	Gatrell	 
pointed	out,	‘entail	a	quest	for	hidden	truths,’	but	it	is	a	quest	worth	taking	as	 
nowhere	else	can	such	information	be	found	on	such	large	numbers	of	the	so	called	 
underclass	(Gatrell	1996,	448).	Due	to	the	petty	and	unremarkable	nature	of	nearly	 
all	of	the	crimes	committed	by	these	offenders,	which	resulted	in	their	selection	 
into	the	sample,	these	juveniles	were	in	many	ways	representative	of	other	 
working-class	juveniles	who	did	not	find	their	way	into	the	courts.	Being	sampled	 
																																																						 5	OBO:	https://www.oldbaileyonline.org/browse.jsp?id=t18290716-103-defend808&div=t18290716-103#highlight		
 
from	the	OBO	these	juveniles	were	London	based.	While	the	large	and	highly	 
populated	city	of	London	is	different	from	anywhere	else	in	England	and	Wales,	it	is	 
also	made	up	of	immigrants	from	all	over	–	making	it	a	more	diverse	and	 
representative	sample.		 
Thanks	to	the	details	given	in	the	proceedings	we	know	information	about	those	 
such	as	George	Fenby	-	including	his	full	name	(in	this	case	an	unusual	surname),	his	 
mother’s	name,	occupation,	as	well	as	both	of	their	ages,	and	their	crime	and	 
sentence.	Such	information,	will	not	only	allow	initial	statistical	analysis	into	who	 
was	brought	before	the	courts	and	for	what	crimes,	it	will	also	aid	the	record-
linkage	of	George	Fenby	enabling	life-course	analysis.	 
	 
Australian	Transportation	Records	 
This	research	traced	all	juveniles	sentenced	to	transportation	to	ascertain	if	they	 
were	actually	sent.	While	it	is	not	certain	that	just	because	they	are	not	present	in	 
the	transportation	records	they	were	not	transported,	as	records	may	be	missing	or	 
incomplete,	it	does	give	an	idea	of	the	disparity	between	those	sentenced	to	 
transportation	and	those	arriving	in	Australia.		 
	 Of	the	150	000	people	transported	to	Australia	between	1788	and	1853,	almost	half	 
were	sent	to	VDL,	but	a	colony	which	changed	its	name	to	Tasmania	to	rid	itself	 
from	the	stigmatization	of	its	convict	past	also	rid	itself	of	much	of	the	 
documentation	detailing	it.	Thankfully,	while	many	records	were	destroyed	or	 
disappeared,	the	central	archive	of	the	Convict	Department	survived	(Frost	2011,	 
19).	Much	of	this	information	has	been	digitized	and	is	available	online.6	Available	 
information	includes;	behavioural	information,	height	data,	details	of	punishment,	 
employment	details	and	progress	in	the	penal	colony.	In	particular,	the	Founders	 
and	Survivors	project	has	gathered	information	about	73	000	convicts	transported	 
to	VDL	between	1803	and	1853	(Shore	&	Johnston	2015,	5).	Indeed,	the	conduct	 
																																																						 6	State	Library	of	Queensland,	Convict	transportation	registers	database,	Found	at	 http://www.slq.qld.gov.au/resources/family-history/convicts	/;	Tasmanian	Government,	Tasmanian	 Names	Index,	Found	at	http://linctas.ent.sirsidynix.net.au/client/en_AU/names/;	Founders	&	 Survivors	,	Founders	&	Survivors:	Australian	Life	course	in	Historical	Context	1803-1920,	Found	at:	 http://foundersandsurvivors.org/pubsearch;	Convict	Records,	Convict	Records	of	Australia,	Found	at:	 http://www.convictrecords.com.au/		
 
registers	initiated	by	Lieutenant-Governor	Arthur	(of	VDL)	running	from	1803,	 
recorded	the	convicts’	offences	from	their	arrival	in	the	colony,	details	of	their	 
conviction,	to	their	behaviour	prior	to	embarkation	(Shore	1999,	136-137).	The	 
system	of	convict	transportation	and	the	detailed	bureaucratic	records	on	individual	 
offenders	it	provided,	allows	the	recreation	of	their	experiences	during	and	after	 
convict	detention	in	the	colony	(Godfrey	2014,	117).7		 
	 Case	Study	Continued…	 According	to	some	historians,	juveniles	were	not	usually	transported	until	‘they	 were	a	suitable	age’	according	to	Duckworth	that	was	fourteen	or	fifteen	years	 old	(2002,	86-87).	If	they	were	younger	upon	conviction	they	would	spend	this	 period	of	 limbo	in	 local	gaols	or	on	the	hulks.	Clearly,	there	were	exceptions	 and	 juveniles	 were	 transported	 under	 fourteen	 years-old	 and	 George	 is	 an	 example.	George’s	trip	aboard	the	Manlius	took	four	months,	meanwhile	his	 mother	was	transported	separately	aboard	the	Eliza.		 
The	Conduct	Records	are	of	particular	use	to	this	research	because	of	the	 information	 on	 the	 perception	 of	 offenders’	 behaviour,	 and	 information	 on	 changing	 locations.	 Changing	 locations	 can	 also	 be	 uncovered	 in	 the	 Appropriation	Records	which	outline	the	assignment	of	convicts	whether	they	 were	assigned	to	an	individual	free	settler	or	put	to	work	on	the	government	 works.	After	being	firstly	assigned	to	Mrs.	Humphreys	for	less	than	two	years,	 George	was	re-assigned	to	a	John	Kerr.	There,	George	began	his	misconduct	 relatively	 unremarkably,	 for	 example,	 he	 received	 twelve	 lashes	 for	 being	 absent	in	1833.	However,	just	a	year	later	his	misconduct	took	on	a	new	form.	 It	 was	 reported	 that	 George	 took	 ‘liberties’	 with	 his	 master’s	 six-year-old	 daughter,	himself	being	approximately	fourteen.	As	a	result,	he	was	placed	in	 the	worst	class	of	boys	at	Point	Puer	(a	juvenile	penal	settlement	1834-1849).	 At	Point	Puer	George	 received	a	 further	 twelve	 lashes	 for	 ‘most	 riotous	and	 improper	conduct	in	the	cells’.	This	was	followed	by	more	absenteeism.	Before	 receiving	his	Certificate	of	Freedom	in	1836,	it	is	possible	to	continually	track	 George	 within	 the	 Muster	 Records.	 These	 records	 inform	 us	 who	 he	 was	 assigned	to.	Particularly	they	inform	us	whether	he	was	at	the	Public	Works	(he	 never	was)	or	in	confinement	(he	was	placed	in	Port	Arthur	Penal	Station	after	 repeated	offences).		 
While	awaiting	transportation,	George	was	imprisoned	on	a	hulk.	Convict	 prison	hulks	were	decommissioned	war	ships	moored	in	harbours.	The	records	 
																																																						 7	Records	available	include	but	are	not	limited	to:	Conduct	Records	CON31/1/14;	Appropriation	Lists	 CON27/1/4	and	CS01/1/444;	Description	Lists	CON18/1/15	and	CON23/1/1;	and	Muster	Rolls	 CS01/1/354	(often	reference	only):	Tasmanian	Government,	Tasmanian	Names	Index,	Found	at	 http://linctas.ent.sirsidynix.net.au/client/en_AU/names/	
 
for	the	male	juvenile	only	Euryalsis	Hulk,	on	which	George	was	kept,	tell	us	that	 he	was	‘not	known	here	before’.	While	this	gives	us	little	detail,	just	knowing	 George	spent	time	on	the	Euryalsis	allows	us	to	place	him	in	the	context	of	the	 numerous,	unfavourable	descriptions	given	by	inmates,	employees	and	visitors	 of	the	hulk	conditions.	 
While	most	of	the	transportation	records	allow	us	to	track	George,	and	the	 Conduct	 Record	 provides	 information	 about	 behaviour	 and	 location,	 the	 Description	 List	 gives	 us	 enough	 information	 to	 enable	 us	 to	 create	 a	 basic	 sketch	of	George	in	our	mind’s	eye	-	humanizing	the	subject.	It	also	informs	us	 that	he	was	a	tailor	by	trade	and	that	he	was	from	the	Parish	of	Shadwell	 in	 London.	 
	 Transport	records	were	unfortunately	written	from	the	perspective	of	the	colonial	 
authorities,	and	were	never	meant	for	public	consumption.	Notwithstanding	the	 
methodological	problems	such	a	dependence	on	official	records	has	(Mahood	1995,	 
14),	as	long	as	the	surveillance	purposes	are	recalled	juvenile	offenders	like	George	 
Fenby	can	be	placed	in	context	with	other	offending	juveniles,	and	questions	can	be	 
approached.	While	criminal	records	are	invaluable,	gaps	in	the	life-narrative	remain.	 
These	gaps	can	be	filled	by	turning	to	other	records	including	newspapers	and	birth,	 
death	and	marriage	records	-	both	from	the	colony	and	home.	 
	 Newspapers	 
In	order	to	gain	a	holistic	and	rounded	understanding	of	juvenile	offenders,	 
especially	their	activities	outside	of	the	criminal	justice	system,	it	is	important	to	 
turn	to	non-criminal	records.	Through	these	records	we	can	gain	information	on	 
such	aspects	as	familial	and	work	life.	Newspapers	tell	us	something	about	how	 
events	were	viewed	by	society.	As	such,	numerous	invaluable	digitised	newspaper	 
archives	were	used.8	Nineteenth-century	newspapers	discovered	that	their	 
readership	required	human	interest	stories;	thus	names	of	individuals	can	be	found.	 
It	is	the	existence	of	these	records,	as	well	as	the	intrinsic	interest	of	the	period	 
which	has	led	to	many	present	day	social	historians	to	concentrate	of	the	period	 
from	the	1840s	onwards	–	as	shown	in	the	work	of	Nineteenth	Century	Cities	 
																																																						 8	British	Newspaper	Archive,	19th	Century	British	Library	Newspaper	collection,	 http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.ac.uk	;	The	Times	Digital	Archive,	1785-2011,	 http://www.gale.com/c/the-times-digital-archive;	Australian	Newspapers	Online,	Trove,	 http://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper		
 
(Winchester	1970,	108).	Yet	newspapers	from	the	early-nineteenth	century	are	 
readily	available.	It	is	important	to	note	that	newspapers	not	only	sensationalise	 
reports,	especially	reports	of	crime,	but	also	only	report	incidents	they	deem	 
newsworthy.	Nevertheless,	they	are	essential	for	providing	details	about	offenders	 
and	offences	which	it	is	not	possible	to	ascertain	in	other	sources.	They	can	also	 
confirm	findings	which	may	be	difficult	to	decipher	due	to	handwriting	or	poor	 
quality	preservation.	Importantly,	it	is	sometimes	possible	to	find	information	of	 
offenders	not	related	to	their	crimes.	 
	 Case	study	Continued…	 Thanks	to	the	Australian	newspapers,	information	can	be	both	confirmed	and	 newly	 gathered	 regarding	George’s	 conduct	 and	movements	 in	 the	 colonies	 before	and	after	release.	Firstly,	we	find	that	the	‘grossly	indecent’	offence	he	 committed	when	he	was	fourteen	years-old	was	reported	in	the	Colonial	Times,	 demonstrating	the	seriousness	of	the	incident	(Figure	No.1).	He	again	appears	 in	 the	papers	 in	August	 1842	having	been	 charged	with	 attempted	highway	 robbery	(Figure	No.2).	A	week	later	we	find	him	and	an	accomplice	were	only	 convicted	of	assault	after	the	Court	of	Quarter	Sessions	found	there	was	not	 enough	evidence	 ‘to	substantiate	the	charge	preferred	against	them’	(Figure	 No.3).	We	can	be	confident	that	it	is	the	correct	George,	because	it	states	his	 alias	was	Timms.	Not	only	was	this	name	on	his	mother’s	death	certificate,	but	 the	connection	is	also	shown	in	a	newspaper	notice	addressed	to	George	Fenby,	 by	his	mother	Hannah	Timms,	in	1850	(Figure	No.4).	Such	family	notices	tell	us	 that	mother	 and	 son	 did	 stay	 in	 touch,	 albeit	 sporadically,	 after	 being	 sent	 separately	 across	 to	 the	 other	 side	 of	 the	 world.	 Therefore,	 it	 is	 not	 only	 criminal	 activities	which	make	 the	 papers.	 It	 is	 also	 possible	 to	 find	 that	 he	 migrated	 to	 Victoria,	 living	 for	 a	 period	 in	 Geelong	 where	 he	 worked	 as	 a	 sawyer.	Not	only	can	we	ascertain	his	year	of	death,	but	we	also	find	that	he	 left	£423	in	his	will	–	which	tells	us,	along	with	the	fact	that	he	left	a	wife	behind,	 that	he	had	formed	a	social	life	in	the	colonies	–	with	both	financial	and	familial	 security	(The	Argus,	October	1893,	3);	implying	he	settled	down.

	 	 Census	Records,	Birth,	Marriage	and	Death	Registers	 
As	well	as	newspapers,	non-criminal	records	key	to	this	research	are	the	census,	 
birth,	marriage	and	death	records.	Given	that	this	research	begins	in	1816,	and	the	 
census	returns	available	for	England	and	Wales	run	between	1841-1911,	those	 
convicted	at	the	beginning	of	the	period	who	remained	in	Britain	are	difficult	to	 
trace.	Additionally,	Prison	Licences	did	not	begin	until	1853.	For	these	reasons,	 
those	who	were	not	transported	were	not	traced	because	they	could	not	be	reliably	 
identified.	The	information	gathered	on	those	individuals	not	traced	fully	was	still	
 
useful	in	understanding	the	types	of	juveniles	brought	before	the	courts,	their	 
crimes,	as	well	as	sentencing.	Nevertheless,	for	those	whom	the	census	data	is	 
available	(those	born	later	in	the	sample)	the	information	that	can	be	gathered	is	 
invaluable.	It	is	possible	to	find	the	juvenile’s	location,	type	of	residence,	family	 
structure	and	occupation	pre-transportation.	Also	used	were	birth,	death	and	 
marriage	parish	records	from	Britain	and	Australia.	These	provided	information	on	 
the	individual’s	location,	personal	relationships,	family	size,	occupation,	child	 
mortality	and	length	of	life.		 
	 Case	Study	Continued…	 George’s	proceeding	stated	that	he	was	nine-years-old	and	his	transportation	 records	state	that	he	was	ten-years-old.	In	fact,	George	was	twelve-years-old	 when	he	first	stepped	foot	in	VDL.	This	was	ascertained	from	his	birth	record	 found	in	the	St.	Pauls	Shadwell	Parish	Register.	Born	in	1818,	one	of	Hannah	 Fenby’s	 five	 children,	 it	 is	 likely	 that	 the	 Fenby’s	 presented	 George	 as	 nine	 during	his	trial	in	the	hope	of	a	lenient	sentence.	 
While	there	are	unknowns	in	periods	of	George’s	life,	what	is	clear	is	that	 he	 lived	 an	 eventful	 seventy-five	 years.	 Marrying	 three	 times	 and	 having	 children	 with	 his	 first	 and	 second	 wives.	 George	 died	 in	 1893	 in	 Corryong,	 Victoria.	George	was	 survived	by	his	wife	Susan,	whom	 it	 is	 reported	 in	The	 Argus	died	aged	ninety-four,	in	Moonee	Ponds,	Victoria	(Argus,	August	1924,	 1).	 
	 Other	Records	 
Not	all	records	used	are	available	for	all	those	in	the	sample,	for	example,	the	 
Criminal	Petitions	for	Clemency	1819	–	1839	(HO	17	and	H0	18)	are	a	very	detailed	 
source	but	are	only	available	for	seventeen	per	cent	of	those	traced.	Yet,	when	they	 
are	available	they	provide	information	on	the	family	unit,	economy	and	general	 
background	of	the	offender.	These	records	provide	details	of	petitions	for	16,309	 
people	for	the	period	1817-1858.	Convicted	criminals,	or	their	family	and	friends,	 
made	a	petition	when	they	wanted	to	mitigate	the	sentence.	While	no	such	effort	 
was	made	for	either	George	or	his	mother,	Margret	Corbett’s	parents	appealed	to	 
the	authorities	on	her	behalf.		 
	 
	
 
	 Partial	Case	Study	of	Margaret	Corbett	 After	being	 indicted	 twice	 in	 the	 same	session	 for	 shop	 theft,	Margaret	was	 sentenced	to	transportation	aged	thirteen.	The	petition	allows	us	a	glimpse	into	 Margaret’s	home	life.	Her	parents,	Mary	and	John,	stressed	poverty,	youth	and	 the	fact	it	was	her	first	offence	in	order	to	gain	a	mitigation	of	her	sentence.	 They	further	claimed	that	Margaret	was	needed	to	help	maintain	the	family.	 Therefore,	 not	 only	 does	 this	 tell	 us	 about	 the	 family	 unit,	 but	 also	 the	 responsibility	 of	 her	 role	 within	 it.	 They	 also	 asserted	 that	 Margaret’s	 codefendant,	 Ellen	 Murphy,	 was	 ‘very	 bad’	 despite	 her	 age.	 Mary	 and	 John	 managed	to	get	several	signatures	on	the	petition	including	that	of	Margaret’s	 former	employer	who	promised	to	continue	to	employ	her	as	a	housemaid	if	 she	 was	 released.	 This	 then	 tells	 us	 about	 Margaret’s	 own	 independent	 economic	 life,	 but	 also	 we	 learn	 of	 her	 friendship	 ties	 and	 her	 parent’s	 disapproval	 of	 them.	 Ultimately	 the	 petition	 failed,	 and	 it	 was	 particularly	 ‘recommended	that	she	be	sent	out	of	the	country’	it	being	pointed	out	that	 she	was	‘rather	idle’.	The	exact	same	phrase	was	used	for	Ellen,	suggesting	the	 pair	 spent	 time	 together	while	 awaiting	 transportation.	 They	were	 certainly	 transported	together	on	the	same	ship	to	VDL	for	their	two	consecutive	seven	 year	sentences.	 
	 	 
Context	 
There	were	other	sources	not	fully	outlined	above,	which	were	used	in	this	research	 
including;	Permission-to-Marry	records	from	the	VDL	convict	department,	the	 
Surgeon	Superintendent	Medical	Journals	from	the	convict	transport,	and	even	 
correspondence	with	the	descendants	of	those	in	the	sample.	Together	with	the	 
varied	records	used	to	uncover	and	trace	individual	juveniles,	must	come	records	 
and	sources	to	put	those	lives	into	context.	The	life-events	and	narratives	of	these	 
juveniles	can	never	be	understood	if	they	are	not	contextualized.	In	order	to	do	this	 
primary	sources	including	the	Official	Statistical	Returns	and	correspondence	of	 
those	in	authority	were	turned	to.	This	allows	aspects	such	as	the	economy,	colonial	 
offending,	education,	health,	mortality	and	population	to	be	explored.	In	this	way	a	 
baseline	by	which	to	measure	the	life-outcomes	of	the	juvenile	transportees	was	 
produced	to	explore	what	life	outcome	a	juvenile	convict,	who	had	been	 
transported	to	VDL	in	the	nineteenth	century,	could	reasonably	expect?	Only	then	is	 
it	possible	to	approach	the	question	of	whether	they	were	able	to	settle	into	their	
 
post-transportation	lives	and	which	factors	affected	life-outcomes	(i.e.	gender	or	 
criminality).	And	how	did	their	lives	compare	with	others	in	the	colony	including	 
fellow	convicts	and	free	settlers?	 
	 This	method	of	concentrating	on	an	individual’s	life-course	is	not	without	its	 
criticism.	The	difficulty	of	concentrating	on	the	whole	life	of	these	juvenile	 
offenders	is	that	their	context	changed	over	time.	While	this	does	not	make	it	 
impossible	to	assess	the	‘success’	of	these	lives,	it	does	make	it	difficult	to	point	to	 
the	contributing	factors.	It	is	not	possible	to	produce	a	hierarchy	of	causation.	Since	 
the	working	factors	which	led	to	the	life-outcomes	of	the	juvenile’s	lives	are	the	 
sum	total	of	all	the	negative	and	positive	conditions	taken	together.	Meaning,	no	 
one	main	cause	or	turning-point	can	be	chosen.	Yet,	as	Gorovitz	(1965,	1969)	 
pointed	out,	differentiated	factors	can	still	be	chosen	as	the	most	important	 
contributing	factors.	These	are	not	arbitrary	choices,	but	they	are	not	objective	 
choices	either.	While	causation	is	ultimately	objective,	the	working	factors	chosen	 
here	will	be	partial	and	pragmatic.	However,	they	will	be	justified	through	a	full	 
outline	of	their	context,	and	explained	in	comparison	with	other	competing	 
contributing	factors	(Rigby	1995).	Certainly	the	context	of	each	individual	changed	 
over	time,	especially	given	that	the	period	in	question	runs	from	1816	to	the	turn	of	 
the	century	–	when	the	last	juvenile	was	known	to	have	died.	Consequently,	factors	 
acting	on	the	lives	of	these	juveniles	will	be	difficult	to	uncover	but	this	is	where	 
biographical	narratives	come	into	importance.	It	will	only	be	possible	to	point	to	the	 
major	contributing	factors	with	any	certainty;	through	a	thorough	understanding	of	 
the	whole	lives	of	these	juveniles	and	their	acting	background	factors.	 
	 In	order	to	fully	assess	the	different	factors	which	may	have	affected	these	juveniles	 
lives	it	will	be	important	to	break	the	sample	into	isolated	cohorts	where	possible.	 
This	is	because	these	juveniles	were	arriving	over	the	period	of	1818-1853	and	 
consequently	will	have	experienced	different	mechanisms	of	control,	economies	 
and	cultures.	This	will	allow	an	understanding	of	whether	individual	initiative	was	 
more	important	than	structural	constraints.	 
	
 
Conclusion	 
As	demonstrated	through	the	case	of	the	George	Fenby,	through	manually,	 
nominally	linking	a	variety	of	digitized	and	non-digitized	records,	it	is	possible	to	 
trace	juvenile	offenders	through	their	life	paths.	While	the	types	and	details	of	the	 
records	available	for	different	juveniles	will	vary,	when	taken	as	a	group	research	 
questions	can	be	approached.	Then,	when	trends	are	identified	biographies	can	be	 
formed	for	those	of	interest	in	order	to	obtain	a	more	detailed	understanding.	 
Based	on	the	life-course	methodologies	set	down	by	the	social	sciences,	and	 
following	closely	the	method	used	by	crime	historians,	this	research	aims	to	 
uncover	juvenile	offenders’	lives	in	order	to	explore	whether	they	settled	into	their	 
new	colonial	lives.	 
	 
	 
	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	 	
 
	 Chapter 4: Crime 
 This	chapter	will	look	at	the	pre-	and	post-transportation	criminal	careers	of	female	 
and	male	juveniles	in	order	to	assess	whether	they	were	able	to	turn	away	from	 
crime.	In	order	to	address	questions	of	recidivism	and	desistance,	juvenile	 
transportees9	will	be	compared	with	other	convicts	transported	to	VDL,	and	the	 
data	contextualised	by	comparison	with	the	Tasmanian	population	crimes	rates.	 
Such	comparisons	will	allow	the	following	questions	to	be	asked;	did	juvenile	 
transportees	commit	a	greater	number	of	offences	or	more	serious	offences	than	 
the	average	convict	arriving	in	VDL.	If	so	why	and	how	did	this	effect	their	life-
outcomes?	Also	of	importance	is	whether	they	were	able	to	turn	away	from	crime	 
after	they	had	served	their	transportation	sentence.	Firstly,	it	is	important	to	 
explore	the	background	of	these	juveniles	before	they	reached	the	colony	in	order	 
to	ascertain	whether	they	had	previous	convictions	and	the	severity	of	the	crimes	 
they	committed	in	England	-	because	it	is	the	whole	lives	which	are	important	to	 
this	research.	 
	 Pre-Transportation	 
	 Prior	to	their	transportation	sentence,	seventy-seven	per	cent	of	the	juvenile	 
transportees	had	previous	convictions	for	which	they	were	imprisoned.	These	 
juveniles	were	imprisoned	for	periods	between	five	days	and	six	months.	 
Imprisonment	was	often	the	first	step	before	transportation.	The	next	stage	in	the	 
punishment	process	for	these	juveniles,	if	they	re-offended,	was	often	a	sentence	of	 
transportation.	Even	so,	not	all	of	those	who	were	sentenced	were	transported.	 
Thirty-eight	per	cent	of	those	sentenced	had	their	sentence	commuted	from	 
transportation;	thirty-two	per	cent	of	female	juveniles	were	actually	transported,	 
compared	with	sixty-four	per	cent	of	males.	Despite	there	being	fewer	females	 
sentenced	to	transportation	in	the	first	place,	a	lower	proportion	of	females	were	 
																																																						 9	The	sample	of	juveniles	transported	to	VDL	for	this	research	will	here	and	hence	forth	be	referred	 to	as	‘juvenile	transportees’.	This	will	remain	the	case	even	when	referring	to	them	in	adulthood	as	 this	will	allow	a	differentiation	between	other	samples	discussed.	 	
 
transported	compared	with	males.	If	females	were	not	transported	they	were	 
generally	sent	to	Millbank	Prison	for	approximately	two	years.	Similarly,	males	 
spent	time	on	the	hulks	and	were	then	released.	The	majority	of	those	transported	 
to	Australia	arrived	in	VDL,	and	those	juveniles	are	the	concentration	of	this	 
research	(see	Appendix	No.1	which	includes	details	of	who	were	actually	 
transported	or	remained	in	the	UK).	 
	 Of	all	the	juveniles	who	were	actually	transported	to	Australia,	ninety-nine	per	cent	 
were	convicted	of	theft.	There	were	only	two	violent	offenders,	one	of	whom	was	 
traced	through	his	life.	Francis	MacDonald	was	charged	with	highway	robbery.	 
Convicted	in	1817,	during	the	course	of	the	offence	Francis	struck	the	victim	on	the	 
chest	and	put	the	victim	‘in	fear’.	This	happened	in	Somerset	Street	where	he	stole	 
a	watch,	its	chain	and	a	key	worth	just	under	five	pounds.	There	was	reportedly	a	 
mob	involved	but	only	Francis	was	convicted.	While	Francis	was	only	convicted	of	 
stealing	from	the	person,	this	offence	was	considered	serious	and	he	was	sentenced	 
to	transportation	for	life.	More	common	offences	were	pickpocketing	and	larceny.	 
While	these	offences	were	certainly	considered	serious	at	the	time,	more	serious	 
offences	which	involved	breaking	into	the	dwelling	house	or	physically	confronting	 
the	victim,	were	less	common	in	this	sample:	only	five	juveniles	were	convicted	of	 
burglary.	 
	 The	place	in	which	the	crime	occurred	influenced	how	serious	contemporaries	 
perceived	the	crime.	In	the	majority	of	cases	the	items	were	stolen	by	these	 
juveniles	from	‘public	spaces’.	That	is,	anywhere	outside	including	shops.	This	is	 
because	juveniles	were	welcome	to	enter	shops	without	direct	invitation	from	the	 
owner.	This	suggests	that	both	male	and	female	juveniles,	as	a	general	rule,	did	not	 
enter	unknown	spaces	to	commit	their	crimes.	Spaces	chosen	were	ones	which	 
juveniles	were	familiar	with.	A	typical	example,	Samuel	Linton	was	found	guilty	of	 
stealing	a	dead	goose	worth	seventy-two	pence	from	a	shop.	The	average	value	of	 
the	stolen	item	for	all	juveniles	was	332	pence,	which	would	have	been	a	fairly	large	 
sum.	However,	the	mode	is	thirty-six	pence.	This	is	because	the	data	is	not	normally	 
distributed.	The	mean	value	of	the	stolen	item	has	been	pushed	up	by	those	few	
 
offenders	who	stole	expensive	items.	This	is	not	to	ignore	those	few	juveniles	who	 
did	steal	items	worth	a	considerable	value,	but	it	is	to	put	them	in	context.	For	 
example,	James	Alder	was	indicted	for	stealing	to	the	value	of	twenty-two	pounds.	 
This	was	the	highest	amount	stolen	in	the	sample	and	was	made	up	of	the	following	 
items;	one	writing	desk,	five	watches,	twenty-three	spoons,	one	pair	of	sugar	tongs,	 
four	broaches,	six	seals	and	two	rings.	These	items	were	all	stolen	from	the	dwelling	 
house	and	resulted	in	fourteen	years’	transportation.	This	was	a	very	serious	 
offence	but	it	was	not	typical.	More	often	(in	over	fifty	per	cent	of	the	cases)	 
juveniles	stole	clothes,	fabric	or	handkerchiefs.	Yet,	some	did	steal	expensive	items	 
such	as	jewellery.	At	least	thirty-six	per	cent	of	juveniles	did	not	steal	items	which	 
were	of	immediate	use	to	them	such	as	food,	money	or	tools	to	work	with.	This	 
means	that	it	is	likely	that	what	they	did	steal,	was	stolen	in	order	to	either	 
exchange,	pawn	or	sell.	While	some	of	these	cases	may	have	been	unplanned,	 
others	would	have	been	stolen	with	a	purpose.	This	is	to	some	extent	organized	 
because	these	juveniles	planned	how	to	fence	their	goods,	whether	that	would	 
have	been	by	giving	it	to	their	neighbour	or	pawning	it	in	a	shop.	Despite	some	 
exceptions,	these	juveniles	generally	stole	relatively	inexpensive	items	from	public	 
spaces	but	they	also	stole	items	which	they	could	later	fence.	Many	juveniles	would	 
have	stolen	due	to	opportunity,	but	it	would	be	wrong	to	suggest	that	some	 
juveniles	did	not	steal	in	response	to	external	demand.	Notwithstanding	the	 
probable	fluidity	and	informality	of	these	exchanges,	a	market	of	goods	cannot	be	 
ignored	and	neither	can	juvenile	agency	(Shore	1999,	12).	While	there	is	some	 
organization,	given	the	circumstances	and	value	of	the	items,	these	crimes	were	 
petty.	However,	many	of	these	juveniles	were	not	first	time	offenders;	at	least	 
seventy-seven	per	cent	had	a	previous	conviction.		 
	 As	research	into	nineteenth-century	crime	history	has	increasingly	shown,	these	 
juvenile	crimes	were	not	always	perpetrated	due	to	poverty	and	distress.	However,	 
they	were	not	hardened	or	dangerous	criminals	either.	As	pointed	out	by	Shore	 
(1999,	47),	juvenile	offending	was	relatively	mundane,	but	the	causes	were	wide	 
and	varied.	Opportunity,	need,	desperation,	peer	pressure	and	excitement	all	 
played	a	role	in	juvenile	offending.	Importantly,	need	through	disease,	abuse	and	
 
neglect	did	not	necessarily	cause	offending,	since	offenders	with	relatively	stable	 
and	‘respectable’	backgrounds	existed	(Shore	1999,	47).	This	is	demonstrated	by	 
juvenile	offenders	whose	parents	arranged	petitions	on	their	behalf.	These	parents	 
often	point	to	their	own	stable	employment	and	family	arrangements.	 
Nevertheless,	there	was	a	contemporary	prevailing	stereotype	of	criminals	and	the	 
idea	of	a	‘criminal	class’	which	was	at	its	height	in	the	nineteenth	century,	and	 
juvenile	offenders	were	a	key	subject	in	the	debate	(Shore	1999,	35;	Muncie	2009,	 
54).	For	example,	pickpocketing,	a	common	juvenile	offence,	was	viewed	as	a	 
progressive	step	into	the	criminal	career	leading	it	to	be	a	capital	offence	until	1808.	 
In	reality	the	average	juvenile	offender	did	not	resemble	these	professional	groups	 
(Shore	1999,	55-59).	Still,	contemporaries	feared	that	juvenile	offenders	would	 
mature	into	burglars	and	this	was	embedded	in	many	arguments	for	penal	reform	 
and	‘colonial	retraining’	(Shore	1999,	61).	Therefore,	while	they	were	not	viewed	as	 
‘serious’	offenders,	they	were	associated	by	contemporaries	with	criminal	 
professionalism	and	as	being	a	breed	apart	(Wiener	1990,	31-33).	Added	to	this	was	 
the	belief	that	juveniles	could	be	saved	and	reincorporated	back	into	respectful	 
society	before	they	became	hardened	adult	criminals	(Shore	1999,	1).	This	all	fed	 
into	the	belief	that	transportation	was	necessary	to	deal	with	this	group	of	 
offenders.	 
	 The	magistrate	Francis	Const.	Esq.	wrote	in	1818	that	those	who	were	actually	 
transported	were	‘…seldom	[sent]	for	the	first	or	second	offence…’	(Evans	&	 
Nicholls	1984,	142).	This	magistrate	also	grouped	‘pickpockets’	with	‘atrocious’	and	 
‘violent’	criminals,	thus	highlighting	the	contemporary	view	of	pickpockets	as	being	 
viewed	as	a	particular	problem.	He	also	added:		 
Though	the	specific	offence	may	be	petty	larceny,	you	sometimes	on	 account	of	badness	of	 character,	 sentence	 them	to	 transportation	 -	 yes	it	is	not	so	much	the	crime,	as	being	well	known	to	be	dangerous	 characters	(cited	in	Evans	&	Nicholls	1984,	142).		 
	 This	magistrate	went	on	to	equate	‘badness	of	character’	with	previous	offences.	 
Certainly	the	majority	of	juvenile	transportees	had	previous	offences	and	many	 
were	pickpockets.	However,	it	was	by	no	means	certain	that	a	pickpocket	would	be	 
sentenced	to	transportation,	or	indeed	be	sent:	sixty-six	per	cent	of	pickpockets	
 
were	sentenced	to	transportation,	and	of	those	only	sixty-nine	per	cent	were	 
actually	sent.	 
Nunn	argues	that	bad	behaviour	and	production	on	the	hulk	was	linked	with	being	 
chosen	for	transportation.	Further	pointing	out	that	the	decision	of	removal	to	a	 
vessel	for	the	voyage	‘seems	to	have	resided	with	the	superintendent	and	his	staff’.	 
During	the	wait,	juveniles	sewed	prison	garments,	and	based	on	the	figures	 
presented	by	the	superintendent,	John	Capper,	‘production	levels	on	the	juvenile	 
hulks	appear	to	have	been	quite	substantial’.	For	example,	in	1825,	Capper	noted	 
that	the	boys	had	produced	15	500	items	of	clothing.	Nunn	argues	that	while	the	 
work	was	unskilled,	there	was	a	vested	interest	in	maintaining	the	most	reliable	 
workers	on	the	Euryalus.	Adding	it	was	‘normal	practice’	to	transport	male	juveniles	 
above	fourteen	years-of-age	(2015,	61).	While	this	research	has	sampled	juveniles	 
who	were	fourteen	years-of-age	and	below,	it	was	found	that	of	those	who	arrived	 
in	VDL,	the	majority	were	at	the	upper	end	of	the	age	range:	eighty	per	cent	of	the	 
males	(and	seventy-seven	per	cent	of	the	females)	were	aged	between	thirteen	and	 
fourteen,	but	clearly	some	were	younger.	Nunn	argues	that	for	those	under	 
fourteen	years-of-age	who	were	transported,	it	was	because	it	was	noted	on	their	 
indent	that	they	were	‘bad’	or	‘very	bad’.	Stating	that:	‘placing	certain	juveniles	on	 
transports	was	an	effective	strategy	of	getting	rid	of	the	most	disruptive	inmates’	 
(Nunn	2015,	61-62).	Of	the	male	juvenile	transportees	under	fourteen	years-of-age	 
who	were	transported	(there	were	eighteen),	there	was	one	juvenile	who	was	 
referred	to	as	‘bad’	and	another	as	‘indifferent	and	artful’.	All	others	were	described	 
in	positive	terms;	‘orderly’,	‘good’,	‘remarkably	well’	and	‘very	good’.	Therefore,	 
there	is	no	evidential	pattern	of	transporting	the	bad	or	non-productive	juveniles	in	 
this	sample.	Indeed,	Mr.	Samuel	Owen	(overseer	of	the	Fortitude	Hulk),	stated	that	 
those	with	the	worst	character	would	be	transported	first,	meaning	those	with	 
previous	‘serious’	offences.	Yet,	none	of	the	juvenile	transportees	had	serious	 
offences	and	the	majority	were	transported	(Evans	&	Nicholls	1984,	142-43).	Why	 
particular	juvenile	transportees	were	chosen	for	transportation	and	others	were	not	 
is	therefore	unclear.	What	is	clear,	is	that	juvenile	offenders	were	viewed	in	a	 
particularly	unfavourably	light	by	contemporaries.	
 
While	most	had	previous	convictions,	many	were	pickpockets	and	they	tended	to	be	 
at	the	upper	end	of	the	age-range,	this	was	by	no	means	necessary	to	be	 
transported.	The	question	remains;	did	their	offending	continue	in	the	colony	and	 
how	did	this	effect	their	lives?	 
	 Offending	Under	Sentence	 	 Male	Juvenile	Transportees	 Male	juvenile	transportees	committed	relatively	few	‘very	serious’	offences	(Table	 
No.1).	This	category	would	include	offences	from	burglary	and	bushranging,	to	 
murder.	There	was	an	average	of	eight	‘very	serious’	offences	per	100	convicts.	 
‘Serious’	offences	were	also	relatively	rare.	This	level	includes	all	thefts	and	 
property	offences	(not	including	burglary	which	is	considered	‘very	serious’)	and	all	 
violent	offences	against	the	person,	provided	the	victim	was	not	a	fellow	prisoner	 
(which	would	make	it	a	‘medium’	offence),	and	provided	it	was	neither	an	attempt	 
to	kill,	nor	did	it	result	in	a	death	(which	would	make	it	a	‘very	serious’	offence).	 
‘Serious’	offences	also	include	sexual	offences.	There	was	an	average	of	three	 
‘serious’	offences	per	convict.	‘Medium’	offences	include	all	offences	related	to	 
escaping	and	avoiding	or	neglecting	work.	While	these	offences	would	have	been	 
considered	relatively	serious	for	a	prisoner	to	commit	and	would	have	resulted	in	 
punishment,	they	are	also	regulatory	offences	which	only	convicts	by	dint	of	their	 
status	could	commit.	Other	offences	in	this	level	include	offences	which,	while	 
violent	in	nature,	are	either	only	threatened,	attempted	or	targeted	at	other	 
prisoners.	Any	consensual	sexual	offences	(not	including	‘unnatural’	acts)	are	also	 
considered	‘medium’	(for	example,	Margaret	Corbet	was	found	‘in	an	indecent	 
situation	with	a	man	in	the	privy’).	As	are	any	offences	involving	an	offender	being	 
somewhere	they	were	not	permitted,	for	example,	in	a	pub	or	on	a	racecourse.	 
‘Medium’	offences	were	the	most	common	level	of	offences.	There	was	an	average	 
of	eight	medium	offences	per	convict.	‘Minor’	offences	are	those	offences	such	as	 
obscene	language,	quarrelling	and	communicating	when	not	authorized.	There	was	 
an	average	of	four	‘minor’	offences	per	convict.	The	average	number	of	total	 
offences	per	male	juvenile	transportee	was	sixteen.

	 This	breakdown	of	offences	is	based	on	contemporary	views	of	crime.	What	they	 
reveal,	unsurprisingly,	is	that	juvenile	transportees	were	more	likely	to	commit	 
‘minor’	and	‘medium’	offences,	than	‘serious’	offences	-	and	that	they	were	even	 
less	likely	to	commit	‘very	serious’	offences.	However,	given	the	unique	 
circumstances	of	transportation	and	the	colonial	penal	settlement	of	VDL,	it	is	 
important	to	ascertain	how	this	compared	with	other	convicts.				 
	 Comparison	Group:	1-in-25	Male	Convicts	 
A	1-in-25	sample	was	systematically	chosen	from	all	male	convicts	arriving	in	VDL	 
whose	Police	Number	ended	06,	33,	56	and	83.	In	total	there	were	2405	convicts.	 
(This	1-in-25	sample	was	transcribed	by	Maxwell-Stewart	and	the	Founders	and	 
Survivors	team	but	coded	by	this	researcher).	The	records	used	were;	Con31,	Con32	 
and	Con33.	(See	Appendix	No.2	for	sampling	criteria).	For	the	purposes	of	this	 
analysis	the	sample	was	looked	at	as	a	whole	and	then	broken	into	the	following	 
groups	for	further	analysis:	the	assignment	period	convicts	who	arrived	between	 
1816	and	1840	(total	1281);	the	probation	period	convicts	who	arrived	between	 
1840	and	1853	(total	1124);	and	those	male	convicts	who	are	known	to	be	nineteen	 
years-of-age	and	under.	Offences	from	all	groups	were	categorized	into	levels	of	 
severity	as	described	for	the	male	juvenile	transportees	above.		 
	 
																																																						 10	The	offence	counts	are	taken	from	information	contained	in	their	Conduct	Records	only.	
 
By	taking	all	known	juvenile	convicts	from	the	1-in-25	sample	(those	nineteen	years-
of-age	and	under)11	it	was	possible	to	compare	them	with	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees	to	ascertain	if	they	were	representative.	Unfortunately,	the	ages	of	 
convicts	in	the	1-in-25	sample	are	only	provided	for	those	arriving	in	the	probation	 
period.	Consequently,	these	juveniles	arrived	from	1840	onwards	(this	gave	177	 
male	juvenile	convicts).	This	is	an	issue	because	the	male	juvenile	transportees	 
arrived	from	1817	to	1848	and	therefore	many	arrived	in	the	assignment	period.	 
The	treatment	of	adult	convicts	under	these	two	different	systems,	the	assignment	 
and	the	probation	period,	was	very	different.	However,	while	it	was	not	always	the	 
case,	juvenile	convicts	were	largely	treated	differently	from	adult	convicts.	 
Therefore,	the	changing	system	of	treatment	for	convicts	affected	juveniles	less	 
than	adults.	This	was	not	only	because	of	their	placement	at	Point	Puer.	It	was	also	 
practice,	when	juveniles	could	not	be	assigned,	to	keep	them	in	the	prisoners’	 
barracks.	They	were	kept	in	the	barracks	for	practicality	and	not	as	an	additional	 
punishment.	12		 
	 
																																																						 11	The	upper	age	limit	of	nineteen	years-of-age	was	chosen	for	this	sample	for	a	number	of	reasons.	 Firstly,	the	upper	age	limit	for	those	held	at	Point	Puer	was	twenty	years-of-age	but	nineteen	was	the	 oldest	age	at	which	the	juveniles	in	my	sample	arrived	in	VDL,	and	secondly,	those	sent	on	juvenile	 transports,	including	the	Lord	Goderich	and	the	Frances	Charlotte,	included	‘juveniles’	of	nineteen	 years-of-age	and	possibly	older	(Jordan	1985,	1095).	The	upper	limit	in	which	a	‘juvenile’	was	classed	 as	a	juvenile	therefore	varied.	(This	is	further	demonstrated	in	Chapter	3	under	the	discussion	on	 sampling).	As	such,	it	was	decided,	when	categorising	the	1-in-25	juveniles,	to	use	the	oldest	age	at	 which	a	juvenile	transportee	in	my	sample	arrived	–	which	was	nineteen	years-of-age.	 12	This	table	includes	offences	recorded	in	Conduct	Records	only.	For	details	of	the	1-in-25	sample	 see	Appendix	No.2.	
 
	 Findings	 
As	can	be	seen	in	Table	No.2,	male	juvenile	transportees	committed	more	offences	 
than	any	other	comparison	group.	The	differences	between	the	1-in-25	sample	 
groups,	when	broken	up	into	probation	and	assignment	period	convicts,	are	 
minimal.	There	was,	slightly	less	offending	in	the	probation	period	group.	Given	that	 
the	probation	period	would	have	resulted	in	more	supervision	it	was	expected	that	 
there	would	have	been	more	offending	(specifically	minor	offending)	in	this	group.	 
This	was	not	the	case.	Under	the	probation	period	there	were	fewer	‘minor’	and	 
‘medium’	offences	than	under	the	assignment	period.	The	level	of	‘serious’	 
offending	was	the	same	but	the	level	of	‘very	serious’	offending	was	slightly	higher	 
in	the	probation	group	(0.036).	 
	 The	1-in-25	juvenile	convicts	committed	more	offences,	on	average,	than	the	 
general	convicts	in	both	the	probation	and	assignment	periods.	However,	they	still	 
did	not	commit	as	many	offences	as	the	juvenile	transportees.	 
	 When	comparing	juvenile	transportees	to	the	whole	1-in-25	male	sample	we	can	 
ascertain	which	group	had	committed	more	offences.	Overall	there	were	more	 
offences	per	juvenile	transportee	than	in	all	comparison	groups.	In	fact,	there	were	 
over	twice	as	many	but	there	are	some	provisos.	The	general	convict	population,	as	 
already	noted,	was	a	1-in-25	random	sample.	However,	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees	were	sampled	differently.	They	were	initially	systematically	chosen	 
from	the	Old	Bailey	Proceedings.	However,	only	those	who	were	able	to	be	traced	 
into	freedom	were	then	included,	not	simply	whether	they	had	a	Conduct	Record	or	 
not,	as	in	the	1-in-25	sample.	There	is	likely	to	be	an	over-representation	of	 
offending	in	the	juvenile	transportee	sample	caused	by	this	sampling	process	(see	 
Chapter	Three).		While	tracing	was	sometimes	assisted	because	of	something	as	 
innocuous	as	an	uncommon	name,	other	times	it	was	due	to	an	extraordinary	life.	 
For	example,	James	Hudson	was	locally	admired	for	his	religious	work	which	led	to	a	 
very	detailed	obituary	in	the	newspaper	(Case	Study	No.19).	Perhaps	more	 
challenging,	it	could	also	be	because	of	a	greater	number	of	offences	or	more	 
serious	offending,	and	therefore	more	documentation.	As	in	the	case	of	Charles	
 
Brewer	(Case	Study	No.3)	who	was	repeatedly	in	the	newspapers	due	to	his	high	 
profile	offending	career	as	a	bushranger	and	pirate.	These	cases	are	exceptional.	 
Nevertheless,	it	is	inevitable	that	those	with	more	offences	will	be	more	readily	 
identified	and	therefore	more	readily	traced.	Consequently,	the	male	juvenile	 
transportee	sample	may	over-represent	the	offending	of	juvenile	convicts	 
transported	to	VDL.		 
	 
In	every	category	the	sampled	juveniles	have	a	higher	rate	of	offending	per	convict	 
than	all	other	comparison	groups.	However,	there	is	only	a	slight	difference	with	 
regards	to	‘very	serious’	offences.	Specifically,	3	in	100	convicts	of	the	1-in-25	 
convict	population	committed	a	‘very	serious’	offence,	compared	to	8	in	100	of	 
juvenile	transportees.	Therefore,	given	there	is	a	higher	rate	of	offending	in	the	 
juvenile	transportee	group	than	in	the	juvenile	convict	population	as	a	whole	(and	 
juveniles	were	only	slightly	more	likely	to	commit	one	of	these	‘very	serious’	 
offences),	the	juvenile	transportees	were	not	markedly	more	likely	to	commit	‘very	 
serious’	offences	as	compared	with	the	whole	convict	population.	However,	juvenile	 
transportees	were	more	likely	to	offend	overall.	While	it	is	difficult	to	uncover	how	 
much	this	rate	is	increased	by	the	sampling	process,	since	there	are	over	twice	as	 
many	offences	on	average	per	person,	these	juvenile	transportees	did	offend	more	 
than	the	general	convict	population.	Yet,	this	greater	rate	of	offending	was	caused	 
by	‘minor’	and	‘medium’,	and	to	a	lesser	extent	‘serious’	level	offending	–	not	‘very	 
serious’	level	offending.		 
	 Summary	 
Why	did	this	group	of	juvenile	transportees	offend	more	than	both	the	general	 
convict	population	and	other	juvenile	convicts?	There	is	the	possibility	that,	as	 
modern	criminologists	have	theorised,	the	more	severe	the	punishment	for	juvenile	 
offenders	the	more	likely	they	were	to	go	on	to	repeat	offending	(McAra	&	McVie	 
2007).	The	impact	of	being	transported	away	from	family,	friends	and	familiarity,	 
may	have	been	greater	on	juvenile	transportees	than	their	adult	counterparts.	 
Certainly	both	juvenile	groups	offended	more.	However,	on	average	the	juvenile	 
transportees	have	seven	more	offences	per	convict	than	the	juvenile	1-in-25	
 
sample.	There	may	be	a	number	of	reasons	for	this.	As	noted,	those	in	the	 
assignment	period	offended	more	than	those	in	the	probationary	period,	and	while	 
the	juvenile	transportees	arrived	from	both	periods,	the	1-in-25	juveniles	arrived	in	 
the	probationary	period	only.	The	juvenile	transportees	and	the	1-in-25	samples	 
also	differ	in	other	important	aspects.	The	juvenile	transportees	were	all	from	 
London,	whereas	the	1-in-25	sample	were	from	all	over	Britain	including	Ireland	and	 
rural	areas.	Rural	offenders	transported,	in	particular,	have	been	shown	to	go	on	to	 
less	offending	in	the	colony	in	comparison	with	London	convicts	(Godfrey	&	 
Maxwell-Stewart,	2016).	While	the	juvenile	transportees	were	all	convicted	of	theft,	 
the	1-in-25	sample	encompassed	a	wider	variety	of	offences	which	led	to	their	 
transportation.	In	many	cases	this	would	have	been	due	to	‘serious’	and	‘very	 
serious’	offences.	Criminologists	have	found	serious	offenders	tend	not	to	go	on	to	 
be	persistent	offenders	(Godfrey	et	al	2010).	Lastly,	juveniles	also	inevitably	spent	a	 
longer	period	in	the	colony	since	they	were	sent	at	a	younger	age.	Juveniles	would	 
have	received	the	same	range	of	sentence	lengths	as	their	adult	counterparts.	 
However,	since	Conduct	Records	were	often	updated	with	convictions	even	after	 
initial	freedom	–	it	is	reasonable	to	assume	they	potentially	had	more	time	to	 
offend	in	the	colony.	Consequently,	the	rate	of	offending	is	important	and	will	be	 
explored	later	in	this	chapter.	 
	 Whilst	sampling	bias	maybe	at	play,	since	the	1-in-25	sample	was	randomly	chosen,	 
and	also	had	a	higher	number	of	offences	than	any	other	group	-	juvenile	males	did	 
commit	more	offences	in	VDL	than	their	adult	counterparts.	Accepting	that	the	 
juvenile	transportees	had	more	offences	than	the	whole	juvenile	population,	allows	 
the	exploration	of	what	is	different	about	this	group.	What	characteristics	do	these	 
male	juvenile	transportees	have	in	common	which	contributed	to	their	increased	 
offending?	And	if	it	is	accepted	that	this	group	consists	of	some	of	the	most	 
persistent	offenders	while	under	VDL	colonial	oversight,	were	they	able	to	desist	 
from	crime	afterwards	and	settle	into	colonial	life	despite	it?		 
	 	 	 	
 
Female	Juvenile	Transportees	 The	females,	unlike	their	male	counterparts,	did	not	go	through	a	second	sampling	 
stage.	All	females	fitting	the	criteria	were	traced.13	As	can	be	seen	in	Table	No.3,	 
they	committed	no	‘very	serious’	offences	and	relatively	few	‘serious	offences’.	The	 
most	common	offence	level	was	of	‘medium’	severity.

Comparison	Group:	Male	convicts	 
Female	juvenile	transportees	committed	fewer	offences	overall	than	male	juvenile	 
transportees	in	all	but	one	severity	level.	They,	on	average,	committed	slightly	more	 
‘medium’	offences	than	their	male	counterparts.	They	also	committed	more	 
offences	than	the	male	1-in-25	samples,	including	juveniles.		 
	 The	female	juvenile	transportee	arrivals	straddled	the	two	convict	management	 
periods,	the	assignment	and	probationary	period.	However,	this	shift	in	 
management	structures	is	of	lesser	concern	for	the	females	because	while	the	 
management	of	female	convicts	did	undergo	modifications	over	time,	the	shift	from	 
assignment	to	probationary	management	was	less	dramatic	for	females	than	males.		 
	 Comparison	Group:	1-in-25	Female	Convicts	 
When	comparing	Table	No.3	and	No.4,	the	female	juvenile	transportees	committed	 
more	offences	on	average	per	convict	than	any	break	down	of	the	1-in-25	female	 
sample.	The	female	juvenile	transportees	did	not	have	any	‘very	serious’	offences	 
recorded	against	them	in	their	Conduct	Record.	Similarly,	only	one	adult	female	in	 
the	probation	period	did.	Surprisingly,	the	probationary	juveniles	committed	the

least	offences.	The	female	juvenile	transportees	committed	over	three-times	as

The	1-in-25	category	which	committed	the	most	offences	per	convict	was	the	 
assignment	period.	The	female	convicts	in	the	probation	period	committed	 
approximately	half	the	number	of	offences	committed	by	the	females	in	the	 
assignment	period.	Moreover,	the	probationary	period	adults	committed	more	 
offences	than	the	juvenile	females	in	the	same	period.	While	the	assignment	period	 
saw	the	greater	number	of	offences	per	convict,	the	number	of	‘serious’	offences	is	 
slightly	higher	for	the	probationary	adults	(0.18).		 
	 When	comparing	the	1-in-25	female	convicts	with	the	1-in-25	male	convicts,	before	 
categorization,	there	are	seven	offences	per	male	convict,	and	six	offences	per	 
female	convict.	When	broken	into	categories	both	males	and	females	have	on	 
average	eight	offences	per	convict.	However,	the	female	probation	period	convicts	 
commit	two	fewer	offences	per	convict	than	the	male	probation	period	convicts.	 
Yet,	the	biggest	disparity	appears	in	the	category	of	juvenile	probation	period
