Summary	 
While	the	female	juvenile	transportees	committed	no	‘very	serious’	offences,	they	 
committed	more	offences	than	all	other	samples	excepting	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees.	Moreover,	they	committed	considerably	more	offences	than	other	 
female	convicts	transported	in	the	probation	period.	As	with	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees,	a	big	difference	in	these	groups	is	their	geographical	origin.	The	1-in-
25	sample	arrived	from	all	over	Britain,	both	rural	and	urban	areas,	whereas	the	 
female	juvenile	transportees	were	all	transported	from	London.	Historians,	 
including	Godfrey	and	Maxwell-Stewart	(2016),	have	argued	that	convicts	sent	from	 
certain	areas,	especially	London,	were	‘worse’	with	regards	to	behaviour	and	skills.	 
Was	this	the	case	for	these	juvenile	transportees	or	are	there	other	explanations	 
such	as	the	differing	management	of	these	convicts	and	different	expectations	 
placed	on	them?	Female	juvenile	transportees	were	also	younger	than	the	 
probationary	female	juvenile	group.	Did	the	fact	that	they	came	from	London	and	 
had	a	generally	younger	profile	mean	that	they	were	less	skilled	and	therefore	 
struggled	more	in	assignment,	leading	to	more	offences	being	recorded	against	 
them	(see	Chapter	Six)?	The	types	of	offences	these	juveniles	were	committing	 
under	sentence	is	just	as	important	as	the	number.	 
	 Common	Offences	 
	 In	all	samples,	being	temporarily	absent	was	the	most	common	offence.	This	 
includes	being	absent	for	the	day	but	coming	back	of	their	own	accord,	and	missing	 
muster	(not	escaping	or	trying	to	permanently	abscond).	While	it	is	the	most	 
common	offence	in	every	sample,	it	is	also	more	common	per	female	juvenile	 
transportee	than	any	other	sample.		 16	 
																																																						 16	This	table	contains	offences	taken	from	the	Conduct	Records	only.	
 
	 The	type	of	offending	by	female	juvenile	transportees’	was	less	varied	and	it	was	 
centred	on	not	being	where	they	should.	This	is	demonstrated	in	the	case	of	Susan	 
Campbell	(Case	Study	No.4).	Moreover,	Table	No.5	further	reveals	that	the	most	 
common	female	offence	was	insolence	and	misconduct.	Therefore,	female	juvenile	 
transportees’	most	common	offences	were	behavioural.	There	were	female-specific	 
offences,	i.e.	offences	which	only	female	convicts	could	commit.	For	example,	 
having	an	illegitimate	child	and	prostitution.	However,	they	were	relatively	 
uncommon	amongst	the	female	juvenile	transportees.	Only	two	were	known	to	 
have	an	illegitimate	child	and	be	punished	for	it	through	imprisonment	in	the	 
female	factory.	And	there	were	only	four	incidences	of	females	being	in	a	brothel	or	 
being	a	prostitute.	All	other	offences	were	not	female	specific.	However,	there	are	 
some	nuances.	A	female	could	also	be	brought	up	before	the	courts	by	her	husband.	 
For	example,	in	the	case	of	Caroline	Watson,	who	struck	her	husband	in	the	 
presence	of	another	man.	As	a	result,	this	offence	was	included	in	her	Conduct	 
Record	and	she	was	punished.	As	highlighted	by	Kavanagh	and	Snowden,	what	was	 
private	for	the	general	population	was	subject	to	scrutiny	for	female	convicts	(2015,	 
201).	Since	none	of	the	male	juvenile	transportees	were	assigned	to	wives,	no	
 
similar	offences	were	committed	by	males	while	under	sentence.	Although	George	 
Pickering	(Case	Study	No.5)	did	go	on	to	be	punished	for	domestic	violence	after	 
freedom.	 
	 Like	the	females,	common	male	offences	were	usually	not	felonies.	In	fact,	a	 
common	theme	of	these	offences	is	that	they	are	all	related	to	regulatory	offences	 
such	as	absences	and	being	drunk.	Refusal	to	work	is	also	relatively	common	in	the	 
1-in-25	sample	but	does	not	appear	in	the	top	five	of	the	male	and	female	 
transportees	most	common	offences.	Moreover,	storing	contraband	was	common	 
for	both	the	male	juvenile	transportees’	and	the	probationary	juveniles.	This	 
involved	having	possessions,	such	as	clothing,	food	or	tobacco	without	 
authorisation.	This	does	not	appear	commonly	in	any	other	group.	It	is	unclear	 
whether	these	juvenile	males	were	more	likely	to	have	contraband	or	alternatively	 
were	more	likely	to	be	punished	for	it.	 
	 Summary	 
The	national	statistics	of	VDL	show	a	rise	in	minor	offences,	such	as	those	common	 
offences	described	above,	and	contemporaries,	as	shown	by	the	statistical	returns,	 
attributed	them	to	convicts	(Anon	1836).	Certainly,	juvenile	transportees	did	 
commit	many	non-serious	offences.	However,	the	same	statistical	returns	also	 
posited	that	this	was	due	to	an	increase	in	the	detection	and	punishment	of	minor	 
offences	largely	attributed	to	the	introduction	of	the	new	police	in	1827-1828.	The	 
increase	in	all	minor	offences,	particularly	from	1827,	was	also	attributed	to	the	 
implementation	of	police	magistrates	(Anon	1836).	The	suggestion	here	is	that	 
minor	crime	did	not	increase,	it	was	simply	more	efficiently	detected.	Given	the	 
minor	nature	of	much	of	the	juvenile	transportees’	offending,	it	may	be	that	many	 
of	these	offences	were	recorded	due	to	similar	administrative	reasons.	Juvenile	 
transportees	were	more	likely	to	be	in	an	institution	and	therefore	be	subject	to	 
easier	detecting	and	processing	of	offences.	It	is	also	possible	that	masters	were	 
more	prone	to	seek	punishment	of	juveniles	than	adults	reflecting	societal	norms.	 
The	chastisement	of	children	was	accepted	in	nineteenth-century	society.	 
Moreover,	there	may	have	been	a	relationship	between	the	skills	of	convicts	and	
 
the	likelihood	of	punishment.	The	more	skill	and	experience	a	convict	had	the	more	 
valuable	they	were	to	an	employer	and	therefore	the	more	likely	the	master	would	 
be	to	overlook	‘minor’	and	‘medium’	level	offending.	When	the	annual	maintenance	 
bill	for	convicts	rose	in	VDL,	the	number	of	convicts	sentenced	to	hard	labour	in	 
road	and	chain	gangs	by	magistrates’	benches	increased:	‘The	effect	was	to	shift	the	 
costs	of	maintaining	convicts	from	the	private	to	the	public	sector	at	the	points	 
when	it	became	most	advantageous	to	disinvest	in	unfree	workers.’	As	Maxwell-
Stewart	points	out,	this	trend	exposes	an	important	issue.	Conduct	Records	are	not	 
the	complete	list	of	all	indiscretions	but	are	instead	the	product	of	a	complex	set	of	 
factors	culminating	in	a	decision	to	prosecute.	That	decision	could	be	affected	by	 
many	things	including	the	convict’s	worth;	thus	convicts	with	skills	that	were	not	in	 
demand	in	the	colonial	economy	were	at	a	greater	risk	of	punishment.	This	is	why	 
the	number	of	charges	brought	against	serving	prisoners	was	inversely	correlated	 
with	colonial	wage	rates	(2016,	426).	Juvenile	transportees	arrived	with	fewer	skills	 
and	certainly	less	work	experience	than	many	of	their	adult	counterparts,	thus	 
increasing	the	chances	that	masters	would	be	willing	to	seek	their	punishment	in	 
order	to	gain	a	replacement	servant.	This	would	lead	to	more	offences	being	 
reported	and	processed	for	juvenile	convicts.	This	might	especially	be	the	case	for	 
convicts	from	urban	areas,	which	all	the	juvenile	transportees	were,	who	were	now	 
expected	to	undertake	unfamiliar	rural	work	(see	Chapter	Six).	 
	 Given	that	juvenile	transportees	were	managed	differently	under	sentence	than	 
their	adult	counterparts,	which	may	have	led	to	an	increased	chance	of	reporting	 
offences	of	the	former,	offences	committed	outside	the	Conduct	Record	were	 
explored.	This	will	allow	for	a	fuller	picture	of	the	offending	of	these	juvenile	 
transportees	when	removed	from	the	VDL	colonial	conduct	recording.	 
		 Offences	Not	Recorded	in	Conduct	Record	 	 The	offending	patterns	so	far	discussed	were	extracted	only	from	the	Conduct	 
Records	and	are	therefore	not	all	the	offences	committed	by	the	juvenile	 
transportees.	If	a	juvenile	transportee	migrated	or	had	long	periods	of	time	before	 
they	reoffended	their	Conduct	Records	were	not	updated.	However,	such	
 
information	can	be	tracked	down	through	the	newspapers	and	official	records	of	 
other	colonial	territories	in	Australia.	There	are	104	offences	by	twenty-four	 
juvenile	transportees	(three	of	which	were	female)	which	were	found	in	this	way.	 
These	are	not	the	only	offences	committed	after	freedom,	these	are	the	offences	 
which	were	committed	that	are	not	included	in	the	Conduct	Record.		 
	 Table	No.6:	Juvenile	Transportee	Offences	Not	in	Conduct	Record	Categorized	by	 
Severity17	 		 All	 Minor		 Medium		 Serious		 Very	Serious		 
All		 104	 10	 45	 45	 4	 
Males		 91	 5	 39	 43	 4	 
Females		 13	 5	 6	 2	 0	 	 Male	Juvenile	Transportees	 
As	can	be	seen	in	Table	No.6,	there	were	ninety-one	offences	committed	by	male	 
juvenile	transportees	that	are	not	included	in	their	Conduct	Record.	Taking	away	 
those	juvenile	transportees	who	died	under	their	initial	servitude	(a	total	of	twelve),	 
on	average	there	was	1.03	offences	per	male	juvenile	transportee.	However,	only	 
twenty-one	males	went	on	to	have	offences	recorded	against	them	outside	of	their	 
Conduct	Record.	The	majority	of	these	offences	were	of	‘medium’	and	‘serious’	 
severity.	This	is	because	‘minor’	offences	were	less	likely	to	reach	the	newspapers	 
due	to	their	less	sensational	nature.	Moreover,	as	the	severity	of	the	offences	 
increased,	the	details	included	in	the	articles	increased,	and	consequently	the	more	 
readily	identifiable	the	offender	becomes.	Therefore,	despite	every	effort	-	it	is	 
impossible	to	assert	that	all	offences	outside	of	the	Conduct	Record	were	either	 
contempariously	recorded	or	subsequently	found.	However,	it	is	reasonable	to	 
assert	that	it	becomes	less	likely	an	offence	is	missed	as	the	severity	of	the	offence	 
increases.	It	follows	then	that	the	four	‘very	serious’	offences,	which	were	only	 
committed	by	male	juvenile	transportees,	are	likely	to	be	the	only	‘very	serious’	 
offences.	These	include	burglary,	bushranging,	piracy	and	murder.	The	latter	was	 
committed	by	James	McAllister	(Case	Study	No.6),	and	the	former	three	offences	 
																																																						 17	The	offences	are	taken	from	newspaper	reports	and	other	records	not	including	VDL	Conduct	 Records.	
 
were	committed	by	one	offender,	Charles	Brewer	(Case	Study	No.3).	Therefore,	 
while	there	are	four	‘very	serious’	offences,	there	are	only	two	‘very	serious’	 
offenders.	There	are	forty-three	‘serious’	offences	committed	by	male	juvenile	 
transportees	outside	of	their	Conduct	Records.	These	include:	theft	(fifteen	 
incidences);	absconding	(nine	incidences);	presenting	a	weapon	(one	incident)	e.g.	 
gun	or	knife;	assaulting	an	authority	figure	(six	incidences)	e.g.	a	member	of	the	 
watch,	police	or	overseer;	violence	towards	another	person	(seven	incidences)	i.e.	a	 
free	person,	not	their	master	or	another	convict	or	member	of	authority;	robbery	 
(two	incidences);	uttering,	forging,	defrauding	(one	incident);	wounding	(one	 
incident);	riot	or	mutinous	conduct	(one	incident).		 
	 It	is	clear	that	offending	outside	of	the	Conduct	Record	is	concentrated	in	a	small	 
number	of	these	juvenile	transportees.	Moreover,	repeated	offending	under	the	 
VDL	administrative	gaze	was	not	necessarily	indicative	of	offending	when	removed	 
from	said	gaze	or	vice	versa.	This	is	exemplified	in	the	case	of	George	Pickering	who	 
had	few	offences	in	his	Conduct	Record,	but	went	on	to	commit	a	number	of	 
offences	after	migration.	 
	 Case	Study	No.5:	George	Pickering	 Aged	thirteen	George	was	convicted	in	1840	of	simple	larceny.	He	stole	a	pair	 of	shoes	worth	one	shilling	and	nine	pence	while	he	was	living	in	Whitechapel.	 George	pleaded	guilty	and	was	given	seven	years’	transportation.	It	was	not	his	 first	offence.	George	had	been	previously	convicted	and	punished	with	six	days’	 imprisonment,	and	before	that	he	had	been	acquitted	of	another	crime.	He	was	 no	 stranger	 to	 the	 authorities.	 His	 father,	 Thomas,	 petitioned	 on	 his	 behalf	 through	 stressing	his	 youth,	 good	character,	 and	blaming	bad	and	designing	 associates.	The	petition	also	pointed	out	Thomas’	own	good	character	and	how	 he	had	done	everything	to	bring	up	his	family	on	an	honest	path.	He	further	 pleaded	 that	George	was	 suffering	 from	remorse	and	wished	 to	 retrieve	his	 character	and	become	a	useful	member	of	society.	Moreover,	he	stated	that	he	 had	heard	 in	 some	cases	 that	mercy	was	 shown	on	 the	grounds	of	 age	and	 hoped	this	would	be	extended	to	George	by	sending	him	to	Parkhurst	Prison	 and	 not	 transporting	 him	 to	 Australia.	 This	 would	 allow	 for	 George	 to	 be	 restored	to	the	‘bosom	of	his	family’	upon	his	release.	The	petition	had	several	 signatories	 -	 including	 the	 prosecutor.	 Nevertheless,	 the	 petition	 failed	 and	 George	was	separated	from	his	family.	He	would	never	see	his	mother	Jane	and	 his	father,	who	was	a	wine	cooper,	or	his	siblings	again.	In	September	1841	the	
 
Lord	Goderich	set	sail	from	Portsmouth	on	a	four-month	voyage	to	Hobart	with	 George	in	the	hold.	 
When	 George	 arrived,	 he	 could	 neither	 read	 nor	 write,	 he	 was	 a	 protestant,	and	was	described	as	‘orderly’	and	‘indifferent’	by	the	hulk	and	ship	 authorities	respectively.	His	first	offence	in	the	colony	was	not	until	April	1847,	 when	he	‘willfully’	assaulted	George	Moore.	For	this	offence	he	received	one	 month’s	 imprisonment	with	hard	 labour.	Later	that	year	he	was	recorded	as	 fighting	in	a	public	street	and	representing	himself	as	free,	for	which	he	was	 given	six	days’	solitary	confinement.	Both	of	these	offences	were	after	he	had	 received	a	ToL	(which	was	in	September	1846).	George	was	free-by-servitude	 in	1847	but	despite	this	initial	low	offending	rate,	he	later	went	on	to	have	many	 more	offences.	 
In	 January	 1856,	 George	 was	 tried	 at	 Melbourne	 Police	 Court	 and	 convicted	of	assault	and	sentenced	to	three	months’	imprisonment	with	hard	 labour.	In	1857	he	was	charged	with	stealing	fourteen	shillings	from	the	bar	of	 Manchester	hotel	where	he	had	been	employed	as	one	of	the	bar	men.	Due	to	 insufficient	 evidence	 the	 case	 was	 dismissed.	 In	 September	 1859	 he	 was	 recorded	as	being	‘idle	and	disorderly’	and	given	twelve	months’	imprisonment	 with	hard	 labour.	 In	 June	1864	he	was	convicted	of	a	more	serious	offence,	 malicious	wounding,	for	which	he	was	given	two	years’	imprisonment.	He	had	 been	 found	 guilty	 of	 stabbing	 James	 Miller	 with	 an	 Oyster	 Knife.	 Both	 the	 accused	and	the	victim	claimed	they	were	not	involved	in	the	incident.	It	was	 two	 witnesses	 who	 said	 they	 saw	 the	 struggle.	 Consequently,	 George	 was	 committed	for	trial	and	Miller	was	detained	for	stealing	boots	which	instigated	 the	 altercation	 (The	 Cornwall	 Chronicle	 May	 1862,	 3).	 The	 newspapers	 described	this	as	a	 ‘serious	case	of	stabbing’.	A	gathering	mob	attracted	the	 attention	 of	 Sergeant	 Lewis.	 As	 he	 approached	 he	 heard	 several	 of	 the	 spectators	shout	out	‘the	man	is	stabbed’,	Miller	was	lying	on	the	ground	with	 a	 deep	wound	 on	 his	 head	 and	was	 covered	 in	 blood.	When	 Pickering	was	 searched	an	oyster	knife	was	found.	Miller	was	sent	to	the	hospital	where	it	 was	ascertained	he	had	also	been	stabbed	 in	 the	back	of	his	 right	 shoulder.	 Though	serious,	they	were	not	dangerous	injuries	and	he	recovered	(The	Age	 May	1862,	5).	George	had	only	been	recently	discharged	from	prison,	and	the	 prosecutor	 himself	was	 a	 ToL	man.	When	 in	 court	Miller	 had	 forgotten	 the	 circumstances	of	the	assault.	The	constable	who	had	arrested	Pickering	stated	 that	 he	 knew	 the	 details	 very	 well	 at	 the	 time	 and	 so	 Miller	 was	 held	 in	 contempt	of	court	to	sharpen	his	memory	(The	Age	March	1862,	6).	 
George	 was	 repeatedly	 in	 trouble	 for	 violent	 behaviour.	 The	 Age	 reported	that;	on	hearing	he	was	going	to	be	arrested	he	declared	he	would	 not	go	without	a	 fight	and	gave	a	violent	blow	to	the	officer’s	chest.	 In	 ‘self	 defence’	he	wielded	himself	vigorously	with	the	help	of	his	friends,	who	were	
 
described	 as	pickpockets	 and	oyster	men.	 Eventually	 he	was	hauled	off.	His	 wife,	at	whose	instance	he	was	arrested,	appeared	against	him.	George	had	just	 been	 released	 from	 the	gaol	 and	went	directly	 to	 the	house	where	his	wife	 resided	and	brutally	ill-treated	her.	His	wife,	who	supported	herself	by	washing,	 had	lots	of	washing	in	the	house	which	George	threw	out	into	the	streets.	They	 had	 two	 children,	 one	 of	 whom	 had	 their	 leg	 broken	 by	 George	 in	 a	 fit	 of	 drunkenness	on	a	previous	occasion.	George	was	sentenced	to	three	months’	 hard	labour	and	at	the	conclusion	of	the	term	was	ordered	to	pay	sureties	of	 twenty-five	pounds	to	keep	the	peace	towards	his	wife	for	twelve	months	(The	 Age	April	1856,	3).	This	would	not	be	the	last	incident	of	domestic	violence.	In	 March	1865	he	was	convicted	of	stealing	money	from	the	person	at	the	General	 Sessions	 in	 Melbourne	 and	 given	 five	 years	 on	 the	 roads.	 In	 1871	 he	 was	 convicted	of	stealing	a	blanket	and	given	three	months’	 imprisonment.	Later	 that	year	he	was	convicted	of	‘intent	to	commit	a	felony’	by	Police	G	Wragge	 Esq	JP.	This	resulted	in	twelve	months’	full	time	hard	labour.	This	was	followed	 by	a	‘robbery	in	company’	in	1875	for	which	he	was	given	seven	years	on	the	 public	works.	 Subsequently,	 he	was	 convicted	of	 the	 less	 serious	 offence	of	 being	 ‘drunk	 and	 disorderly’	 for	 which	 he	 was	 given	 only	 three	 days’	 imprisonment.	 	 Domestic	violence	was	a	repeat	offence	by	George	and	took	varied	forms.	 As	already	noted	George	brutally	assaulted	his	daughter	(The	Argus	July	1852,	 3).	George	was	also	brought	up	on	a	warrant	charged	with	using	threatening	 language	 to	 his	 wife	 and	 was	 remanded,	 but	 his	 wife	 did	 not	 appear	 to	 prosecute	(The	Age	22	January	1855;	5,	The	Age	23	January	1855,	5).	Recently	 out	of	gaol	for	beating	his	wife	and	charged	with	threatening	her	again,	he	was	 let	off	after	a	promise	never	to	insult	her	again	(The	Argus	23	January	1855,	5).	 On	another	occasion,	described	in	The	Age	as	‘a	violent	character,	who	had	the	 appearance	of	a	digger’,	George	was	charged	with	threatening	to	stab	his	wife	 and	assaulting	a	constable.	Again	his	wife	did	not	appear	against	him	and	so	he	 was	discharged	with	a	caution	from	the	Bench.	His	Worship	observing	that	if	 George	came	again	before	them	he	would	most	likely	be	sent	to	the	gaol	for	six	 months	 (4	 September	 1855,	 5).	 Shortly	 after	 George	 was	 brought	 up	 on	 a	 warrant	 for	 wife	 desertion	 and	 destroying	 the	 clothes	 of	 his	 children	while	 intoxicated.	He	was	required	to	find	sureties	of	fifty	pounds	each	and	to	keep	 the	 peace	 for	 twelve	 months	 (The	 Age	 17	 April	 1854,	 3).	 The	 Argus	 simultaneously	 reported	 that	he	was	a	wife	beater	and	 ‘a	violent	vagabond’	 who	had	previously	been	before	the	City	Court	on	charges	of	ill-using	his	wife.	 Adding	that	it	took	five	constables	to	take	him	to	the	watch	house	(24	July	1856,	 5).	As	 late	as	 the	early	1860s	he	was	 still	 being	 convicted	of	 similar	 charges	 against	 his	 wife.	 He	 was	 convicted	 of	 an	 aggravated	 case	 of	 assault	 and	 simultaneously	 described	 as	 ‘a	 rough	 looking	 middle	 aged	 man’,	 and	 was	
 
charged	by	his	wife	of	deserting	her	and	her	child	for	two	years,	and	providing	 no	 kind	 of	 subsistence	 for	 them.	 Giving	 him	 another	 chance,	 his	 wife	 Jane	 brought	her	husband	up	from	Geelong	to	her	residence	in	Little	Lonsdale	street,	 in	the	hope	he	would	remain	and	support	his	family.	Instead	‘he	got	mad	drunk	 and	beat	his	wife	fearfully	about	the	head	and	shoulders	and	kicked	her	in	the	 abdomen’.	 His	wife’s	 cries	 fortunately	 brought	 help,	 one	 or	more	 of	whom	 attempted	to	separate	George	from	his	wife.	The	constable	arrived	but	a	man	 named	Christopher	Collis	then	saved	George	Pickering	from	another	young	man	 named	George	Ward.	George	Ward	had	been	holding	George	Pickering	for	the	 constables’	arrival.	Collis	attacked	Ward	ferociously	with	his	fists	and	ultimately	 Pickering	 got	 away.	Ward	 ran	 to	 get	more	 police	 when	 he	was	 again	most	 brutally	 attacked	 by	 friends	 of	 Pickering	 and	 Collis.	 Both	 were	 shortly	 afterwards	taken	into	custody.	Pickering	was	fined	forty	shillings	and	ordered	 to	find	sureties	of	twenty	pounds	to	keep	the	peace	to	his	wife	for	six	months.	 He	 ‘stoutly	 intimated	 to	 the	bench	 that	 he	was	unable	 to	 do	 this’,	 and	was	 informed	 the	 alternative	 was	 six	 months’	 imprisonment	 (The	 Age	 3	 August	 1860,	7).	The	following	year	George	was	again	charged	with	being	drunk	and	 threatening	 the	 life	 of	 his	 wife	 and	 ordered	 to	 find	 sureties	 of	 twenty-five	 pounds	to	keep	peace	for	six	months	(The	Age	7	February	1861,	6;	The	Argus	7	 February	1861,	6).	He	was,	on	top	of	these	domestic	incidences,	time	and	time	 again	fined	for	drunkenness.	 
In	October	1857	George	was	described	in	the	newspapers	as	‘a	savage’	 and	was	charged	by	Mr.	Hogan	with	violently	ill-using	his	wife.18	She	was	beaten	 and	driven	out	of	her	house.	She	fled	for	refuge	to	the	Russell	Street	Barracks.	 George	then	proceeded	to	tear	up	her	dresses	and	break	her	crockery.	On	being	 taken	into	custody	he	assaulted	a	constable.	George	is	described	as	being	‘no	 stranger	to	the	police	court’.	Mr.	Stuart	stated	that	the	court	was	at	a	loss	as	to	 know	what	to	do	with	George,	or	how	to	‘devise	the	means	of	saving	his	wife	 and	family	from	further	brutality’.	 It	was	finally	decided	to	bind	the	prisoner	 over	for	six	months	in	two	sureties	of	fifty	pounds.	George	stated	he	could	not	 procure	the	sureties.	Mr.	Stuart	said	‘it	would	be	a	matter	of	surprise	to	him	if	 he	 could’;	 such	 ‘conduct	 as	 his	 deserved	 that	 he	 should	 meet	 with	 imprisonment	as	the	alternative’	(The	Age	24	October	1857,	6).		 	 George	was	a	prolific	offender	after	his	migration	 to	Melbourne,	he	did	 have	 a	 family	 but	 he	 abused	 them,	 but	 he	 does	 seem	 to	 have	 held	 down	 employment.	George	was	described	as	a	fisherman,	seaman	and	oysterman	at	 different	 points.19	 While	 being	 only	 forty-eight	 inches	 when	 he	 was	 
																																																						 18	This	report	names	George	Pickering’s	wife	as	‘Ann’,	since	his	only	known	wife	is	‘Jane’	this	may	be	 a	misprint	or	he	may	have	remarried	and	no	record	has	been	found.	 19	It	has	been	suggested	that	‘oystermen’	is	a	euphemism	for	working	as	‘pimp’	or	having	a	 connection	with	a	brothel	but	it	is	not	confirmed	George	had	such	a	connection.	
 
transported,	he	grew	to	sixty-five	inches	by	adulthood.	His	ill-treated	wife	Jane	 (formerly	Askeet)	married	him	 in	1852.	 This	marriage	 took	place	only	 a	 few	 years	 before	 his	 offending	 began	 on	 the	 mainland.	 They	 had	 at	 least	 two	 children,	but	George	died	alone	 in	the	Benevolent	Society	 in	August	1884	of	 progressive	paralysis,	aged	sixty.		 
	 	 Female	Juvenile	Transportees	 
Only	one	female	did	not	survive	until	freedom	and	therefore	did	not	have	the	 
opportunity	to	commit	offences	and	have	them	recorded	outside	of	her	Conduct	 
Record.	The	number	of	offences	per	female	juvenile	transportee	is	0.76.	However,	 
the	majority	of	female	juvenile	transportees	did	not	offend	outside	of	their	Conduct	 
Record.	The	majority	of	these	offences	were	‘medium’	level	offences,	only	two	 
offences	were	‘serious’	(theft	and	violence	towards	another	person	i.e.	a	free	 
person)	and	one	was	‘minor’.	 
	 Summary	 
The	details	of	these	offences	tell	us	that	twenty-three	per	cent	of	juvenile	 
transportees	carried	on	offending	–	not	simply	after	freedom	–	but	also	outside	of	 
the	ties	of	their	convict	life.	Of	those	males	who	did	have	offences	recorded	outside	 
of	their	Conduct	Record,	fifty-two	per	cent	had	migrated	and	one	had	headed	for	 
the	bush.	Of	the	female	juvenile	transportees	who	had	offences	recorded	outside	of	 
their	Conduct	Record,	two	had	migrated	out	of	the	three.	Despite	many	of	these	 
juveniles	migrating,	they	were	unable	to	achieve	the	fresh	start	they	sought.	 
However,	these	offences	were	concentrated	amongst	a	few	juveniles	suggesting	 
that	most	juvenile	transportees,	when	removed	by	time	and/or	space,	were	able	to	 
achieve	a	‘fresh	start’.	 
	 It	can	be	argued	that	the	offences	not	included	in	their	Conduct	Record	cannot	be	 
identified	in	their	entirety,	which	is	indeed	likely	to	be	the	case.	Nevertheless,	it	is	 
fair	to	assert	that	the	majority	(at	least)	did	stop	offending.	Moreover,	for	those	 
juvenile	transportees	whose	offences	were	located	outside	of	their	Conduct	Record,	 
it	is	unlikely	that	any	but	the	very	minor	offences,	which	would	be	less	likely	to	be	 
recorded,	were	not	evidenced	in	the	newspapers.	There	is	no	reason	to	suggest	that	 
some	offences	could	not	be	found	when	others	could	for	previously	identified	
 
individuals.	Still,	the	number	of	offences	located	outside	of	the	Conduct	Record	may	 
under	represent	the	number	of	offences	despite	the	great	care	taken.	 
Simultaneously,	since	the	male	juveniles	were	only	traced	if	information	after	 
freedom	was	found,	the	amount	of	offending	by	this	group	is	likely	to	over	 
represent	male	juvenile	convict	offending	after	freedom.	Therefore,	on	balance,	the	 
wider	picture	of	offending	after	freedom	for	the	male	juvenile	transportees	is	that	 
the	majority	stopped	offending	in	adulthood	when	removed	from	VDL	colonial	 
oversight.		 
	 Rate	of	Offending	 
	 Since	the	total	number	of	offences	committed	by	an	offender	is	affected	by	the	 
length	of	time	they	had	to	commit	offences,	this	chapter	will	now	turn	to	the	rate	of	 
offending.	Table	No.7	shows	the	rate	of	offending	for	male	and	female	juvenile	 
transportees	calculated	at	different	points	including:	the	rate	of	offending	within	 
their	Conduct	Record	when	they	were	under	VDL	colonial	oversight	(pre-	and	post-
freedom);	the	rate	of	offending	for	their	colonial	offending	period	(up	until	their	last	 
known	offence);	and	the	rate	of	offending	for	their	whole	life	(from	birth	to	 
death).20	 
	 The	juvenile	transportees	rate	of	offending	will	be	contextualised	by	comparison	 
with	the	1-in-25	samples	(Table	No.8)	This	can	only	be	achieved	for	the	life-course	 
point	within	their	Conduct	Record	since	offences	outside	of	their	Conduct	Records	 
and	their	death	dates	are	unknown	to	the	researcher.

This	is	because	it	is	not	possible	to	exclude	these	 individuals	in	the	1-in-25	sample.	*This	includes	juvenile	transportees	whose	death	dates	are	known	 only.

As	can	be	seen	in	Table	No.7,	the	male	juvenile	transportees’	rate	of	offending	was	 
higher	during	the	time	that	their	Conduct	Records	were	updated	as	compared	with	 
their	rate	of	offending	over	their	whole	lives.	While	this	was	not	true	of	all	 
offenders,	such	as	George	Pickering	(Case	Study	No.5),	this	was	the	general	trend.	 
The	rate	of	offending	of	those	who	had	offences	recorded	outside	of	their	Conduct	 
Records	(looking	at	only	that	offending)	was	0.15.	This	shows	that	those	who	did	 
carry	on	offending,	when	removed	from	the	time	and/or	space	of	their	conduct	 
recorders,	offended	at	a	lower	rate.	This	suggests	that	when	the	offenders	were	 
removed,	either	through	time	and/or	space	from	VDLs	penal	authority,	not	only	did	 
the	majority	(seventy-nine	per	cent)	stop	offending,	but	also	even	if	they	carried	on	 
offending	the	rate	slowed	down.	The	rate	of	offending	over	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees	whole	lives	is	also	lower.	This	highlights	that	these	juvenile	 
transportees	rarely	offended	up	until	their	deaths	and	when	they	did	the	rate	 
slowed	markedly.		 
	 While	the	rate	of	offending	within	the	Conduct	Record	is	revealing,	especially	in	 
terms	of	comparison	with	other	samples	–	the	offending	rate	over	the	offender’s	 
whole	life	is	more	informative.	This	can	be	seen	in	the	following	case	study:	 
	 Case	study	No.7:	John	Patching	 Born	in	approximately	1816,	John	Patching	was	thirteen	years-of-age	when	he	 was	convicted	of	pickpocketing	a	handkerchief	worth	three	shillings,	in	Regent	 Street,	 from	 an	 attorney	 named	Nathaniel	 George.	 For	 this	 offence	 he	was	 given	 a	 sentence	 of	 fourteen	 years’	 transportation.	 There	 were	 two	 accomplices	to	this	crime	but	they	were	neither	named	nor	caught.	There	are	 no	previous	offences	known	to	be	committed	by	John.	While	kept	on	the	hulk	 
																																																						 21	The	offending	rate	for	the	1-in-25	sample	could	only	be	calculated	here	for	those	whose	arrival	 date	was	recorded.	For	further	information	on	1-in-25	Sample	see	Appendix	No.3	
 
he	was	described	as:	‘bad	twice’.	He	was	transported	aboard	the	Gilmore	after	 a	 sixty-five-month	wait,	 in	1834.	 John	arrived	 in	Hobart	after	a	 three-month	 journey	 in	 1835.	 He	was	 described	 as	 being	 sixteen	 years-of-age	 on	 arrival.	 Unfortunately,	we	do	not	know	whether	he	was	able	to	read	and	write	before	 he	was	transported.	However,	he	did	go	on	to	get	married	and	was	able	to	sign	 the	marriage	register.		 
John’s	 first	offence	 in	 the	colony	was	 for	disobedience	of	orders	and	 insolence	while	on	assignment.	For	this	he	was	punished	with	six	weeks	on	the	 treadmill.	Within	the	first	year	he	was	moved	to	a	road	party	after	a	series	of	 absences.	After	 this	he	had	his	original	 sentence	extended	by	 two	years	 for	 absconding.	Later,	due	to	‘refusing	to	work	until	he	received	some	clothing’	he	 was	imprisoned	with	labour	in	Richmond,	and	it	was	further	recommended	that	 he	be	put	 in	a	chain	gang.	Again	he	absconded	and	he	had	his	original	 term	 extended	by	three	years.	It	was	still	only	1834	by	this	point.	After	breaking	out	 of	Richmond	Gaol	 to	abscond,	he	was	 sent	 to	Port	Arthur	 for	 two	years.	By	 1835,	now	in	Port	Arthur,	he	was	ordered	to	be	placed	in	irons.	After	a	series	 of	offences	involving	the	damaging	and	losing	of	government	property	he	was	 then	 insolent	 to	his	overseer,	he	was	 idle	and	he	had	 stolen	property	 in	his	 possession,	then	he	was	under	‘strong	suspicion	of	[a]	felony’.	This	latter	charge	 was	dismissed	and	he	was	placed	back	 in	 the	assignable	party	 in	 June	1838.	 Unfortunately,	by	October	he	was	brought	before	the	court	on	a	charge	of	theft	 for	which	he	was	found	guilty	and	sentenced	to	Port	Arthur	for	three	years	in	 irons.	His	last	offence	was	in	April	1840,	again	for	absenteeism	for	which	he	was	 given	two	days’	solitary	confinement.		 
Finally,	John	was	free-by-servitude	in	March	1847,	after	144	months	in	 the	 colony.	 After	 just	 four	 months	 of	 freedom,	 John	 made	 his	 way	 from	 Launceston	to	Port	Fairy	via	the	Essington	ship.	He	did	not	go	alone.	Before	his	 freedom	he	was	married	in	November	1842	to	Mary	Ann	Miley.	Also	a	convict,	 Mary	was	seventeen	when	they	married	at	Launceston.	While	they	may	have	 had	 children,	 given	Mary’s	 age,	 none	 were	 recorded.	 Unusually	 for	 convict	 marriages	–	Mary	Ann	and	John’s	marriage	made	the	papers.	The	couple	were	 the	first	to	be	wed	in	their	church.	John	died	in	Great	Western,	Victoria	in	1882	 aged	sixty-seven.	During	his	years	of	freedom	there	were	no	offences	recorded	 against	him.	As	a	result,	his	offending	rate	dropped	from	five	 in	his	Conduct	 Record,	to	0.5	when	including	his	whole	life.	 
	 Comparison	Group:	1-in-25	Sample		 
The	male	juvenile	transportee	rate	of	offending,	based	on	the	offences	in	their	 
Conduct	Record	only,	is	higher	than	all	1-in-25	sample	comparisons.	It	is	therefore	 
immediately	clear	that	the	greater	number	of	offences	committed	by	male	juvenile	
 
transportees	is	not	simply	due	to	their	being	in	VDL	for	longer	periods	than	adult	 
convicts.	 
	 The	1-in-25	juvenile	convicts	(those	nineteen	years-of-age	and	under)	had	a	similar,	 
but	higher,	offending	rate	as	adults	under	assignment.	This	highlights	that,	while	the	 
male	juvenile	transportees	may	have	been	biased	through	the	sampling	process	in	 
favour	of	higher	offending,	juveniles	did	have	a	higher	rate	of	offending	than	their	 
adult	counterparts.	 
	 Female	Juvenile	Transportees	 
Female	juvenile	transportees’	rate	of	offending	was	lower	than	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees	but	higher	than	all	comparison	categories.	Moreover,	the	pattern	of	 
their	rate	of	offending	was	the	same	as	the	male	juvenile	transportees.	When	 
female	juvenile	transportees	were	removed	from	time	and/or	space	in	which	the	 
Conduct	Records	were	updated,	their	offending	decreased	(when	looking	at	those	 
offences	only).		 
	 When	compared	with	the	female	1-in-25	category	samples	it	becomes	clear	that	 
female	juvenile	transportees	had	a	higher	rate	of	offending	(looking	only	at	the	 
Conduct	Record).	This	suggests	that	it	was	not	their	longer	time	in	the	colony	which	 
resulted	in	them	having	a	higher	number	of	offences.	The	female	juvenile	 
transportees	includes	all	of	the	females,	there	is	no	sampling	bias	which	would	 
account	for	the	increased	offending	rate	in	this	sample	over	the	1-in-25	probation	 
juvenile	females.	This	means	other	aspects	need	to	be	turned	to.	The	youngest	 
probationary	juvenile	was	sixteen,	whereas	the	juvenile	transportees	were,	in	fifty	 
per	cent	of	the	cases,	under	sixteen	years-of-age.	This	reflects	the	practice	of	 
transporting	London	juvenile	offenders	at	younger	ages.	This	may	have	affected	 
their	ability	to	cope	in	assignment.	If	they	lacked	the	skills	and	experience	of	being	a	 
domestic	servant	or	nurse	maid,	their	masters	may	have	been	more	prone	to	report	 
non-serious	offences.	Certainly	the	female	juvenile	transportees	were	recorded	as	 
committing	many	‘minor’	and	‘medium’	offences	which	led	to	them	being	returned	 
by	their	masters	–	who	rarely	took	them	back	after	their	punishment.	 
	
 
Desistance?	 	 
Criminal	desistance	is	important	in	understanding	the	lives	of	these	juvenile	 
transportees.	Vital	to	this	understanding	is	the	point	at	which	desistance	is	 
measured	from.	Under	conditions	where	bad	language	and	falling	asleep	in	church	 
were	recorded	as	offences	–	it	is	perhaps	surprising	that	ten	per	cent	of	these	 
juvenile	transportees	managed	to	avoid	committing	any	offence	at	all.	The	low	bar	 
for	reoffending	while	under	sentence	therefore	needs	to	be	accounted	for.	As	can	 
be	seen	in	Table	No.9,	by	focusing	on	Summary	Offences	heard	by	the	police	and	 
superintendents	of	convicts	during	1848,	it	is	possible	to	compare	offences	 
committed	by	convicts	and	the	free	population.	It	is	immediately	clear	that	convicts	 
under	sentence	committed	more	offences	than	free	persons.	This	reflects	the	added	 
surveillance	and	restrictions	placed	on	convicts.	Consequently,	desistance	here	will	 
be	measured	as	follows;	did	these	juvenile	transportees	carry	on	committing	 
offences	up	until	their	death	and	if	so,	did	they	slow	down	in	their	offending.	 
Meaning	did	they	commit	fewer	offences	as	time	went	on	and/or	did	the	severity	of	 
those	offences	decrease.

The	opening	of	convict	institutions,	such	as	Hobart	Barracks	in	the	1820s,	marked	 
the	beginning	of	the	end	of	certain	freedoms	convicts	had	enjoyed	including	having	 
their	own	houses	and	domestic	arrangements	–	this	was	a	direct	assault	by	 
Governor	Bigge	on	the	convict	private	sphere.	Now,	convicts	found	out	of	 
institutions	or	away	from	the	property	of	their	assigned	employers	were	more	likely	 
to	be	regarded	with	suspicion	and	thus	as	legitimate	targets	of	police	action	(Reid	 
2007,	131).	When	looking	at	the	summary	offences	for	VDL	as	a	whole,	the	 
following	six	offences	markedly	decreased	from	1838;	absconding,	absence	without	 
leave,	disobedience	of	orders,	drunkenness,	insolence	and	neglect	of	duty	(at	a	rate	 
of	36%,	80%,	248%,	59%,	131%	and	159%	respectively).	Whereas,	the	remaining	 
offences	increased;	insubordination,	idleness	and	misdemeanors	(Ewing	1843,	XV).	 
These	changes	reflect	the	change	in	management	of	convicts	whereby	there	was	 
increased	surveillance	and	decreased	freedoms.		 
	 Governor	Arthur	addressed	the	inability	to	punish	convicts	further	by	systematically	 
expanding	the	police	and	judiciary,	and	splitting	the	colony	into	districts.	With	the	 
formal	separation	of	VDL	from	NSW	and	the	establishment	of	the	Courts	of	Quarter	 
Sessions	and	Supreme	Court	in	1824,	the	Governor’s	authority	was	more	secure.	 
This	coincided	with	the	creation	of	a	number	of	criminal	offences	some	of	which	 
were	exclusively	aimed	at	convicts,	and	the	institution	of	summary	jurisdiction	over	 
convict	servants.	All	leading	to	an	increased	difficulty	for	masters	to	overlook	their	 
servants’	offences	(Reid	2007,	129).	From	1820	onwards,	the	punitive	resources	of	 
the	state	expanded	with	gaols,	watch	houses,	convict	barracks	and	houses	of	 
correction,	for	both	female	and	male	convicts,	as	well	as	penal	settlements	for	 
males	(Reid	2007,	130).	This	demonstrates	the	increased	ability	for	the	state	to	 
control	and	punish	convicts.	 
	 The	ten	per	cent	of	juvenile	transportees	with	no	reoffending	equates	to	only	nine	 
individuals,	five	of	which	died	under	sixteen	years-of-age,	none	of	whom	had	the	 
chance	to	offend	due	to	either	dying	on	the	voyage	or	soon	after	arrival.	This	leaves	 
only	four	individuals	who	actually	did	not	offend	in	the	colony.	There	is	no	doubt	 
that	the	added	surveillance	of	the	penal	colony	increased	offending.	Therefore,	a	
 
more	important	question	than	the	number	of	offences	is;	did	they	carry	on	 
offending	up	until	their	death?		 
	 Excluding	the	female	who	died	en-route,	no	female	offended	up	until	death.	 
However,	twenty-nine	per	cent	of	males	continued	offending	until	death.	Of	those	 
who	offended	throughout	the	whole	of	their	lives,	all	apart	from	ten	individuals	 
slowed	down	in	their	offending.	Therefore,	ten	per	cent	of	male	juvenile	 
transportees	carried	on	offending	up	until	their	death	and	they	did	not	slow	down.	 
One	of	these	juveniles	who	did	not	slow	down	was	Charles	Brewer	(Case	Study	 
No.3).	 
	 The	majority	of	juvenile	transportees	did	not	continue	offending	in	adulthood	–	this	 
is	reflected	in	the	findings	of	Godfrey	et	al	(2017)	who	found	that	nineteenth-
century	English	juvenile	crime	history	was	‘a	“crime	history”	dominated	by	 
desistance’.	This	is	in	contrast	to	adult	experiences	of	desistence	detailed	in	cognate	 
historical	studies	(Godfrey	et	al	2007;	2010)	and	more	contemporary	studies	 
(Maruna	2001).		 
Conclusion	 	 
Male	juvenile	transportees	were	more	likely	to	commit	‘minor’	and	‘medium’	 
offences	than	‘serious’	and	‘very	serious’	offences.	They	also	committed	more	 
offences,	on	average,	than	any	other	comparison	group	including	the	1-in-25	 
juvenile	probation	sample.	It	is	acknowledged	that	the	male	juvenile	transportees	 
were	biased	in	favour	of	over	representing	high	offending.	However,	since	the	1-in-
25	probation	juvenile	sample	also	committed	more	offences	than	their	adult	 
counterparts,	this	confirms	that	male	juveniles	were	more	likely	to	have	a	higher	 
number	of	offences	than	adult	convicts.	In	comparison	with	the	1-in-25	sample,	the	 
male	juvenile	transportees	committed	more	offences	but	they	did	not	commit	more	 
‘very	serious’	offences	while	under	sentence.	Yet,	because	the	offending	rate	of	 
these	male	juvenile	transportees	was	also	higher	than	all	comparison	groups	it	 
confirms	that	their	higher	number	of	offences	was	not	simply	due	to	a	longer	period	 
in	the	colony.	Nonetheless,	when	removed	from	the	colonial	gaze	of	VDL,	the	 
majority	of	male	juvenile	transportees	did	not	offend.	However,	of	those	who	did,	
 
the	majority	were	‘serious’	offenders	and	there	were	two	offenders	who	went	on	to	 
become	‘very	serious’	offenders.	The	rate	of	offending	of	male	juvenile	transportees	 
was	higher	while	their	recording	of	their	Conduct	Record	continued.	Not	only	did	 
the	majority	of	the	juveniles	not	have	offences	recorded	outside	of	their	Conduct	 
Record,	but	also	the	offending	rate	slowed	down	for	those	who	did.	Despite	some	 
exceptions,	the	offending	rate	of	their	whole	lives	was	also	lower.	Therefore,	male	 
juvenile	transportees	were	generally	frequent	petty	offenders	while	under	 
sentence,	but	most	stopped	offending	after	freedom	and	removal	from	their	 
colonial	servitude.	 
	 The	female	juvenile	transportees	present	a	different	offending	picture.		They	 
committed	no	‘very	serious’	offences,	but	similarly	to	the	male	juvenile	 
transportees	most	commonly	committed	‘medium’	and	then	‘minor’	level	offences.	 
They	committed	fewer	offences	per	convict	overall	than	male	juvenile	transportees.	 
However,	they	committed	more	offences,	on	average,	than	the	male	and	female	1-
in-25	samples	(including	juveniles).	The	majority	of	female	juvenile	transportees	did	 
not	go	onto	offend	after	removal	from	the	colonial	gaze,	and	of	those	who	did	they	 
mainly	committed	‘minor’	and	‘medium’	level	offences.	Only	two	females	went	on	 
to	commit	‘serious’	offences,	and	both	who	offended	in	this	way	slowed	down.	 
None	of	the	female	juvenile	transportees	carried	on	offending	throughout	their	 
lives.	Despite	the	higher	number	of	offences	and	the	quicker	offending	rate,	female	 
juvenile	transportees	both	slowed	down	and	ultimately	stopped	offending	before	 
death.	Maxwell-Stewart	(2016,	427)	found	that	female	expirees	were	less	likely	to	 
be	rearrested	than	males.	This	is	significant	since,	when	looking	at	all	female	 
convicts,	females	confessed	to	worse	offending	prior	to	transportation.	Maxwell-
Stewart	argues	that	transportation	was	effective	at	breaking	cycles	of	female	 
offending	(2016,	427).	While	it	is	true	that	all	female	juvenile	transportees	 
eventually	stopped	offending,	it	would	be	wrong	to	suggest	that	transportation	 
broke	their	offending	cycle.	Both	female	and	male	juvenile	transportees	offended	 
repeatedly	and	in	quick	succession	for	much	of	their	servitude.	This	included	 
‘serious’	offences	in	both	groups.	However,	despite	this,	after	freedom	most	turned	 
away	from	crime.	
 
It	is	likely	that	the	high	number	of	‘minor’	and	‘medium’	offences	in	both	male	and	 
female	juvenile	transportees	while	under	sentence,	was	affected	by	the	assignment	 
masters	and	the	increased	time	sent	in	institutionalized	settings	(in	female	factories	 
and	Point	Puer	particularly).	Both	situations	led	to	the	reporting	of	relatively	non-
serious	offending	in	juveniles	more	likely.	This	increased	tendency	to	report	 
juveniles	is	likely	to	be	due	to	a	mixture	of	increased	surveillance	of	the	group	and	a	 
decreased	willingness	to	overlook	the	offences	observed.	This	decreased	likelihood	 
to	overlook	offences	is	likely	to	be	due	to	the	normalisation	of	reprimanding	 
children	for	poor	behaviour	and	performance,	as	well	as	the	decreased	likelihood	 
that	these	juveniles	would	possess	the	skills,	experience	and	competencies	that	 
were	wanted.	As	already	noted,	the	less	skill	a	convict	had	the	greater	the	likelihood	 
that	a	convict	would	be	reported	for	offending.	This	reasoning	is	further	enforced	by	 
the	finding	that	most	juvenile	transportees	did	not	go	on	to	offend	outside	of	their	 
Conduct	Record,	and	even	of	those	who	did	most	desisted	from	crime	before	death.	 
                            
 
Chapter 5: Punishment 	 
Where	 a	 master	 in	 England	 finds	 fault,	 the	 master	 in	 Australia	 threatens	the	 lash;	where	the	master	here	grows	angry,	 the	master	 there	 swears,	 and	 invokes	 the	 lash;	where	 here	 he	 talks	 of	 turning	 away,	there	he	procures	the	infliction	of	the	lash;	for	idleness,	the	lash;	 for	carelessness,	the	lash;	for	insolence,	the	lash;	for	drunkenness,	the	 lash;	 for	 disobedience,	 the	 lash;	 wherever	 there	 is	 reason,	 and	 wherever	there	is	not	reason,	the	lash.	Ever	on	the	master’s	tongue,	 and	 ever	 in	 the	 prisoner’s	 ear,	 just	 as	 he	 himself	 urges	 his	 drowsy	 bullocks,	sounds	the	lash,	the	lash!	-	the	lash!	(Bishop	Ullathorne	cited	 in	Wolter	2014,	202)		 
	 
The	punishments	endured	by	the	juvenile	transportees	will	be	investigated	to	 
further	understand	their	experience	under	servitude	and	to	ascertain	if	this	related	 
to	their	life-outcomes.	From	hard	labour	and	flogging	to	confinement	in	the	cells	 
and	extended	sentences	-	what	did	these	juvenile	transportees	experience?	 
Governor	Arthur’s	scale	of	punishment	was,	as	he	explained	in	1830,	as	follows:	 
	 ‘on	 the	 one	 hand	 [it	 descends]	 from	 the	 least	 severe	 species	 of	 punishment,	 in	the	service	of	 the	settlers,	by	regular	steps,	 through	 the	 usual	 public	 service,	 road-gangs,	 chain-gangs,	 the	 penal	 settlements	of	Port	Arthur	and	Macquarie	Harbour	(a	last	alteration,	 next	 to	 capital	 punishment),	 and	 ascending	 on	 the	 other,	 by	 encouraging	to	reform,	through	the	links	of	probationary	service	in	the	 field,	and	other	descriptions	of	duty	in	the	public	service,	distinguished	 by	some	mark	of	conferring	different	degrees	of	liberty	by	conditional,	 and	lastly	by	absolute	pardons’	(cited	in	Reid	2007,	130).		 
	 The	hierarchy	of	punishment	at	Point	Puer,	from	the	point	of	view	of	the	authorities	 
was	as	follows;	first,	confinement	to	the	muster	ground	or	to	a	particular	separate	 
part	of	the	jail,	depriving	them	of	their	usual	hours	of	play,	and	confinement	to	a	 
more	limited	space	than	the	General	Class	is	allowed;	second,	sleeping	in	a	silent	 
apartment	which	included	confinement	to	the	cell	except	during	the	hours	of	 
labour;	third,	confinement	to	the	‘Old	Jail’	which	prevented	them	from	mixing	with	 
the	General	Class	at	trades	or	at	school,	and	restricted	their	play.	They	were	then	 
taught	for	one	hour	in	the	morning,	employed	during	the	day	in	breaking	up	new	 
ground	or	in	working	on	the	land	and	during	their	spare	time	they	were	confined	to	 
the	Yards.	They	were	expected	to	labour	for	two	hours	a	day	longer	than	the	
 
General	Class,	and	no	dumpling	was	allowed	at	dinner,	but	an	equal	weight	of	bread	 
was	given	instead;	fourth,	confinement	to	the	crime	jail	where	they	may	have	be	 
sentenced	to	chains.	They	are	then	employed	during	the	day	in	breaking	stones;	 
fifth,	solitary	confinement	on	bread	and	water	for	any	period	not	exceeding	 
fourteen	days;	sixth,	corporal	punishment	to	the	extent	of	thirty-six	lashes;	seventh,	 
in	‘very	bad	cases’	they	were	transferred	to	the	Port	Arthur	(Horne	1843,	5).	 
	 Knowing	how	the	authorities	‘ranked’	punishment	informs	us	which	punishments	 
they	thought	the	most	severe,	but	since	none	of	the	juvenile	transportees	left	 
behind	diaries	or	written	testimony	–	we	cannot	know	how	individual	experience	 
differed.	Helen	Johnston	(2008,	78)	argues	that	prison	policy	and	practice	was	 
‘ambiguous,	contradictory	and	paradoxical’	in	Britain,	and	that	this	is	exemplified	by	 
prison	officers	working	in	these	institutions.	The	same	can	be	said	of	overseers	and	 
masters	in	VDL.	Johnston	points	out	that,	while	the	magistrates	and	policy	makers	 
may	sentence	offenders,	it	was	the	officers	who	had	most	contact	with	the	 
offenders.	Unfortunately,	as	with	the	prisoners,	there	is	little	information	left	from	 
the	accounts	of	these	individuals	(Johnston	2008,	78).	However,	it	is	inevitable	that,	 
whether	a	warder	or	overseer,	individual	officers	were	different	and	so	punishment	 
for	the	offenders	under	these	individuals	will	have	differed,	and	therefore	so	did	the	 
experience	of	punishment.	For	example,	at	Birmingham	Gaol	the	governor,	surgeon	 
and	visiting	justices	were	severely	admonished	for	the	cruel	regime	which	had	 
resulted	in	the	death	of	a	fifteen-year-old	prisoner,	Edward	Andrews.	Because	of	 
this	incident	some	of	the	subordinate	officers	were	dismissed	while	one	warder	in	 
particular	was	praised	for	the	‘great	sympathy’	he	exhibited	towards	the	prisoners	 
(Johnston	2008,	89).	This	demonstrates	how	in	one	institution,	at	one	time,	there	 
were	varying	practices.	Such	a	phenomenon	would	be	amplified	at	an	earlier	period	 
in	the	colonies.	Moreover,	as	found	by	Ginneken	and	Hayes	in	their	2017	study	of	 
contemporary	offenders	‘there	is	no	agreement	among	offenders	in	their	 
interpretation	of	punishment’	and	‘the	experienced	severity	of	a	punishment	is	 
contingent	on	the	interpretation	of	punishment’	as	well	as	individual	circumstance.	 
Punishment	in	practice	is	the	interaction	between	offender	and	the	punishment	 
itself	and	as	such	differs	between	offenders	(2017,	74).	If	their	perception	of	the	
 
punishment	is	different	so	too	will	the	effects	of	the	punishment	differ	both	in	the	 
short	and	long	term.	 
	 Direct	numerical	comparison	between	the	male	juvenile	transportees	and	the	male	 
1-in-25	samples	is	not	possible	because	of	the	sheer	variety	of	not	only	different	 
punishments	(see	Table	No.10),	but	also	in	the	way	those	punishments	were	 
recorded	and	the	resulting	ambiguity.	For	instance,	in	the	1-in-25	sample	many	of	 
the	probation	period	punishments	which	were	recorded	as	‘hard	labour’	would	 
have	been	sent	to	the	road	party.	Yet	it	is	often	impossible	to	know	when	this	 
applied,	and	where	they	were	sent.	However,	it	is	still	possible	to	build-up	a	picture	 
of	the	experience	of	punishment	for	these	juvenile	transportees	and	how	this	 
broadly	compared	with	other	samples.	It	is	important	to	look,	in	turn,	at	each	 
punishment.	 
	 Male	Juvenile	Transportees	 	 Building	up	a	picture	of	the	punishments	convicts	endured	is	important.	This	is	 
because	any	punishment	would	have	affected	the	convict	lives	and	possibly	their	 
life-outcomes	from	their	recidivism	or	desistance,	to	marriage	and	migration.	Table	 
No.10	shows	the	punishments	endured	by	male	juvenile	transportees,	and	Table	 
No.11	shows	incidences	of	re-transportation	and	executions.	Broadly	speaking,	the	 
most	common	type	of	punishment	for	male	juvenile	transportees	was	hard	labour,	 
flogging	and	confinement	to	the	cells,	whereas	the	punishment	of	the	treadmill	and	 
fines	were	relatively	uncommon.

explored	in	turn	and	compared	with	other	samples.	 
	 Lashes	at	the	Breech	 
On	average	the	male	juvenile	transportees	received	sixty-two	lashes	each	during	the	 
period	their	Conduct	Records	were	updated.	However,	the	spread	of	the	 
punishment	was	not	equal.	Thomas	Mihan	received	425	lashes,	compared	with	 
another	who	received	only	twelve.	This	highlights	the	marked	difference	in	 
experience	for	these	juvenile	transportees.	Table	No.14	demonstrated	that	while	 
the	majority	of	these	juveniles	(sixty-five	per	cent)	were	flogged,	and	the	majority	of	 
those	who	were	flogged	(sixty-nine	per	cent)	had	under	one-hundred	lashes;	twenty	 
male	juvenile	transportees	were	flogged	over	100	times.

As	Maxwell-Stewart	points	out,	it	is	hard	to	‘comprehend	the	savagery	of	such	a	 
punishment’.	The	convict	would	be	stripped	to	the	waist,	legs	splayed	and	arms	 
secured	above	the	head,	and	fixed	to	a	frame.	The	lash	was	made	of	nine	whipcord	 
strands	with	knots	that	had	been	stiffened	with	wax	or	wire	(2008,	79).	Often	for	 
juvenile	males	stationed	at	Point	Puer,	the	punishment	differed	slightly.	The	male	 
juvenile	punishment	usually	involved	being	struck	on	the	breech	with	a	bundle	of	 
sticks	forming	a	‘birch	rod’.	Boys	were	strapped	to	a	birching	pony,	where	they	were	 
bent	over	and	stripped	naked	from	the	waist	downwards.	This	of	course	 
‘heightened	the	humiliation’	(Nunn	2017,	163).	This	sample	would	have	endured	 
both	scenarios.	Despite	Booth’s	declaration	that	he	‘never	resorts	to	the	lash	except	 
as	a	measure	of	dernier	resort’,	corporal	punishment	was	frequently	used	Point	 
Puer.	In	1839,	2	709	offences	were	committed	at	Point	Puer,	of	which	374	were	 
punished	with	corporal	punishment	(Nunn	2017,	163).	Whilst	the	punishments	for	 
juvenile	transportees	were	not	carried	out	all	at	one	time	(the	fewest	number	of	 
lashes	given	at	one	time	was	twelve)	the	most	common	number	given	at	one	time	 
was	twenty-five.	This	would	have	inflicted	severe	physical	pain	and	caused	both	 
bruising	and	bleeding.	After	examining	a	seven-year-old	boy	who	had	received	only	 
four	strokes	of	the	‘lesser’	punishment	of	the	birch,	Sir	Walter	Foster,	a	medical	 
doctor,	described	the	effects:	 
I	saw	the	boy	two	of	three	days	after	the	infliction	of	this	 punishment,	and	his	little	back	was	covered	with	wounds	which	 extended	right	through	the	skin	to	the	muscles,	and	not	only	was	his	 back	a	mass	of	rawness,	but	the	wounds	had	come	round	to	the	front	 of	the	abdomen,	and	they	had	cut	down	to	the	muscle	on	the	front	 of	his	frame	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	717).	 
																																																						 26	This	table	excludes	the	two	male	juvenile	transportees	who	died	on	transport.	
 
While	flogging	is	seen	as	abhorrent	in	todays’	society	and	was	contested	by	some	 
contemporaries,	it	was	a	common	punishment.	Despite	some	opponents,	the	 
arguments	for	flogging	were	that	it	allowed	for:	the	infliction	of	immediate	physical	 
pain	(although	this	was	seen	as	the	remnants	of	medieval	torture	by	its	opponents);	 
humiliation	(though	it	was	seen	as	brutalising	by	its	opponents);	what	Bentham	 
termed	a	‘characteristic	punishment’	which	was	a	punishment	appropriate	to	the	 
perceived	nature	of	the	offender	as	a	distinct	criminal	type;	the	punishment	was	 
quick	and	cheap	(an	aspect	humanitarians	preferred	to	the	alternative	in	which	 
offenders	lingered	in	gaols);	‘active	public	revulsion’;	and	lastly	its	deterrent	role	for	 
those	witnessing	the	spectacle	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood,	1990;	699-702).	Only	from	 
1862	was	flogging	in	public	abolished	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	689).	However,	it	 
had	ended	for	females	in	1817	(after	being	in	decline	since	the	1770s)	and	had	 
declined	for	men	from	as	early	as	the	1830s	(Old	Bailey	Online,	2017).	Yet,	even	as	 
late	as	1874,	it	was	believed	by	some	that	flogging	exercised	‘perhaps	stronger	 
moral	influence	than	any	other	power	in	the	world…the	lessons	which	are	taught	by	 
discomfort	and	suffering	are	wonderfully	valuable’	as	written	by	barrister	Fitzjames	 
Stephen	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	702).	Indeed,	it	was	not	until	1920	that	a	Home	 
Office	Report	concluded	that	corporal	punishment	of	juveniles	was	largely	 
ineffective	as	a	means	of	deterring	youths	from	re-offending.	Although	it	remained	 
in	widespread	use	for	boys,	rising	significantly	during	the	two	World	Wars	until	the	 
passage	of	the	Criminal	Justice	Act	in	1948	(Gard	2009,	115-123).	Still,	despite	its	 
advocates,	over	the	course	of	the	nineteenth-century	attitudes	were	changing.	 
Referring	to	juveniles	in	particular,	Horne	pointed	out:		 
	 Corporal	punishment	has	the	same	effect	here	[Point	Puer]	as	 elsewhere.	It	tends	to	degrade	and	harden,	and	after	having	been	 twice	or	thrice	inflicted	is	evidently	useless.	Some	boys	take	a	pride	 in	enduring	all	that	can	be	given	them,	and	consider	flogging	a	manly	 sort	of	punishment	as	it	is	generally	inflicted	upon	grown	up	 Convicts.	When	anyone	seems	to	feel	its	severity	he	loses	caste	in	the	 eyes	of	his	companions	who	jeeringly	tell	him	that	they	could	take	as	 much	upon	their	faces	(Horne	1843,	6).		 	 
Alexander	Maconochie,	a	penal	reformer,	asserted	that	settlers	had	developed	a	 
taste	for	flogging	and	hard	labour	and	that	such	punishments	were	ordered	lightly	
 
for	non-serious	offences.	Flogging,	in	particular	was	preferred	because	it	resulted	in	 
less	work	interruption	(Reid	2007,	170).	‘The	“effect	of	the	lash	is	not	confined	to	 
the	marks”	on	a	man’s	“back”	but	rather	“enters	his	soul”’	stated	former	colonist	 
Charles	Rowcroft	(Reid	2007,	171).	Flogging	was	deemed	to	have	powerful	 
debilitating	effects.	It	was	said	to	defy	natural	masculine	independence.	It	also	 
violated	the	corporeal	integrity	of	the	convict:	‘the	wiry	cords	struck	and	eat	their	 
fill	of	the	flesh	and	gore	of	the	wretched	man’	remarked	Ullathorne	–	‘the	scourge	 
drinks	the	blood	of	their	flesh’	and	‘devours	the	spirit	of	their	manhood’	(Reid	2007,	 
229).	Flogging,	declared	the	exiled	Chartist	leader	John	Frost,	was	a	contest	 
between	flogger,	a	man	who	‘felt	a	gratification	in	inflicting	and	witnessing	human	 
misery’,	and	the	man	who	still	retained	his	natural	feelings	of	pride	and	self-respect	 
(Reid	2007,	230).	Frost	also	asserted	that	convicts	were	flogged	routinely	for	 
breaches	of	regulations	so	minute	that	they	were	impossible	for	any	man	to	 
remember	to	obey	(Reid	2007,	230).	Nevertheless,	according	to	Shergold	the	lash	 
was	used	judiciously	in	colonial	Australia	and	he	asserts	that	there	is	little	evidence	 
of	a	society	terrorized	by	corporal	punishment	(1988,	11).		 
	 Selecting	1835	as	a	starting	point,	the	peak	year	of	floggings,	the	probability	of	 
being	beaten	every	year	during	a	five-year	sentence	was	0.001,	and	roughly	two	 
thirds	of	all	convicts	received	one	or	no	floggings	during	servitude.	The	official	 
statistics	on	corporal	punishment	disprove	the	popular	picture	of	convictism	as	a	 
society	where	workers	were	demoralized	physically	and	psychologically	by	the	whip.	 
Physical	violence	in	Australia	was	no	greater	than	in	the	British	army	or	navy,	and	 
less	than	for	American	slaves	(Shergold	1988,	11).	Compared	with	the	convict	 
system,	drunkenness,	absence	without	leave,	and	violence	towards	officers	earned	 
the	death	sentence	in	the	army	(Nicholas	1988,	181).	Physical	violence	against	child	 
workers	and	apprentices	was	a	daily	occurrence	in	early	nineteenth-century	Britain	 
(Shergold	1988,	11).	However,	in	an	official	report	to	the	Molesworth	committee,	it	 
stated	that	fifty	lashes	with	the	regulation	cat	were	equal	to	one	hundred	lashes	 
using	a	military	cat	(Evans	&	Nicholls	1984,	56).	Nevertheless,	the	picture	here	is	 
that	flogging	was	uncommon	for	the	general	convict	population.	Yet,	it	was	not	 
uncommon	for	these	juvenile	transportees.	
 
Summary	 
The	juvenile	transportees	certainly	underwent	more	lashes	on	average	than	the	1-
in-25	samples.	Similarly,	at	Point	Puer,	one	third	of	the	boys	were	flogged	in	1835	 
and	1836,	and	in	1837	and	1838	half	were.	They	were	subject	to	severe	corporal	 
punishment	(Shaw	1998,	244).	Therefore,	it	was	not	just	the	juvenile	transportees	 
but	also	juveniles	at	Point	Puer	who	were	flogged	relatively	frequently.	While	it	 
cannot	be	ignored	that	juveniles	did	offend	more,	there	is	a	suggestion	that	it	was	 
seen	as	more	acceptable	to	flog	juveniles	to	discipline	them.	Despite	opposition	to	 
flogging	of	adults,	often	those	same	individuals	did	not	oppose	flogging	the	young.	 
Unlike	Horne,	many	in	authority	did	not	feel	the	degrading	effect	flogging	had	on	 
adults	extended	to	juveniles.	This	was	largely	because	‘the	chastisement	of	the	 
young	was,	by	tradition,	a	well-established	method	of	child	discipline’.	Flogging	for	 
adult	men	was	seen	as	a	last	resort,	but	for	juveniles	it	was	placed	at	the	other	end	 
of	the	scale.	The	idea	being	that	a	‘short,	sharp	punishment’	was	better	than	 
periods	of	imprisonment	for	the	young	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	712).	Indeed,	as	 
Rowbotham	points	out,	corporal	punishment	was	influenced	by	.	.	.	‘a	range	of	 
factors,	with	class	and	gender	considerations	ranking	very	high’.	A	number	of	 
leading	commentators	on	juveniles	including	Matthew	Hill,	alongside	evangelical	 
didactic	authors	like	Silas	Hocking	and	Hesba	Stretton,	were	doubtful	that	lower	 
class	juvenile	delinquents	could	count	as	children	–	their	depravity	(which	included	 
a	high	degree	of	self-assertive	independence)	had	aged	them	and	the	only	way	to	 
redeem	them	was	to	reduce	them	to	childhood	once	again,	‘by	force	if	necessary’	 
(2017,	101).	Many	studies	of	Victorian	and	Edwardian	childhood	agree	that	corporal	 
punishment	was	a	significant	factor	in	child-rearing	strategies	(Rowbotham	2017,	 
102).	It	was	held	that	a	parent	was	behaving	lovingly	in	chastising	the	young,	to	 
discipline	their	hearts	and	minds	through	the	infliction	of	physical	pain	so	that	they	 
would	become	useful	members	of	society,	full	of	moral	rectitude	and	respect	for	 
authority	(Rowbotham	2017,	105).	Such	normalisation	of	punishment	against	 
juveniles	in	the	home	was	also	reflected	in	the	courts:		 
	 	 	
 
‘the	 ordering	 of	 judicial	 corporal	 punishment	 (JCP)	 by	 the	 courts	 endured	 until	 the	 Criminal	 Justice	 Act	 1948.	 The	 majority	 of	 the	 sentences	for	JCP	were	passed	on	those	considered	to	be	children,	up	 to	14;	it	was	used	more	rarely	for	adults…’	(Rowbotham	2017,	105).	 
	 Moreover,	it	was	expected	that	the	probationary	groups	would	have	less	flogging	 
sentences	because	the	use	of	the	lash	was	increasingly	phased	out	in	the	move	 
towards	confinement.	This	partially	explain	why	the	1-in-25	probationary	convicts	 
had	fewer	flogging	incidences	than	the	assignment	period	convicts.	 
	 Confinement	 
There	were	on	average	thirty-one	days	of	confinement	for	each	male	juvenile	 
transportee,	and	seventy-one	juveniles	(seventy-two	per	cent)	actually	received	a	 
sentence	of	confinement	to	the	cells;	as	can	be	seen	in	Table	No.15.	Nonetheless,	 
the	majority	of	those	(seventy-five	per	cent)	only	spent	between	one	and	fifty	days	 
in	the	cells.	Only	seven	of	these	male	juvenile	transportees	spent	over	100	days	 
confined	to	the	cells.

	 Solitary	confinement	was	a	punishment	in	which	offenders	were	confined	in	the	 
cells	alone	and	communication	was	prohibited.	Seen	as	the	‘penal	panacea’,	by	the	 
late	1830s	there	was	serious	consideration	to	set	up	a	separate	system	of	 
confinement	throughout	Britain	as	an	alternative	to	transportation	(Radzinowicz	&	 
Hood	1990,	490-1).	As	early	as	1842	there	were	‘voices	of	dissent’,	including	Charles	 
Dickens,	who	was	unconvinced	by	the	‘miracles’	brought	by	isolation.	Noting	 
instead	the	consecutive	phases	of	‘initial	shock,	through	depression,	over-
sensibility,	detachment	from	reality,	placid	adjustment,	down	to	helpless	mental	 
																																																						 27	Excludes	two	male	juvenile	transportees	who	died	en-route.	
 
state	of	dissolved	responsibility’	by	discharge.	While	Dickens	was	eventually	proven	 
right,	generally	his	views	were	ignored	at	the	time	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	492).	 
Henry	Mayhew	and	John	Binny	argued	that	separate	confinement	eventually	 
produced	‘long	suffering	and	deep	mental	affliction’.	Indeed,	the	Pentonville	 
Chaplain,	Joseph	Kingsmill,	admitted	the	number	of	converted	was	over-rated	 
(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	503).	However,	not	only	could	solitary	confinement	(in	 
the	early	days	especially)	be	enforced	to	different	degrees,	but	also	Conduct	 
Records	did	not	always	specify	‘solitary’	when	recording	the	sentencing	of	convicts	 
sent	to	the	cells.	Another	issue	was	the	availability	of	appropriate	buildings.	For	 
example,	there	was	no	means	of	solitary	confinement	at	Port	Arthur	until	1835	 
(Shaw	1998,	211).	 
	 Horne,	in	referring	to	Point	Puer,	stated	that	‘solitary	confinement	is	a	punishment	 
which	seems	more	severely	felt	when	of	any	duration,	as	the	diet	is	merely	bread	 
and	water	and	communication	with	their	companions	is	as	much	as	possible	 
prevented’	(Horne	1843,	6).	Yet,	he	also	pointed	out:	 
	 There	are	also	some	small	detached	buildings	near	the	jail,	formed	 into	cells	opening	into	an	inner	passage,	for	separate	confinement,	 and	some	wooden	erections	resembling	sentry	boxes	for	what	is	 commonly	called	solitary	confinement.	As	to	their	strength	and	 adaptation	to	the	purpose	I	can	only	say	that	two	boys	are	 sometimes	found	in	one	of	the	separate	cells	in	the	morning,	and	 that	I	have	heard	the	boys	in	the	solitary	cells	keep	up	a	conversation	 at	the	full	pitch	of	their	voices	during	the	middle	of	the	day.	They	 sometimes	break	out	of	them	and	abscond,	and	at	other	times	 remove	boards	so	that	provisions	may	be	conveyed	to	them	from	 without.	In	short	the	whole	is	a	mockery	of	separate	or	solitary	 confinement	(Horne	1843,	2-3).	 
	 It	would	be	wrong	to	suggest	that	all	incidences	of	‘to	the	cells	24	hours’	or	even	 
‘one	month	in	separate	working	cells’	were	true	solitary	confinement.	When	 
speaking	of	prisons	in	Britain,	Johnston	pointed	out	that	although	these	prisons	 
claimed	to	operate	a	silent	regime	it	is	difficult	to	see	how	the	prisoners	would	have	 
been	prevented	from	communicating	at	all	times,	especially	in	larger	prisons	with	 
low	staff	levels.	This	suggests	that	‘despite	growing	ideas	of	the	use	of	different	 
regimes,	to	ensure	the	conformity	and	possible	reform	of	prisoners,	practice	varied	
 
considerably’.	Whilst	the	prisons	of	Coldbath	Fields	and	Pentonville	embraced	the	 
silent	and	separate	punishment	regimes,	many	rural	prisons,	observed	John	 
Howard:	‘still	suffered	problems	of	poor	management,	dilapidated	buildings	and	 
were	ill	constructed	for	the	new	philosophies	of	punishment’.	The	opposing	system	 
of	separation	could	be	imposed	with	fewer	staff,	but	the	required	architectural	 
alterations	cost	money.	While	Johnston	is	considering	Britain,	the	same	can	be	said	 
of	VDL:	there	was	considerable	difference	in	the	experience	of	punishment	 
(Johnston	2008,	81).	Some	prisoners	did	live	a	solitary	existence	for	the	duration	of	 
their	punishment,	but	the	practice	of	keeping	convicts	in	solitary	was	not	uniform	 
through	different	institutions.	That	is	not	to	say	that	confinement	in	the	cells	for	 
long	periods	was	not	arduous	on	the	body	and	mind	–	whether	they	managed	to	 
have	the	odd	conversation	or	not.	It	was	still	a	punishment.	Nevertheless,	the	 
degree	of	rigor	would	have	depended	on	the	time	and/or	place	of	the	punishment.	 
While	Conduct	Records	clearly	record	the	date	of	such	punishments,	they	often	do	 
not	clarify	where	the	confinement,	solitary	or	not,	took	place.	Therefore,	for	the	 
purposes	of	exploring	punishments	here,	all	incidences	of	confinement	to	the	cells,	 
whether	specified	as	solitary,	separate	or	neither,	will	be	grouped	as	being	 
‘confined	to	the	cells’.	While	true	solitary	confinement	is	attributed	to	mental	 
breakdown	in	both	contemporary	and	secondary	sources,	we	cannot	say	which	 
convicts	here	endured	true	solitary	confinement.	Nevertheless,	the	punishment	of	 
being	confined	to	the	cells,	even	for	a	convict	under	servitude	would	have	resulted	 
in	a	loss	of	certain	freedoms.	There	would	have	been	a	starker	contrast	between	 
confinement	in	the	assignment	period	as	compared	with	the	probation	period,	as	 
the	former	would	have	seen	a	greater	loss	of	freedom.		 
	 When	broadly	comparing	the	samples,	the	number	of	incidences	of	to	the	cells	 
increases	from	the	1-in-25	assigned	males,	the	probation	males,	the	juvenile	 
probation	males	and	lastly	(with	the	most	number	of	incidences)	the	juveniles	 
transportees.	This	does	not	directly	reflect	the	number	of	offences	committed	by	 
these	samples.	While	the	1-in-25	assigned	sample	committed	more	offences	than	 
the	probation	sample,	there	were	fewer	incidences	of	being	ordered	to	the	cell.	
 
Instead	this	pattern	reflects	changing	punishment	practices	where	flogging	was	 
overtaken	as	a	primary	punishment	for	males	by	confinement	to	the	cells.	 
	 Hard	Labour	 
As	can	be	seen	in	Table	No.16,	the	majority	(eighty-two	per	cent)	of	male	juvenile	 
transportees	did	undergo	hard	labour.	While	sixty-two	of	these	juvenile	 
transportees	underwent	under	1000	days	of	hard	labour,	eighteen	underwent	over	 
1000	days	–	approximately	three-years	hard	labour.	Moreover,	thirty	male	juvenile	 
transportees	underwent	at	least	one-year	of	hard	labour.

In	parliament	the	work	carried	out	in	Portland	was	described	as	insufficiently	 
laborious	and	the	convicts	‘pampered’.	Meanwhile,	convicts	labouring	to	excavate	 
the	new	naval	dockyard	at	Chatham	was	simultaneously	described	as	of	an	‘arduous	 
character’	and	a	‘waste,	misapplication	and	indolence’	(Radzinowicz	&	Hood	1990,	 
505).	Hence,	hard	labour	could	vary	within	the	British	Isles	in	the	same	period	and	 
so	it	is	reasonable	to	assert	that	hard	labour	in	VDL	would	also	have	varied.	Some	 
offenders	would	have	endured	more	severe	working	conditions	than	others	 
sentenced	to	the	same	period	of	hard	labour.	This	means	that	only	a	broad	 
comparison	between	the	juvenile	transportees	and	the	1-in-25	sample	is	possible.	 
	 The	incidence	of	punishment	through	hard	labour	increased	as	the	number	of	the	 
offences	in	the	separate	samples	increased,	as	follows;	1-in-25	Probation	sample,	1-
in-25	assignment	sample,	1-in-25	juvenile	probation	sample	and	with	the	most	 
incidences	(and	the	most	offences)	the	male	juvenile	transportees.	It	is	also	clear	 
that	punishment	by	hard	labour	was	a	common	punishment	for	juveniles.

Treadmill	 
There	were	twelve	male	juvenile	transportees	who	were	sentenced	to,	between	ten	 
and	seventy	days	on	the,	treadmill.	While	six	transportees	spent	at	least	a	month	on	 
the	treadmill,	it	was	not	a	common	punishment.		 
	 Treadmills	became	very	popular	as	a	form	of	punishment	in	the	early-nineteenth	 
century.	This	was	especially	the	case	following	the	construction	of	a	treadmill	in	 
Suffolk	County	Gaol	in	1819,	which	allowed	fifty-six	prisoners	to	be	punished	at	 
once.	By	1842	over	half	of	the	200	gaols	and	houses	of	correction	in	Britain	had	 
treadmills.	While	initially	such	machines	were	used	to	generate	power	in	the	use	of,	 
for	example,	grinding	grain,	it	quickly	became	a	machine	for	generating	‘useless’	 
toil.	The	punishment	of	‘grinding	rogues	honest’,	as	Bentham	termed	it,	could	only	 
be	carried	out	in	areas	where	a	treadmill	was	available	(Maxwell-Stewart	2008,	142-
3).	This	accounts,	partly,	for	the	scarcity	of	colonial	punishments	involving	 
treadmills.	However,	it	is	likely	that	the	want	of	labour	for	the	benefits	of	the	colony	 
weighed	in	on	the	decision	also.	Given	the	increasing	popularity	of	the	treadmill	in	 
England	up	to	the	1840s,	this	does	not	seem	to	be	reflected	in	the	punishments	 
meted	out	to	convicts	as	specified	in	their	Conduct	Record.	This	may	also	be	an	 
issue	of	nomenclature;	where	instead	of	specifying	a	punishment	of	the	treadwheel,	 
it	was	recorded	as	hard	labour.	 
	 The	recording	of	the	treadmill	as	a	punishment	is	almost	the	same	for	the	1-in-25	 
assigned	convicts	and	the	male	juvenile	transportees,	both	have	the	highest	number	 
of	incidences,	this	is	followed	by	the	probationary	group	and	lastly	the	juvenile	 
probation	group.	However,	it	was	not	very	common	in	any	group.	While	recording	 
practices	may	have	influenced	this	result,	the	practical	considerations	of	such	a	 
punishment	would	also	have	influenced	its	use.

per	cent	who	did	–	see	Table	No.17.

death	sentences;	as	many	as	two	per	cent	of	these	juvenile	transportees	were
